Chapter 2

National Affairs

Key national policies, statutory amendments, central welfare schemes, judicial pronouncements, and governance milestones.

Political / National A昀昀airs Chinmaya & Related Developments

  • Political / National A昀昀airs Chinmaya Amrit Mahotsav Global Sammelan
  • Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurated the Sammelan on October 23, 2026 at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi.
  • The 23: 25 October event marks the culmination of year-long celebrations commemorating 75 years of the Chinmaya Mission.
  • It was expected to bring together over 9,000 participants from India and abroad.
  • The Prime Minister interacted with a holographic representation, or “Holobot,” of Swami Chinmayananda.
  • He recalled their 1993 meeting in Vadodara, which focused on youth empowerment and building a strong India.
  • He highlighted Swami Chinmayananda’s Gita Gyana Yagna, which brought the teachings of the Bhagavad Gita, Upanishads and Vedanta to the public.
  • His address emphasised cultural preservation, social unity, self-reliance and youth participation in achieving Viksit Bharat by 2047.
  • Swami Chinmayananda Saraswati was a spiritual teacher who spread the teachings of Vedanta, the Upanishads and the Bhagavad Gita.
  • Born on May 8, 1916, as Balakrishna Menon, he passed away on August 3, 1993.
  • Founded the Chinmaya Mission in 1953 to spread the timeless wisdom of Advaita Vedanta.
  • He launched Gita Gyana Yagnas to make spiritual knowledge accessible to the public. UDAN Completes 10 Years
  • RCS: UDAN completed 10 years on October 21, 2026.
  • RCS: UDAN stands for Regional Connectivity Scheme -Ude Desh ka Aam Nagrik.
  • Launched on October 21, 2016 , it follows the National Civil Aviation Policy, 2016.
  • It promotes affordable and economically viable air connectivity to unserved and underserved regions.
  • The 昀椀rst UDAN 昀氀ight connected Shimla and Delhi in April 2017.
  • By October 2026, the scheme had operationalised 687 regional routes and 95 aerodromes, including 17 heliports and two water aerodromes.
  • It facilitated over 3.68 lakh 昀氀ights , carrying 1.72 crore passengers.
  • India’s operational airports increased from 74 in 2014 to 166 in 2026. India is the world’s third-largest domestic aviation market.
  • Modi昀椀ed UDAN , launched on 4 July 2026 , has an outlay of ₹28,840 crore for FY 2026–27 to FY 2035–36.
  • It envisages developing 100 airports and 200 modern helipads.
  • Its priorities include sustainable regional operations, stronger infrastructure and indigenous aircraft manufacturing. Internet Access and Children’s Rights
  • On October 15, 2026, the Supreme Court delivered its order in Just Rights for Children Alliance v. S. Harish.
  • The Bench comprised Justices J.B. Pardiwala and K. Vinod Chandran.
  • It recognised internet access and use as a fundamental right under Article 21 read with Article 19(1)(a).
  • Children enjoy this right irrespective of age.
  • The Court rejected blanket restrictions on children’s internet access as disproportionate and unproven.
  • It suggested parental supervision, dedicated child modes, private-by-default accounts and restrictions on messages from unknown adults.
  • Restrictions on inherently harmful content and services remain permissible.
  • The Centre must create a National Hash & URL List Database to detect and remove Child Sexual Exploitation and Abuse Material (CSEAM). RTI Act Completes 21 Years
  • The Right to Information (RTI) Act, 2005 completed 21 years of full implementation on October 12, 2026.
  • It received Presidential assent on 15 June 2005 and became fully operational on 12 October 2005.
  • The Right to Know derives from Article 19(1)(a), which guarantees freedom of speech and expression.
  • In State of U.P . v. Raj Narain (1975), the Supreme Court recognised citizens’ right to know about public acts of government.
  • In PUCL v. Union of India (2003), it upheld voters’ right to information about electoral candidates.
  • The Act replaced the Freedom of Information Act, 2002.
  • It enables citizens to obtain information held by public authorities, subject to statutory exemptions.
  • It established the Central Information Commission and State Information Commissions.
  • Its central objectives are transparency, accountability, informed participation and prevention of corruption. SARAS Mela 2026 SARAS Melas, organised under the Central Government’s Deendayal Antyodaya Yojana– National Rural Livelihoods Mission (DAY-NRLM), connect rural women entrepreneurs with wider markets, buyers and business opportunities.
  • The event is being held from 13 to 31 October 2026 at Punnami Ghat, Vijayawada . The Vijayawada edition is the 昀椀rst National SARAS Mela organised outside the Delhi–National Capital Region (Delhi-NCR).  Key Facts
  • Around 1,500 women Self: Help Group (SHG) entrepreneurs and Lakhpati Didis from 34 states and Union Territories are showcasing their products through more than 650 stalls.
  • Products include regional textiles, handicrafts, natural and processed foods, and other rural products.
  • A major attraction is a 16: foot installation titled “SHAKTI–The Spirit of Lakhpati Didi.”
  • SARAS Melas provide a practical bridge between these needs and market opportunities by bringing SHGs, consumers, institutional buyers and other stakeholders together.  SARAS Melas began in 1999, when the 昀椀rst National SARAS Mela was organised in Delhi with approximately 65 bene昀椀ciaries.  To date, 117 National SARAS Melas have been organised, with annual sales exceeding ₹200 crore. Inauguration of a Section of Chennai Metro Rail Phase II Prime Minister Narendra Modi visited Tamil Nadu on 11 October 2026 . He inaugurated the Poonamallee–Vadapalani stretch of Phase II of the Chennai Metro Rail Project , built at a cost of approximately ₹4,900 crore. He also laid the foundation stones for and inaugurated key National Highway projects worth approximately ₹3,700 crore.
  • A distinctive feature of this Chennai Metro corridor is its 3.7-kilometre-long double-decker structure.
  • It also incorporates advanced signalling systems designed to support driverless operations.
  • Among the National Highway projects, the Prime Minister inaugurated the 36-kilometre, four-lane Vadugapatti–Therkuvenganallur section of NH-744.
  • He also inaugurated the 30: kilometre, four-lane Madurai Ring Road section of NH-744A.
  • He laid the foundation stone for the four-lane Thiruvarur Bypass on the Nagapattinam– Thanjavur section of NH-83.
  • He also inaugurated and dedicated to the nation railway infrastructure projects worth over ₹750 crore.
  • These included the Karaikal: Peralam railway line, which he dedicated to the nation.
  • He inaugurated 昀椀ve Amrit Stations , redeveloped under the Amrit Bharat Station Scheme : Palani, Vellore Cantonment, Ambasamudram, Paramakkudi and Namakkal.
  • At Chennai Port, he inaugurated four infrastructure projects: a Paved Storage Yard , four Export– Import (EXIM) Godowns , an upgraded Cruise Terminal and a Seafarers Club.
  • He inaugurated and laid foundation stones for eight major development projects at V .O. Chidambaranar Port . He also inaugurated the Coal Berth-3 project at Kamarajar Port.
  • He dedicated to the nation the Sudha Gopalakrishnan Brain Centre (SGBC) at the Indian Institute of Technology Madras (IIT Madras). Deen Dayal Upadhyaya–Grameen Kaushalya Yojana 2.0 The Ministry of Rural Development will begin training batches under Deen Dayal Upadhyaya– Grameen Kaushalya Yojana (DDU-GKY) 2.0 in most states and Union Territories from October 2026.
  • According to the DDU: GKY 2.0 portal, 24 states and Union Territories have allocated training targets covering 5.6 lakh candidates across more than 1,200 projects to Project Implementing Agencies (PIAs).
  • Approximately 2,015 training batches for around 70,000 rural youth are expected to begin across these 24 states and Union Territories during October 2026.  Key Facts
  • DDU: GKY is a Centrally Sponsored Scheme that provides placement-linked skill training to poor rural youth.
  • Training courses range from three to twelve months.
  • Under DDU: GKY 2.0, training targets covering more than nine lakh candidates have been allocated to all 31 participating states and Union Territories for the two-year period 2026–28.
  • DDU: GKY was launched on 25 September 2014 under the National Rural Livelihoods Mission (NRLM).
  • Since its launch in 2014: 15, more than 18.47 lakh candidates have received training for over 800 types of jobs, and more than 12.43 lakh candidates have secured employment.
  • The scheme provides placement: linked skill training to youth aged 15–35 years from poor rural households.
  • The Government issued revised DDU: GKY 2.0 guidelines in May 2025.  Progress in States and Union Territories
  • Goa has emerged as a leading state in preparations to start training batches under DDU-GKY 2.0.
  • Andhra Pradesh has commenced training for more than 12,000 candidates in just three months.
  • Jammu and Kashmir has allocated 100% of its assigned training targets and commenced training against 91% of the total allocation. Integrated Transport & Logistics Authority (ITLA) On October 6, 2026 , the Union Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi , approved the establishment of the Integrated Transport & Logistics Authority (ITLA) as a Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV).
  • Its principal objective is to strengthen research, planning, project appraisal, monitoring and impact assessment across the transport and logistics sectors.
  • ITLA will strengthen coordination among these sectors and promote integration across road, rail, water and air transport. This will help make transport infrastructure development more effective, economical and sustainable.
  • ITLA will function as the national apex institution for integrated transport and logistics planning, research, project appraisal and monitoring, policy support and data analytics.

It will prepare a comprehensive & Related Developments

  • It will prepare a comprehensive National Transport Master Plan with a planning horizon of ten years or more.
  • It will evaluate the transport ministries’ short-term sectoral plans covering approximately 昀椀ve years, as well as their annual plans.
  • ITLA will undertake the technical appraisal of Government of India infrastructure projects costing ₹500 crore or more.
  • ITLA will develop a National Transport Data Repository (NTDR) , bringing together transport and logistics data from multiple sources.
  • Major data sources will include GST Network (GSTN) e-way bills, FASTag, Vahan, GPS-based systems and urban traf昀椀c management systems. 100 Years of the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) The Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) completed 100 years on 1 October 2026. Its institutional journey began on 1 October 1926 , when India’s 昀椀rst Public Service Commission was established.
  • At that time, it was an advisory body whose Chairman and members were appointed by the Secretary of State for India in London.
  • Various programmes and activities were organised throughout the year to mark the UPSC’s centenary. The year-long celebrations began on 1 October 2025 and continued until 1 October 2026.  Key Facts
  • The UPSC organised a two: day centenary event titled ‘Manthan’ at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi, from 30 September to 1 October 2026.  The Journey
  • The Indian Civil Service (ICS) examination began in London in 1855, replacing the East India Company’s nomination system with open competition.
  • In 1862, 21: year-old Satyendranath Tagore , the elder brother of Rabindranath Tagore, passed the examination in 1863 and joined the service in 1864.
  • He thus became the 昀椀rst Indian to join the ICS . The British referred to it as the ‘heaven-born service’.
  • The Government of India Act, 1919 , enacted following the Montagu–Chelmsford Reforms , provided for the establishment of a Public Service Commission.
  • In 1922, the ICS examination was held in India for the 昀椀rst time, alongside London. Its Indian examination centre was Allahabad, now Prayagraj.
  • In 1924, the Lee Commission, chaired by Arthur Hamilton Lee , recommended the immediate establishment of a statutory Public Service Commission.
  • The Commission was established under the Public Service Commission (Functions) Rules, 1926 , framed under Sections 96B and 96C(2) of the Government of India Act, 1919.
  • Sir Ross Barker, a member of the United Kingdom’s Home Civil Service, was its 昀椀rst Chairman.
  • The Commission’s of昀椀ce was located at Metcalfe House in Delhi.
  • The Indian examination centre was shifted to Delhi in 1928.  Major Milestones Year Major milestone 1937 On 1 April, the Commission was renamed the Federal Public Service Commission. 1938 Combined competitive examinations were introduced for several services, marking the beginning of integrated recruitment to multiple services. 1947 Shri H. K. Kripalani became the first Indian Chairman following independence; the first examination was held in December and the IAS replaced the ICS. 1950 On 26 January , the Federal Public Service Commission was renamed the Union Public Service Commission. Shri R.N. Banerjee assumed charge on January 14, 1949, and continued as Chairman following the Institution’s Constitutional transition on January 26, 1950. 1951 The All India Services Act was enacted. 1979 The three-stage Civil Services Examination— Preliminary Examination, Main Examination and Interview—was introduced. 2011 The Civil Services Aptitude Test (CSAT) was introduced.   • These national ambitions are distinct from the projected outcomes of ECMS projects. Special Constitutional Safeguards for Ladakh
  • At a meeting on September 9, 2026 , the Union Home Ministry reportedly proposed Article 371- K to provide special constitutional safeguards for Ladakh. Representatives of the Leh Apex Body (LAB) and Kargil Democratic Alliance (KDA) participated in the discussions.
  • The proposed arrangement envisages a directly elected Union Territory-level body with legislative powers over speci昀椀ed local matters, including land, culture, language, forests, environment and natural resources.
  • It would follow a “sui generis” model, meaning a unique governance arrangement tailored to Ladakh’s circumstances. It would not automatically grant statehood or create a conventional Union Territory legislature.
  • Ladakh became a Union Territory without a legislature on October 31, 2019 , following the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019.
  • Local organisations seek stronger protection for tribal identity, land, employment, culture and natural resources, alongside greater participation in governance.
  • Their principal demands include statehood, Sixth Schedule protection, employment safeguards and separate Lok Sabha constituencies for Leh and Kargil.
  • The Sixth Schedule, linked to Articles 244(2) and 275(1), provides special administrative arrangements for tribal areas in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.
  • It provides for Autonomous District and Regional Councils, with legislative, administrative, judicial and 昀椀nancial powers over speci昀椀ed subjects. Extending this framework to Ladakh would require appropriate constitutional changes.
  • Article 371: K remains a proposal ; its 昀椀nal constitutional structure and distribution of powers require agreement and parliamentary approval. Assam Uniform Civil Code Act, 2026 The Uniform Civil Code, Assam, Bill, 2026, was introduced in the Assam Legislative Assembly on May 25, 2026, by Parliamentary Affairs Minister Atul Bora on behalf of Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma
  • The Assam Legislative Assembly passed the Bill by voice vote on 27 May 2026.
  • Presidential assent was given on September 29, 2026.
  • With this, Assam became the first state in the North- east and the third state in India after Uttarakhand and Gujarat to adopt such UCC legislation at the state level.
  • The idea of a Uniform Civil Code is linked to Article 44 of the Constitution, which directs the State to endeavour to secure a uniform civil code for citizens throughout India.
  • It also repeals the Assam Compulsory Registration of Muslim Marriages and Divorces Act, 2024.
  • STs are excluded from the application of Assam’s UCC.  Marriage-Related Provisions
  • The Act mandates monogamy as the legal rule for marriage.
  • Bigamy and polygamy shall attract imprisonment of up to seven years.
  • The act fixes the legal age of marriage at 21 years for grooms and 18 years for brides.
  • Couples must submit a marriage memorandum to the Sub-Registrar within 60 days of the marriage ceremony and within 90 days outside Assam.  Divorce-Related Provisions
  • The Act codifies uniform grounds for divorce.
  • Grounds for divorce include cruelty, desertion, and mutual consent.
  • The Act ensures that custody of children below five years of age remains with the mother (However, the Court remains free to consider the best interests of the child).

National Affairs · Part 4

  • Class: 1 heirs will include the spouse, children, and parents of the deceased.  Live-In Relationship Provisions
  • The Act makes registration of live: in relationships mandatory within one month, including for non- residents.
  • Failure to register a live: in relationship within one month may attract imprisonment of up to three months or a fine of up to `10,000 (and continued failure may attract six months of imprisonment or `25,000 or both).
  • Any child born out of a live: in relationship will be considered fully legitimate.  Penalties Under the Act
  • Marriage within prohibited relationships, unless protected by valid customs, shall be punishable with imprisonment of up to six months and a fine of up to `50,000.
  • Non: registration of marriage or divorce within the prescribed period shall attract a penalty of `10,000 (and `25,000 after first notice).
  • Forged documents in registration matters may lead to imprisonment of up to three months, or a fine of up to `25,000, or both.  Gujarat Uniform Civil Code 2026 President Droupadi Murmu assented to the Gujarat Uniform Civil Code Bill on 17 September 2026. Gujar at became the second state after Uttarakhand to adopt a new UCC framework.
  • The Gujarat Assembly passed the Bill on March 24, 2026.
  • The committee chaired by retired Supreme Court judge Justice Ranjana Prakash Desai made recommendation for UCC.
  • Scheduled Tribes and groups with constitutionally protected customary rights are exempt.  Major provisions
  • Monogamy is compulsory: neither party may have a living spouse. The framework therefore prohibits bigamy.
  • Minimum marriage age: men 21 years; women 18 years.
  • Marriages covered by the Act after its commencement require a registration memorandum within 60 days; wilful non-compliance attracts monetary penalties.
  • Grounds for divorce include adultery, cruelty, desertion for at least two years, etc.

Status of Policing in India Report 2026 The Status of Policing in India Report (SPIR) 2026 examines cybercrime, victims’ experiences and the response of the police and banks. Released by Common Cause and Lokniti - CSDS in New Delhi on 24 September 2026, it highlights unequal access to redressal and the association of bribery and personal in昀氀uence with the recovery of lost money. Its theme is “Cybercrime—Victim Perspectives and Systemic Responses”.
  • Survey Coverage: 8,306 citizens across 15 States and Delhi (a UT) examining digital exposure, victimisation, reporting, police action and 昀椀nancial recovery.  Cybercrime Trends and Digital Exposure
  • Registered cases: NCRB data show an increase from 86,420 cybercrime cases in 2023 to 1,01,928 in 2024, a rise of 17.9%. These are registered cases, rather than the total number of incidents experienced by citizens.
  • Common scam calls: 33% of respondents received calls about unordered deliveries, 31% about high-return investment opportunities and 27% from persons posing as bank of昀椀cials seeking account details.
  • Internet use and risk: Moderate-to-high scam exposure was reported by 46% of heavy internet users, compared with 19% of non-users.
  • Overall victimisation: 13% of respondents reported experiencing cybercrime in the previous two to three years.
  • Financial loss: Digital 昀椀nancial fraud accounted for 54% of cybercrime victims. Among digital 昀椀nancial fraud victims, 23% lost more than ₹20,000.  Informal channels and 昀椀nancial recovery Informal channel Full recovery % No recovery % Paid a bribe 38 38 Did not pay a bribe 12 75 Used personal contacts 28 48 Did not use personal contacts 8 72 National Co-operative Development Corporation (Amendment) Act, 2026 The National Co-operative Development Corporation (Amendment) Act, 2026, amends the NCDC Act, 1962, expanding its mandate and 昀椀nancing powers without additional Central Government budgetary assistance. The Bill was introduced in the Lok Sabh a on 10 August 2026 and passed by the Lok Sabha on 11 August and the Rajya Sabha on 12 August. The President assented to the Act on 14 August 2026. Section 1(2) requires a separate commencement noti昀椀cation, which was not located in of昀椀cial sources examined up to August 22, 2026.
  • The amendment provides 昀氀exible 昀椀nancing for diversi昀椀ed cooperative-sector needs and widens institutional channels for infrastructure, technology, processing and marketing.  About National Co-operative Development Corporation
  • NCDC is a statutory organisation established in 1963 under the 1962 Act and administered by the Ministry of Cooperation. It plans, promotes and 昀椀nances cooperative development, including agriculture, dairy, 昀椀sheries, processing, storage and marketing.  Major Provisions of the Amended Act
  • The amended Act allows direct loans and grants to any cooperative society or eligible entity engaged in cooperative development, alongside State Government 昀椀nancing. Share-capital investment in single-State cooperatives and other eligible entities requires prior Central Government approval.
  • It expands “foodstuffs” to include processed food, other edible products and noti昀椀ed items, removes the rural-area restriction on eligible cooperative industrial activities, permits credit-information exchange with the Central Government, RBI, banks and noti昀椀ed 昀椀nancial institutions, and authorises activities addressing emerging technological and sectoral needs.
  • The 97 th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2011, recognised the right to form cooperative societies under Article 19(1)(c), introduced Article 43B and added Part IXB. Article 43B promotes voluntary formation, autonomy, democratic control and professional management. Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Act, 2026
  • The Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Act, 2026, raises the number of puisne judges from 33 to 37, excluding the Chief Justice of India (CJI).
  • The total sanctioned strength increases from 34 to 38 judges. This is the 昀椀rst increase since 2019.
  • Section 2 of the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Act, 1956, initially permitted 10 judges excluding the CJI, giving a total strength of 11.  Background to the Bill
  • The Union Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, approved four additional puisne judges on 5 May 2026.
  • The Lok Sabha passed the Bill by a voice vote without debate on 3 August 2026. Presidential assent was given on 11 August 2026.  Need for Increasing Judicial Strength
  • The government cited increasing case pendency as the main reason for expansion. On 1 January 2026, the Court had 92,101 pending cases.
  • During 2025, it received 75,410 cases but disposed of 65,615, leaving a gap of 9,795. By 30 April 2026, pendency had reached 92,823, according to the National Judicial Data Grid.
  • This gap continued despite the Court functioning close to its sanctioned strength. The increase seeks to improve disposal capacity and deliver speedy justice. The Tribunals Reforms Act, 2026
  • The Tribunals Reforms Act, 2026 seeks to establish an independent, transparent, ef昀椀cient and professionally administered tribunal system through a judiciary-led National Tribunals Commission (NTC).
  • It seeks to reduce executive discretion, establish uniform service conditions and implement the Supreme Court’s Madras Bar Association principles.
  • Introduced by Union Law Minister Arjun Ram Meghwal, the Bill passed the Lok Sabha by voice vote on August 10, 2026, without detailed debate amid Opposition protests.
  • It received presidential assent on August 13, 2026, and came into force on August 25, 2026.
  • The Act repeals and replaces the 2021 Act and applies to 16 tribunals, appellate tribunals and authorities without altering their jurisdiction or adjudicatory powers.  Background and Objectives
  • The Supreme Court has repeatedly emphasised that tribunals performing judicial functions must remain independent of the executive.
  • In Madras Bar Association v. Union of India, (2026) 2 SCC 1, the Supreme Court struck down provisions of the 2021 Act for violating judicial independence, separation of powers and earlier judicial standards.
  • The new Act seeks uniform appointments, 昀椀nancial and administrative autonomy, expert assessment and institutional accountability.  National Tribunals Commission
  • The Act establishes the National Tribunals Commission as the central institutional body responsible for appointments and oversight in the tribunal system.
  • The Commission will replace the fragmented and predominantly executive-controlled administrative framework established under the 2021 Act.
  • Its headquarters will be located in New Delhi.
  • The Commission will consist of one Chairperson and four members, producing a total strength of 昀椀ve.
  • The NTC Chairperson and members will serve for 昀椀ve years or until the age of 70, whichever is earlier.  Search cum Selection Committees
  • Section 13 provides separate committees for selecting tribunal Chairpersons and members. The NTC Chairperson heads the committee for Chairpersons, which includes a retired High Court Chief Justice nominated by the NTC Chairperson.
  • An NTC Judicial Member heads the committee for Members, which includes a retired High Court Judge nominated by the NTC Chairperson.
  • The committee Chairperson has a casting vote when votes are equal. Nasha Mukt Yuva for Viksit Bharat Sankalp Abhiyan Prime Minister Narendra Modi launched the ‘Nasha Mukt Yuva for Viksit Bharat Sankalp Abhiyan’ on 2 August 2026 to mobilise young people and communities for building a drug-free India.
  • The campaign links the physical and mental well- being of India’s youth with the national objective of transforming the country into Viksit Bharat by 2047.  Key Facts
  • The nationwide campaign was launched through a large video conference involving more than one crore young people from over 28,000 locations across India.
  • More than 125 spiritual and public organisations, educational institutions, non-governmental organisations and industrial associations supported the programme.
  • The initiative originated as a pilot project in Kashi, Uttar Pradesh, in the previous year 2025.
  • The pilot initiative was supported by spiritual organ- isations and several non-governmental organisations under the Kashi Declaration before being expand- ed into a nationwide campaign.
  • The Prime Minister described India’s young population as the “Amrit generation”.  Major Features
  • The campaign will continue for 100 weeks, covering 100 consecutive Sundays.
  • Every Sunday, participating organisations and communities will conduct activities related to art, culture, sports, meditation, spirituality, community service and public awareness.
  • These 100 Sundays are intended to become 100 sustained steps towards a drug-free India.
  • The campaign places young people at the centre of the movement against substance abuse.
  • The campaign promotes open communication between parents and children about the risks associated with substance abuse.
  • The Prime Minister described those who overcome addiction as “true warriors” who deserve respect and a second opportunity in life. Mines and Minerals Development and Regulation Amendment Act 2026 The Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026 was passed by both Houses of Parliament on August 13, 2026. The Act amends the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957. The President assented to Ac t No. 20 of 2026 on August 17, 2026. The Act came into force August 22, 2026.
  • The MMDR Act, 1957, is the principal mining legislation. The Centre regulates major minerals, conservation and royalty rates.
  • In Mineral Area Development Authority v. Steel Authority of India, a nine-judge bench ruled by 8:1 in July 2024 that royalty is a contractual payment, not a tax.
  • States may tax mineral rights under Entry 50, subject to parliamentary restrictions absent from the existing MMDR Act.  Major Provisions of the Act
  • Union Regulation of Mineral Bearing Land: The amendment to Section 2 brings mineral- bearing land, de昀椀ned as land containing minerals under Central parameters, within Central regulatory control.
  • Restrictions on State Levies: Section 9D restricts State taxes, cesses and similar levies on mineral rights and mineral-bearing lands, including levies based on mineral quantity, value or royalty. States may impose them only under Central conditions or restrictions.
  • Treatment of Past Dues: Unpaid or unrecovered State levies for periods before commencement will become invalid. Amounts already deposited or recovered will not be refunded.
  • Central Rule Making Power: The amendment to Section 13 authorises Central rules prescribing conditions and restrictions for future State levies.  Evolution of the MMDR Framework
  • The 2015 amendment introduced mandatory auctions, the District Mineral Foundation and the National Mineral Exploration Trust. The 2016 amendment de昀椀ned the leased area and permitted certain captive lease transfers.
  • The 2020 reforms opened coal and lignite auctions to companies without prior coal-mining experience. In 2021, captive mines could sell up to 50% of their annual output after meeting linked end-use requirements. Protection for Women in Live-in Relationships In Dr. Lokesh B.H. & Others v. State of Karnataka & Another, decided on 3 August 2026, the Supreme Court held that protection against domestic cruelty under Section 498A of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) is not con昀椀ned to women in legally valid marriages.
  • The protection may extend to a woman in a live-in relationship when the relationship is “in the nature of marriage” and the parties have the intention to marry.  What Is Section 498A of the IPC?
  • Section 498A of the IPC criminalised cruelty committed against a woman by her husband or a relative of her husband.
  • The provision prescribed imprisonment for up to three years and a fine.
  • Following the replacement of the IPC by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) , the corresponding offence is contained in Section 85 of the BNS.  Supreme Court’s Ruling
  • The Supreme Court held that Section 498A is not restricted exclusively to relationships based on a legally valid marriage.
  • It can apply to a live: in relationship that legally qualifies as a relationship in the nature of marriage.
  • However, the woman must also establish that the relationship involved a genuine intention to marry.
  • The relationship must be between consenting adults and must satisfy the legal characteristics of a marriage-like domestic partnership.  Essential Conditions for Invoking Section 498A
  • A woman in a live: in relationship must initially establish two essential requirements:  The live-in arrangement must constitute a relationship in the nature of marriage.  The relationship must involve an intention to marry.
  • The initial burden rests on the woman seeking protection under Section 498A.
  • In Indra Sarma v. V .K.V . Sarma (2013) , the Supreme Court recognised that a live-in relationship between consenting adults is not an offence. Samudra Manthan: National Offshore Exploration Scheme On July 31, 2026, the Union Cabinet approved Samudra Manthan - the National Offshore Exploration Scheme - with a Phase-I outlay of ₹84,084 crore up to FY 2030–31.
  • It is a Central Sector Scheme of the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas.
  • It seeks to unlock India’s offshore oil and gas potential through better geological data, risk-sharing, deepwater drilling, shared infrastructure and indigenous manufacturing.
  • The Cabinet: approved outlay remains ₹84,084 crore, and no subsequent of昀椀cial revision has been announced.
  • Prime Minister Narendra Modi articulated the vision of a modern-day “Samudra Manthan” from the Red Fort on Independence Day 2025.
  • The scheme aims to accelerate oil and gas exploration in India’s deepwater, ultra-deepwater and frontier offshore basins.
  • It seeks to identify and add more than 600 MMTOE (Million Metric Tonnes of Oil Equivalent) of hydrocarbon reserves.
  • It aims to increase the domestic production of crude oil and natural gas.  Major Components
  • Accelerated Offshore Exploration: ₹43,200 crore has been allocated for 60 wells, with government assistance covering up to 50% of eligible costs, capped at ₹675 crore per well.
  • Offshore Data Acquisition: ₹28,534 crore will support seismic surveys and data analysis to identify potential hydrocarbon reserves and reduce geological risks.
  • Common Infrastructure Hubs: ₹10,000 crore will fund shared facilities for faster and more cost- effective offshore oil and gas production.
  • Manufacturing and Services Zone: ₹2,000 crore will promote domestic equipment manufacturing, specialised services and reduced import dependence. India’s First Telecom Manufacturing Zone in Gwalior The Department of Telecommunications (DoT) and the Government of Madhya Pradesh signed a Memorandum of Understanding on July 30, 2026, in New Delhi to establish India’s 昀椀rst Telecom Manufacturing Zone (TMZ) at Gwalior, Madhya Pradesh.
  • It supports the national visions of Aatmanirbhar Bharat and “Make in India, Make for the World.”
  • According to government information, the bhumi pujan of the project will be held in Gwalior on October 29, 2026.
  • The zone aims to transform India from a predominantly telecom services market into a major telecom-product manufacturing hub.
  • It seeks to increase domestic value addition in telecom and mobile-phone manufacturing.
  • The manufacturing zone is envisaged as an integrated 350-acre plug-and-play industrial cluster, designed to provide world-class infrastructure.
  • The Central Government has approved ₹493 crore for Phase-I core infrastructure.
  • One account places cumulative committed investment at ₹5,500 crore.
  • Investment is expected to cross ₹10,000 crore in the second phase.
  • The Government of Madhya Pradesh will hold 51% equity in the SPV , while the Department of Telecommunications will hold 49%.
  • The zone will cover mobile phones, telecom equipment, optical 昀椀bre, semiconductors, electronic components and 5G-6G technologies.
  • India’s mobile: phone production has reportedly risen from ₹18,000 crore to ₹6.2 lakh crore during FY 2014-15 to FY 2025-26.

Mobile & Related Developments

  • Mobile: phone exports have reportedly increased from ₹1,500 crore to ₹2.59 lakh crore. Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act 1971
  • Enacted on 23 December 1971, the Act extends to the whole of India and protects the National Flag, Constitution and National Anthem. Section 2 addresses insults to the Flag and Constitution in a public place or within public view. Section 3 currently protects the singing of the Nat ional Anthem. The Public Examinations Prevention of Unfair Means Amendment Act 2026 The Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment Act, 2026, amends the 2024 Act, which came into force on June 21, 2024.
  • Dr. Jitendra Singh introduced the Bill in the Lok Sabha on July 27, 2026. It passed the Lok Sabha on July 29 and the Rajya Sabha on July 30, and received presidential assent on July 31, 2026.  Public examination authorities covered
  • The Act covers examinations conducted by the Union Public Service Commission, Staff Selection Commission, Railway Recruitment Boards, Institute of Banking Personnel Selection, National Testing Agency, Central Government ministries and attached of昀椀ces, and other authorities noti昀椀ed by the Central Government.  Major provisions  Enhanced penalties
  • For individuals using unfair means, imprisonment increases from 3–5 to 5–10 years, and the maximum 昀椀ne increase from ₹10 lakh to ₹50 lakh. For service providers, the maximum 昀椀ne rises from ₹1 crore to ₹5 crore and debarment expands from up to four years to eight years. Proportionate examination costs shall also be recovered.
  • Directors, senior managers or persons in charge who consent to or connive in an offence face 5–10 years’ imprisonment and a ₹5 crore 昀椀ne, compared with 3–10 years of imprisonment and a 昀椀ne of ₹1 crore earlier. Organised crime attracts 7–10 years’ imprisonment and a minimum ₹10 crore 昀椀ne, compared with 5–10 years of imprisonment and a 昀椀ne of a minimum ₹1 crore 昀椀ne under the 2024 Act.  Investigation
  • The amendment introduces a two: month investigation period, counted from the date of recording information for police investigations, referral for central agencies, and the date of the noti昀椀cation constituting a Special Task Force (STF).  Special Fast Track Courts
  • Every state and Union Territory must designate one or more Courts of Session as Special Fast- Track Courts in consultation with Chief Justice of the relevant High Court. Trials must be completed within three months of 昀椀ling the charge sheet, or within three months of transfer in pending cases. State governments and UT administrations must appoint Special Public Prosecutors under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023.  Appeals
  • Appeals lie before a two: judge High Court bench, normally within 30 days, with an absolute 90-day limit. Appeals should be disposed of, as far as possible, within three months of admission. The reports assess school education performance at two administrative levels: PGI-S covers all 36 States and Union Territories, and PGI-D covers 784 districts.  Evolution and Objectives of PGI

Delhi Electric Vehicle Policy 2.0 The Delhi Government has notified the Delhi Electric Vehicle Policy 2.0, effective from July 1, 2026 to March 31, 2030. Chief Minister Rekha Gupta defended the decision to stop fresh registrations of petrol two- wheelers from April 2028. The policy was approved by the Cabinet on June 29, 2026.  About the Policy and Its Objectives
  • Delhi EV Policy 2.0 promotes electric mobility in the National Capital Territory to reduce vehicular emissions, improve air quality and make Delhi a leading electric mobility hub.

  • From 1 January 2027, only electric three-wheelers and N1-category trucks will be registered in Delhi.
  • From 1 April 2028, only electric two-wheelers will be registered. Existing petrol and other fossil-fuel vehicles may complete their full life cycle, allowing a gradual transition.
  • School buses must convert at least 10% of their 昀氀eet to EVs within two years of policy noti昀椀cation. The target is to electrify at least 30% of the school-bus 昀氀eet by 31 March 2030.

Electric three-wheelers receive ₹50,000, ₹40,000 and ₹30,000, respectively (No incentive shall be given to e-autos with a battery capacity of less than 4 kWh.). N1 commercial trucks receive up to ₹1 lakh in the 昀椀rst year.

India Ranks Ninth in Global Internet Blackout Preparedness India has been ranked ninth globally among nearly 100 countries considered least vulnerable to a majo r internet blackout or digital infrastructure breakdo wn, according to a study by TRG Datacenters, a United States-based colocation and digital infrastructure provider acquired by Tallvine Partners.  India’s Position

Ken-Betwa River Link Project Tribal families and farmers renewed their protest on July 3, 2026 beside the Barana River near Kupi village, Chhatarpur, alleging that assurances made in April remained unful昀椀lled. Participants included people affected by the Ken-Betwa, Majhgawan, Runjh, Neguwan or Naiguwa, and NTPC-linked projects.
  • Protesters stood in the river during the Jal Satyagraha, women lay on symbolic pyres during the Chita Andolan and wore symbolic nooses during the Faansi Satyagraha, while soil represented their attachment to ancestral land during the Mitti Satyagraha. Activists began an inde昀椀nite hunger strike.  Revision of the Rehabilitation Package
  • After the April protest, a fresh survey added around 750 families to rehabilitation plans for the Majhgaon and Runjh projects.
  • The Madhya Pradesh Cabinet approved an increase of approximately ₹202.50 crore increase in the package.
  • Compensation rose from ₹5 lakh to ₹12.5 lakh per affected family. Protesters were advised to raise remaining concerns with Panna’s administration.  Background of the Project
  • Launched by Prime Minister Narendra Modi on 25 December 2024, the Ken-Betwa Link Project is the 昀椀rst of 30 proposed river-linking projects under the National Perspective Plan.
  • It seeks to transfer surplus Ken basin water to the water-de昀椀cit Betwa basin, addressing shortages in Bundelkhand across Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh.
  • The Ken and Betwa rivers are tributaries of the Yamuna River.  Phase I
  • Phase I proposes the 77: metre-high Daudhan Dam, two powerhouses and a 216.46-kilometre link canal, including a 2-kilometre tunnel.
  • The reservoir’s dead and full reservoir levels will be 240 and 288 metres; respectively, dead and gross storage capacities will be 169 and 2,853 million cubic metres respectively.
  • Annual gross water yield up to Daudhan is estimated at 6,590 million cubic metres (MCM) at 75% dependability.
  • The canal will divert 1,377 million cubic metres annually. Of this, 220.77 million cubic metres will be used at the RD 18-kilometre pumping station, 1,010.51 million cubic metres for irrigating 1,93,899 hectares en route and 94.79 million cubic metres for drinking.
  • The remaining 50.93 million cubic metres will enter the Betwa upstream of Parichha Weir for drinking water and irrigation in Lalitpur.  Phase II
  • Phase II includes the Lower Orr Dam, Kotha Barrage and Bina Complex. These will meet water requirements in water-de昀椀cit areas of the Betwa basin within Madhya Pradesh’s allocated share at Rajghat Dam. Accidental Deaths and Suicides in India 2024 Report Accidental Deaths and Suicides in India 2024 (ADSI 2024) is an annual report published by the National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB) on May 6, 2026 under the Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India.  Key Findings of the Report  Accidental Deaths in India
  • In 2023, the total number of accidental deaths in India was 4,44,104.
  • In 2024, the total number of accidental deaths in India increased to 4,67,857.
  • The rate of accidental deaths was 31.9 in 2023.
  • The rate of accidental deaths increased to 33.3 in 2024.
  • The maximum number of accidental deaths in 2024 was reported in the age group of 30 to below 45 years.
  • This age group accounted for 1,46,370 deaths, which represented 31.3% of total accidental deaths.  Major Causes of Deaths Due to Forces of Nature
  • Out of the 7,903 accidental deaths attributable to forces of nature, 35.7% were due to lightning.
  • Out of the 7,903 accidental deaths attributable to forces of nature, 23.2% were due to heat or sunstroke.   • A total of 25.6% of suicide victims were educated up to the matriculation level.
  • Only 5.6% of total suicide victims were graduates or had higher quali昀椀cations. Election Commission Announces Special Intensive Revision Phase III
  • The Election Commission of India announced Phase III of the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls to be conducted in a phased manner on May 14, 2026 beginning on May 30, 2026.
  • As of September 2026, Special Intensive Revision (SIR) was being implemented in phases across India. Phase III covered 16 States and 3 Union Territories. Odisha, Mizoram, Sikkim and Manipur were scheduled to publish their 昀椀nal electoral rolls on September 6, while other regions had later deadlines extending into October, November and December 2026.  Constitutional and Legal Basis
  • The SIR exercise is based on the Election Commission’s constitutional and statutory powers. Article 324 and 326 of the Constitution gives the Election Commission superintendence, direction and control over the preparation of electoral rolls and the conduct of elections. Section 16, 19, 21 and 22 of Representation of the People Act 1950 are also invoked.
  • On May 27, 2026, the Supreme Court in Association for Democratic Reforms & Ors. vs. Election Commission of India & Ors. (2026) held that SIR falls within the ECI’s statutory mandate and is consistent with its constitutional responsibility to ensure free and fair elections.  Key Highlights
  • More than 3.94 lakh Booth Level Of昀椀cers is participating in the revision process during Phase III.

It is also signi昀椀cant because 2024 was the year in which the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita was used along with the Indian Penal Code framework.
  • NCRB is an attached of昀椀ce of the Ministry of Home Affairs. It was established in March, 1986.  Key Highlights
  • According to the report, India recorded 58,85,867 criminal cases in 2024 (a declined of ~ 6% compared with 2023).
  • This was a 6 percent (~5.7%) decline from 62.41 lakh cases recorded in 2023.
  • The overall crime rate declined from 448.3 cases per lakh population in 2023 to 418.9 cases per lakh population in 2024.
  • Out of all criminal cases, 35,44,608 cases were registered under the Indian Penal Code/Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
  • A total of 23.41 lakh cases were registered under Special and Local Laws.  Impact of Legal Reclassi昀椀cation
  • Cases under the hurt category declined sharply by 30.58 percent.

The number of cases under & Related Developments

  • The number of cases under IPC Sections 325, 326 and 329–335 declined from 6.36 lakh in 2023 to 4.41 lakh in 2024.  Rise in Cybercrime
  • Cybercrime continued to rise sharply in 2024.
  • India recorded 1,01,928 cybercrime cases in 2024.
  • This was a 17.9 percent increase over 86,420 cases in 2023.
  • Cybercrime cases had already increased by 31.2 percent in 2023 over 65,893 cases in 2022.
  • Out of 1,01,928 cybercrime cases , 73,987 cases were related to financial fraud.
  • Financial fraud accounted for 72.6 percent of all registered cybercrime cases in 2024.
  • Sexual exploitation accounted for 3.1 percent, with 3,190 cases.  Economic Offences
  • Economic offences increased by 4.6 percent in 2024.
  • India reported 2,14,379 economic offence cases in 2024.
  • In 2023, the number of economic offence cases stood at 2,04,973.
  • 1,92,382 cases were related to forgery, cheating and fraud.
  • This category accounted for nearly 90 percent of total economic offences.
  • Authorities seized 8,21,100 fake currency notes in 2024.
  • The total face value of these seized fake currency notes was `54.61 crore.  Crimes Against Women
  • Crimes against women declined slightly by 1.5 percent in 2024.
  • The crime rate under this category fell from 66.2 to 64.6 per lakh female population.
  • However, the total number of cases remained very high at 4.41 lakh.
  • “Cruelty by the husband or his relatives” accounted for 1,20,227 cases.
  • This category acconted for 27.2 percent of total crimes against women.
  • Kidnapping and abduction of women accounted for 67,829 cases (15.4 percent of total crimes against women).
  • Uttar Pradesh reported the highest number of crimes against women, with 66,398 cases.
  • Nagaland, Sikkim and Manipur recorded the lowest numbers of such cases.
  • Uttar Pradesh also recorded the highest number of dowry deaths cases (2038) with 2,057 victims.  Crimes Against Children
  • Crimes against children increased by 5.9 percent in 2024.
  • India recorded 1,87,702 cases of crimes against children.  Atrocities Against Scheduled Tribes
  • Crimes against Scheduled Tribe communities declined by 23.1 percent in 2024.

  • Crimes against Scheduled Caste communities declined by 3.6 percent in 2024.
  • Cases fell from 57,789 in 2023 to 55,698 in 2024.
  • The crime rate for crimes against Scheduled Castes stood at 27.7.
  • Rape accounted for 7.6 percent of cases.
  • Uttar Pradesh recorded the highest number of crimes against Scheduled Castes with 14,642 incidents.  Murder Cases
  • India recorded 27,049 murder cases in 2024.
  • This was a marginal decline of 2.4 percent from 2023.
  • Murder cases had also declined by 2.8 percent in 2023 compared to 2022.  Deaths by Suicide
  • The farming sector recorded 10,546 suicide deaths.
  • This included 4,633 farmers or cultivators.
  • It also included 5,913 agricultural labourers.

  • Deaths due to drug overdose increased sharply by 50 percent in 2024.

  • Tamil Nadu recorded the highest number of drug overdose deaths with 313 cases.  Crimes Against the State
  • Cases under offences against the State increased by 6.6 percent in 2024.

  • Kerala filed charge: sheets in 94.5 percent of cases.
  • Puducherry followed with 91 percent charge- sheeting efficiency.  Arrests and Convictions
  • More than 26.72 lakh people were arrested under the IPC and BNS.
  • More than 10.71 lakh people were convicted. The Prevention of Insults to National Honour Amendment Act, 2026 President Droupadi Murmu on August 11, 2026 gave assent to The Prevention of Insults to National Honour (Amendment) Bill, 2026 which has become a law.
  • The law making the intentional disruption or prevention of the singing of the national song ‘Vande Mataram’ a criminal offence, granting it the same legal protection as the National Anthem.
  • The Lok Sabha passed the Bill on July 30, 2026 while the Rajya Sabha had cleared it earlier.
  • The legislation grants Vande Mataram the same status as the National Anthem, ‘Jana Gana Mana’.
  • The Union Cabinet gave approval on May 5, 2026 to amend The Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971.
  • Any insult to Vande Mataram or intentional obstruction to its singing is proposed to be made punishable.

  • The Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971 was enacted to prevent insults to national honour.
  • The Act currently covers insults to the National Flag and the Constitution of India.  V ande Mataram: National Song and Freedom Struggle
  • Vande Mataram was composed by Bankim Chandra Chatterjee and 昀椀rst published in Bangadarshan (1875), later included in Anandamath (1882).

  • It was launched at the National Summit on Innovation and Inclusivity - Best Practices Shaping India’s Health Future.

The Constitution (One Hundred & Thirty-First Amendment) Bill, 2026 The Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026 was introduced in the Lok Sabha on 16 April 2026, but on 17 April 2026, it failed to pass in the Lok Sabha as it could not secure the required special majority.
  • During the vote, 298 members voted in favour and 230 members voted against.
  • A total of 528 members were present and voting, therefore 352 votes were required for its passage.
  • The central idea of this Bill was to bring representation closer to population.
  • If the population of a state has increased signi昀椀cantly, then the representation of its voters should increase proportionately.
  • On the one hand, it strengthened the idea of “one person, one vote, one value” , and on the other hand, it raised concerns among those states that had made serious efforts towards population control.  Main Objectives of the Bill
  • The Bill was based on four major objectives:  To increase the strength of the Lok Sabha  To restart delimitation on a new basis  To give Parliament the power to decide which census would be used  To implement one-third reservation for women at an earlier stage
  • An amendment to Article 81 was proposed.
  • The maximum strength of the Lok Sabha was proposed to be increased from 550 to 850.
  • Of these a maximum of 815 members would be from the states and 35 members from Union Territories.
  • A new de昀椀nition of “population” was proposed in Articles 55, 81, 170, 330, 332 etc.
  • Population would mean the census determined by Parliament through law.
  • An amendment to Article 82 was proposed.
  • Under the new proposal, delimitation would be done based on the census determined by Parliament.
  • This work would be carried out by the Delimitation Commission.
  • An amendment to Article 170 was proposed.
  • The total number of seats and constituencies in State Legislative Assemblies would be re-determined. Plastic Waste Management (Amendment) Rules, 2026 The Plastic Waste Management (Amendment) Rules, 2026 are an important step in India’s plastic-waste governance. They do not replace the Plastic Waste Management Rules, 2016; rather, they further amend them.
  • The Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change noti昀椀ed the amendment on March 31, 2026.  Revised De昀椀nitions and Scope
  • The de昀椀nition of End: of-Life Disposal has been expanded to include energy recovery methods such as co-processing, waste-to-energy, waste-to-oil, and road construction.
  • Processes converting plastic into feedstock or new plastic are now classi昀椀ed strictly as recycling, not disposal.
  • The de昀椀nition of Plastic Waste Processors has been broadened to include both recyclers and end- of-life disposal entities.
  • New terms such as Registered Environment Auditor, Reuse, and Seller have been introduced to improve regulatory clarity.
  • The scope of local governance has been widened to include all relevant authorities beyond traditional local bodies.
  • All recycled plastic packaging must comply with Indian Standard IS 14534:2023.
  • Packaging must carry mandatory labeling indicating recycled content. India’s First National Counter Terrorism Policy The Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) released India’s 昀椀rst national counter-terrorism policy , and strategy, PRAHAAR, on 23 February 2026.
  • The policy comes after the government announced in November 2024 that a comprehensive national counter-terrorism strategy would be framed, and it follows recent security concerns including the April 2025 Pahalgam terror attack.
  • It seeks to provide a uniform, coordinated and technology-aware framework to deal with terrorism, terror 昀椀nancing, radicalisation, cyber- attacks, drone-based threats, and attacks on critical infrastructure.  Key Highlights
  • The policy states that India faces terrorist threats across land, air and water, along with growing risks in the cyber domain.
  • It speci昀椀cally warns that criminal hackers and nation- states are targeting India through cyber-attacks.
  • The document underlines that India continues to face sponsored terrorism from across the border.
  • The policy identi昀椀es groups such as Al-Qaeda and ISIS as entities trying to incite violence in India through sleeper cells and extremist propaganda.
  • PRAHAAR notes the use of drones, encrypted messaging apps, social media, dark web platforms, and crypto wallets by terrorist groups for communi- cation, propaganda, recruitment and 昀椀nancing.
  • It also 昀氀ags the danger of misuse of CBRNED materials—Chemical, Biological, Radiological, Nuclear, Explosive and Digital—as well as robot- ics and drone systems. Age-Based Social Media Restrictions for Children On March 6, 2026, Karnataka announced in its Budget speech that social media use would be banned for children below 16. On the same day, Andhra Pradesh said it would prohibit access for children below 13 within 90 days and was also considering rules for the 13–16 age group.
  • At the Union level, the Economic Survey 2025–26 recommended age-based access limits and stronger platform responsibility, and an NHRC discussion on March 16, 2026 (Press release on March 18, 2026) showed that the matter is now being treated as a serious governance issue.  Global Context
  • The strongest global precedent has come from Australia.  Australia enacted the Online Safety Amendment (Social Media Minimum Age) Act, 2024.  Under this law, from 10 December 2025 , age- restricted platforms must take reasonable steps to prevent children under 16 from creating or retaining accounts.  The Australian eSafety regulator has indicated that platforms such as Facebook, Instagram, Snapchat, Threads, TikTok, Twitch, X, YouTube, Kick and Reddit fall within the age-restricted category, though the list may change. Defence Forces Vision 2047 The Raksha Mantri, Rajnath Singh , released “Defence Forces Vision 2047: A Roadmap for a Future-Ready Indian Military” on 10 March 2026 in South Block, New Delhi . Prepared by the Headquarters Integrated Defence Staff (HQ IDS), the document presents a long-term blueprint for transforming India’s armed forces into a modern, integrated, technologically advanced, and self-reli ant military by the centenary of Independence.
  • In 2025, the Ministry of Defence declared the year as the “Year of Reforms” to push jointness, integration and future-readiness.
  • The Ministry’s Year End Review 2025 had also said that the Armed Forces Vision 2047 was prepared in two parts and that Part I would be released publicly soon.  Phased Roadmap to 2047 One of the major strengths of the document is that it sets out a calibrated timeline for transformation. 1. Era of Transition (till 2030)
  • This phase focuses on restructuring the military and strengthening deterrence.
  • It gives importance to rapid adoption of indigenous technologies, especially in areas such as drones and surveillance. 2. Era of Consolidation (2030–2040)
  • This phase aims to deepen integration of cyber and space capabilities.
  • It seeks to operationalise layered air and missile defence systems. 3. Era of Excellence (2040–2047)
  • This 昀椀nal phase envisions a fully integrated, self- reliant, all-domain military force.
  • It aims to make India’s armed forces globally respected, technologically advanced, and combat ready. Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM) 2.0 Under the chairmanship of Narendra Modi, the Union Cabinet approved Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM) 2.0 on 10 March 2026. Its objective is to transform Jal Jeevan Mission from being limited to infrastructure creation into a service-based model.  Key Facts
  • The Cabinet has approved an increase in the total expenditure for this restructuring to `8.69 lakh crore , of which the central government’s contribution will be `3.59 lakh crore.
  • This amount is higher than the earlier approved `2.08 lakh crore by the Centre in 2019–20, meaning that an additional `1.51 lakh crore of central assistance has been included.  In this direction, an integrated national digital platform named “Sujalam Bharat” was developed by March, 2026.  Under this, each village will be assigned a unique Sujal village/service area ID , through which a complete digital mapping of the supply system from water source to household tap will be prepared.
  • To enhance transparency and accountability, active participation of Gram Panchayats and Village Water and Sanitation Committees will be ensured through the “Jal Arpan” initiative.
  • Gram Panchayats will certify project completion only when adequate arrangements for operation and maintenance have been ensured by the state government; only thereafter will a village be declared as “Har Ghar Jal”.
  • To strengthen community participation, “Jal Utsav” will be developed as an annual programme.  Progress and Coverage
  • The Functionality Assessment 2024 covered 19,812 Har Ghar Jal Villages and 2,37,608 househoulds; 76% received water meeting prescribed quality standards.
  • It is noteworthy that in 2019, only 3.23 crore (about 17%) rural households had tap water connections, whereas now more than 12.56 crore additional households have been provided this facility.
  • At present, out of a total of 19.36 crore rural households, approximately 15.80 crore (about 81.61%) households have access to tap water (as on March, 2026).  Targets and Implementation

Under JJM 2.0, the target & Related Developments

  • Under JJM 2.0, the target is to provide tap water connections to all 19.36 crore rural households by December 2028 and to ensure that all Gram Panchayats receive “Har Ghar Jal” certi昀椀cation.
  • This mission is now moving beyond an infrastructure-based approach towards a utility- based service delivery model , which will ensure 24×7 rural drinking water supply and strengthen the goal of “Viksit Bharat @2047”.  Quick Facts
  • Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM) was launched by Narendra Modi on 15 August 2019.
  • It had an ambitious target of providing tap water supply to every rural household by 2024.
  • At the time of its launch, only 3.23 crore (17%) rural households had access to tap water connections. Regional Connectivity Scheme – Modi昀椀ed UDAN Approved The Union Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi approved the launch and implementation of the Regional Connectivity Scheme – Revised UDAN on March 25, 2026 for a period of ten years from FY 2026–27 to 2035–36.
  • The total cost of the scheme is `28,840 crore, which will be borne through budgetary support from the Government of India.
  • The major components of the scheme are as follows:
  • Under the Revised UDAN scheme, it is proposed to develop 100 airports from existing unserved airstrips to enhance regional connectivity.
  • A total provision of `12,159 crore has been made for this over the next eight years.
  • Considering the high recurring O&M costs and limited revenue of airports operated under the Regional Connectivity Scheme (RCS), the scheme proposes O&M support for three years.
  • This support will be up to `3.06 crore per airport per year and `0.90 crore per heliport/water aerodrome. An estimated total of `2,577 crore is proposed for approximately 441 aerodromes.  Major Facts
  • The UDAN scheme was launched in October 2016 with the objective of making air travel affordable and strengthening connectivity to Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities.
  • During nine years of implementation, as of June, 2026, operations had been conducted on 665 routes across 95 airports, heliports, and water aerodromes.
  • More than 3.5 lakh 昀氀ights had been operated, carrying 1.64 crore passengers. Republic Day 2026 Republic Day is observed on 26 January to mark the day the Constitution of India came into force (January 26, 1950). Supreme Court stays 2026 UGC Equity Regulations In a significant order affecting India’s higher education governance, the Supreme Court on 29 January 2026 has kept in abeyance the newly noti昀椀ed UGC (Promotion of Equity in Higher Education Institutions) Regulations, 2026.
  • These Regulations were designed to create a time- bound, enforceable anti-discrimination framework on campuses. The Court raised concerns about vagueness, possible misuse, and exclusion, and has directed that the older 2012 UGC Equity Regulations would continue to operate for now.
  • The UGC Equity Regulations, 2026, were framed pursuant to the Supreme Court’s directions in Abeda Salim Tadvi v. Union of India (2019).
  • A Bench of Justices Surya Kant and Ujjal Bhuyan had directed the UGC to notify enforceable regulations to:  Address caste-based discrimination  Prevent student suicides  Rectify the ineffective implementation of the 2012 regulations.  Key Provisions of the UGC Regulations, 2026
  • Broad Coverage of Caste: Based Discrimination: The regulations de昀椀ne caste-based discrimination as any unfair or biased treatment against Scheduled Castes (SCs), Scheduled Tribes (STs), and Other Backward Classes (OBCs), thereby explicitly extending legal protection to OBCs and correcting a major omission in the earlier draft framework.
  • Mandatory Equal Opportunity Centres (EOCs): Every higher education institution is required to establish an Equal Opportu - nity Centre (EOC) to promote equity, social inclusion, and equal access, and to address com - plaints related to discrimination on campus.  Each institution must form an Equity Committee under the EOC, chaired by the head of the institution, with mandatory representation from SCs, STs, OBCs, persons with disabilities, and women, ensuring inclusive decision-making.  The Equity Committee is required to meet within 24 hours of receiving a complaint and submit its report within 15 working days , after which the head of the institution must initiate action within 7 days.
  • The UGC will establish a national monitoring com - mittee comprising representatives from statutory bodies and civil society to oversee implementation, review complaints, and suggest preventive measures, with the committee meeting at least twice a year. Water Budgeting in Aspirational Blocks NITI Aayog, in collaboration with GIZ India, has released a report titled “Water Budgeting in Aspirational Blocks”, aimed at enhancing water security at the local level, improving resource planning, and aligning with the vision of Viksit Bharat@2047. The report provides a comprehensive analysis of water availability, demand, and sector-speci昀椀c challenges across 18 Aspirational Blocks in 10 states and a UT (11 states and UT), using a digital platform for water budgeting.  Key Findings
  • Water Deficits: Several blocks are facing severe water shortages. Notable examples include:  Namchi (94% deficit)  Gangiri (60% deficit)  Baldeogarh (53% deficit)
  • Over: extraction of Groundwater: Blocks like Kotri and Abu Road in Rajasthan are over-extracting groundwater beyond recharge levels, leading to unsustainable water use.
  • Under: utilization of Runoff: Some regions, such as Fatehpur in Bihar, generate runoff but fail to utilize the stored water effectively. Bihar Legislative Assembly Election Results, 2025 The Bihar Legislative Assembly Election, 2025 was held in two phases (6 and 11 November) , the election witnessed a landslide victory for the National Democratic Alliance (NDA). In the 243-member Assembly, the NDA secured 202 seats, while the main opposition Mahagathbandhan was reduced to just 35 seats.
  • On November 20, 2025, Nitish Kumar took oath as the Chief Minister of Bihar for the 10th time, becoming the longest-serving Chief Minister of the state . Along with him, Samrat Choudhary and Vijay Kumar Sinha took oath as Deputy Chief Ministers.
  • Nitish Kumar of昀椀cially resigned from his post as the Chief Minister of Bihar on April 14, 2026.
  • Samrat Chaudhary took the oath of of昀椀ce on April 15, 2026, to become the 昀椀rst Chief Minister of Bihar from the Bhartiya Janata Party (BJP). Bihar Governor Syed Ata Hasnain administered the oath of of昀椀ce to Mr. Choudhary at Lok Bhawan in Patna.  Key Highlights
  • The Election Commission of India (ECI) successfully conducted the Bihar Legislative Assembly Election, 2025, with a voter turnout of 67.25%, the highest since 1951.  This included 71.77% female turnout and 62.73% male turnout.  The gender gap was about 9.04 percentage points in favour of women.  It is noteworthy that during Special Intensive Revision (SIR), the 昀椀nal electoral roll in Bihar included a total of 74,526,858 voters (November, 2025).
  • According to the election results, the National Democratic Alliance recorded a historic victory with 202 seats.  The NDA comprised the BJP , Janata Dal (United), Lok Janshakti Party (Ram Vilas), Hindustani Awam Morcha (Secular), and Rashtriya Lok Morcha.
  • The BJP emerged as the largest party in the state by winning 89 seats, while JD(U) secured 85 seats.
  • Folk singer Maithili Thakur (BJP) won from the Alinagar constituency (youngest MLA in Bihar).
  • According to the election results, the Rashtriya Janata Dal (RJD) secured the highest vote share at 23%.  Important Dates Phase I II Number of constituencies 121 seats 122 seats Date of noti昀椀cation October 10, 2025 October 13, 2025 Date of polling November 6, 2025 November 11, 2025 Date of counting — November 14, 2025 Bihar Legislative Assembly Election Results: Party-wise Position Party Name Seats Won Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) 89 Janata Dal (United) 85 Rashtriya Janata Dal (RJD) 25 Lok Janshakti Party (Ram Vilas) 19 Indian National Congress 6 Total 243 Kashi Tamil Sangamam 4.0 Kashi Tamil Sangamam (KTS) 4.0 is a Government- led cultural and educational exchange that deepens the civilisational connect between Tamil Nadu and Kashi (Varanasi). The 4 th edition was held in Varanasi from 2 to 15 December 2025, and it put a special focus on Tamil language learning and youth engagement under the theme “Let Us Learn Tamil – Tamil Karkalam.” The valedictory ceremony of Kashi Tamil Sangamam 4.0 was held on December 30, 2025, graced by the Vice President of India C.P . Radhakrishnan.  About Kashi Tamil Sangamam?
  • KTS is designed as a “knowledge bridge” and people-to-people platform to celebrate the long- standing movement of ideas, spirituality, learning and culture between Tamil Nadu and Kashi.
  • It is aligned with the spirit of Ek Bharat Shreshtha Bharat (EBSB).
  • KTS is anchored by the Ministry of Education , with IIT Madras and Banaras Hindu University (BHU) as principal knowledge partners, and participation from multiple ministries (including Railways, Culture, Tourism, Textiles, Youth Affairs & Sports) along with the Government of Uttar Pradesh.  Kashi Tamil Sangamam
  • KTS 1.0 (2022): Held from November 16 – December 16, 2022; large-scale cultural immersion with curated tours and academic-cultural interactions.
  • KTS 2.0 (Dec 2023): Held 17–30 Dec 2023 at Namo Ghat, Varanasi; included real-time Tamil translation of the PM’s address; exhibition sales and high public footfall were reported.
  • KTS 3.0 (Feb 2025): Held 15–24 Feb 2025; thematic focus on Sage Agastya; workshops connected ancient knowledge systems with contemporary education aligned with NEP 2020 emphasis on Indian knowledge traditions. Union Cabinet Approves 2027 Census
  • India is conducting Census 2027 after the last completed Census of 2011. It will be the sixteenth Census of India and the eighth since Independence.
  • The Union Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, approved the scheme on 12 December 2025, at an estimated cost of ₹11,718.24 crore.
  • The Census is a Union subject under Entry 69 of the Union List in the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution. Its legal framework comprises the Census Act, 1948, and the Census Rules, 1990, as amended.
  • The Office of the Registrar General and Census Commissioner, India , under the Ministry of Home Affairs, conducts the Census with state governments and Union Territory administrations.
  • The initial declaration under Section 3 of the Census Act was issued on 16 June 2025 . A notification dated 5 September 2026 superseded it and introduced an additional regional reference date.
  • Census operations will take place across 2026 and 2027 in two phases: Houselisting and Housing Census, followed by Population Enumeration.
  • Phase I records housing conditions, household amenities and assets. Its original national window was 1 April–30 September 2026, normally involving 30 days of fieldwork in each state or Union Territory.
  • Subsequent notifications deferred Phase I in Manipur until a further declaration and extended houselisting in Assam’s Charaideo and Sivasagar districts until 31 October 2026.
  • Phase II—Population Enumeration generally remains scheduled for February 2027, with separate schedules for specified regions.
  • In the entire Union Territory of Ladakh and specified snow-bound non-synchronous areas of Jammu and Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand, Population Enumeration was scheduled for 1–30 September 2026 , followed by revision on 1–5 October 2026 . Self-enumeration was scheduled for 17–31 August 2026.
  • The reference date, meaning the point in time to which the population count relates, is generally 00:00 hours on 1 March 2027.
  • Population Enumeration covers demography, religion, language, literacy, education, economic activity, migration and fertility . Its notified schedule contains 40 questions, including questions on disability and digital literacy.
  • The Cabinet Committee on Political Affairs decided on April 30, 2025 to include caste enumeration. Caste information will be collected electronically during Population Enumeration, and Question 10 concerns SC, ST and caste.
  • Census 2027 will be India’s first Census conducted by digital means , using enumerator mobile applications available on Android and iOS , while continuing house-to-house visits.
  • Optional online self: enumeration enables house- holds to submit information before the enumerator’s visit. For Phase I, the normal window is 15 days before fieldwork , and the generated Self- Enumeration ID helps enumerators confirm submitted details.
  • About 30 lakh field functionaries are envisaged.
  • Census 2021 was postponed following the COVID-19 outbreak. News in Short  Unlocking Growth in Tourism and Hospitality Sector

  • Reduces natural gas and potash imports; promotes circular economy  Approval of Proposal to Rename ‘Kerala’ as ‘Keralam’
  • The Kerala Legislative Assembly passed a resolution on June 24, 2024 to change the name of the state from “Kerala” to “Keralam.” Under the chairmanship of Narendra Modi, the Union Cabinet approved the proposal on 24 February 2026 to change the name of the state “Kerala” to “Keralam.”  BCCI Is Not a Public Authority Under RTI Act
  • The Central Information Commission has held that the Board of Control for Cricket in India is not a “public authority” under the Right to Information Act, 2005.

  • Poshan Pakhwada 2026 is a nationwide campaign of the Ministry of Women and Child Development to strengthen nutrition awareness, early childhood care and development and community participation under Mission Poshan 2.0.

  • To reduce fatalities due to road accidents, the scheme was launched by Prime Minister Narendra Modi on February 13, 2026 , and it was of昀椀cially named “Prime Minister – Road Accident Victims’ Hospitalisation and Assured Treatment (PM- RAHAT) Scheme” through a noti昀椀cation issued on February 19, 2026.
  • As per the statutory provisions provided under Section 162 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, this scheme was noti昀椀ed on 5 May 2025.

  • Bharat: VISTAAR is a farmer-centric, AI-powered agricultural Digital Public Infrastructure launched on February 17, 2026 in Jaipur by Union Minister for Agriculture and Farmers’ Welfare, and Rural Development, Shivraj Singh Chouhan, in the presence of Rajasthan Chief Minister Bhajanlal Sharma.

  • It has deployed over 350 AI language models to facilitate translation, speech recognition, and conversational AI services.  Uttar Pradesh “Gharauni Act” 2025
  • The Uttar Pradesh Rural Abadi Records Act (popularly called the “Gharauni Act”) was taken up and passed by the Uttar Pradesh Legislature (assented to by the Governor on January 2, 2026), to provide a clear legal framework for rural residential (“abadi”) property records created under the SVAMITVA programme.
