Chapter 3

International Affairs

Bilateral relations, prime ministerial and presidential visits, global indices, rankings, and multilateral conventions.

India and It’s Neighbours; Other & Related Developments

  • India and It’s Neighbours; Other Asian Countries India–Switzerland President Guy Parmelin’s State Visit to India Swiss Confederation President Guy Parmelin visited India from October 5–7, 2026 , marking the first anniversary of the India–European Free Trade Association (EFTA) Trade and Economic Partnership Agreement (TEPA) . On 5 October, he paid tribute to Mahatma Gandhi at Rajghat, New Delhi, held bilateral talks with Prime Minister Narendra Modi at Hyderabad House , and met President Droupadi Murmu at Rashtrapati Bhavan . Both countries emphasised cooperation in the 3Ts—Trade, Technology and Talent, alongside developing resilient global supply chains.
  • India: EFTA Agreement: Established in 1960, EFTA comprises Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland. Switzerland is not a member of the European Economic Area (EEA).
  • India: EFTA TEPA was signed on 10 March 2024 and entered into force on 1 October 2025. It aims to facilitate US$100 billion in investments and one million direct jobs in India over 15 years.
  • Five Major Agreements and Arrangements: 1. Migration and Mobility Partnership Memorandum of Understanding (MoU): Promotes legal migration and professional mobility, including multiple-entry visas valid for up to 昀椀ve years. 2. Young Professionals Exchange Agreement: Provides for the exchange of 300 professionals annually from each country , expandable to 500, through temporary employment. 3. Transport Technology MoU: Signed between India’s Ministry of Road Transport and Highways and Switzerland’s Federal Department of Economic Affairs, Education and Research A. International Relations (EAER) to promote sustainable transport, electric vehicles, ropeways and tunnel technologies. 4. Research Letter of Intent (LoI): Signed between India’s Department of Science and Technology (DST) and the Swiss National Science Foundation (SNSF) to strengthen long-term scienti昀椀c research. 5. Innovation Implementation Arrangement: Signed between DST and the Zurich University of Applied Sciences (ZHAW) to promote technology transfer, entrepreneurship and the Indo- Swiss Academia–Industry Training (AIT India) programme for early-stage startups.
  • The inaugural Indo: Swiss Research Flagship Event was held in New Delhi on 6 October 2026, attended by President Parmelin and Union Minister Dr. Jitendra Singh.
  • The Indo: Swiss Research Framework (ISRF) aims to strengthen scienti昀椀c networks, knowledge exchange and academia–industry collaboration. Bilateral scienti昀椀c cooperation began in 2003, followed by the Indo-Swiss Joint Research Programme in 2005.
  • The Second India: EFTA Prosperity Summit was held at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi, on 7 October 2026 , reviewing TEPA implementation and investment opportunities.
  • India: Switzerland relations are rooted in the Treaty of Friendship signed on 14 August 1948. India-Japan Shinzo Abe Memorial Corridor Inaugurated in Varanasi On October 7, 2026, Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath and Akie Abe, wife of former Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe, jointly inaugurated the Abe Memorial Corridor at the Rudraksh International Cooperation and Convention Centre in Varanasi.
  • The corridor commemorates Shinzo Abe’s contribution to India–Japan relations and his association with Varanasi.
  • It displays photographs and memories of his visits to India and his friendship with Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
  • In December 2015, Abe visited Varanasi with Prime Minister Modi and participated in the Ganga Aarti.
  • The visit strengthened cultural cooperation between Varanasi and Japan’s ancient city of Kyoto.
  • Rudraksh Convention Centre: Inaugurated by Prime Minister Modi on 15 July 2021, the centre was constructed with Japanese assistance.
  • Its concept was discussed during Abe’s 2015 Varanasi visit, making it a symbol of India–Japan cultural cooperation.
  • Abe served as Japan’s Prime Minister during 2006– 07 and 2012–20.
  • India honoured him with the Padma Vibhushan in 2021 in the field of Public Affairs.
  • Uttar Pradesh plans to develop a 500-acre Japan City in the Yamuna Expressway Industrial Development Authority (YEIDA) region to attract Japanese investment.
  • Cooperation with Japan’s Yamanashi Prefecture also includes green hydrogen, research and skill development, with a proposed Centre of Excellence involving IIT (BHU), IIT Kanpur and other institutions.
  • Japan supports major Indian projects, including the Mumbai–Ahmedabad High-Speed Rail, Dedicated Freight Corridor and Delhi–Mumbai Industrial Corridor. 16th India–Japan Annual Summit 2026 Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi visited New Delhi from 1 to 3 July, 2026 for the 16th India–Japan Annual Summit. The main meeting with Narendra Modi was held on 2 July. The visit marked 20 years of annual, alternating leadership visits.
  • The summit strengthened the Special Strategic and Global Partnership established in 2014, focusing on defence and security, economic partnership and people-to-people exchanges.
  • It produced 16 official outcomes. The separately announced UNICORN defence co-development initiative was outside this list.
  • Mineral cooperation focuses on upstream exploration, technical knowledge and collaboration between the Geological Survey of India and the Japan Organization for Metals and Energy Security (JOGMEC).
  • Japan’s Free and Open Indo: Pacific (FOIP) approach broadly aligns with India’s Indo-Pacific Oceans Initiative (IPOI) and Mutual and Holistic Advancement for Security and Growth Across Regions (MAHASAGAR), supporting sovereignty, international law and a rules-based region.
  • The fourth 2+2 Foreign and Defence Ministers’ Meeting is scheduled to be held in Tokyo before the end of 2026.
  • Cooperation covers JAIMEX 25, satellite-based maritime awareness, naval maintenance in India and defence technology under Make in India.
  • The Unified Complex Radio Antenna (UNICORN) combines communication antennas into one structure, reducing radar signature and improving naval communication.
  • AI outcomes included a joint statement and IndiaAI Mission–Japan’s Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry cooperation with GENIAC.
  • IIT Bombay, BharatGen and Japan’s National Institute of Informatics will develop large language models with scientific-reasoning capabilities.
  • SarvamAI and Preferred Networks will cooperate on foundation models and the complete AI technology stack.
  • The target is to invite 500 highly skilled Indian AI professionals to Japan by 2030.
  • AI cooperation will be guided by the Hiroshima AI Process and New Delhi Declaration on AI Impact.
  • Digital cooperation includes the proposed FOIP Digital Corridor and the NIXI–JPNIC agreement on internet registries, IPv6, security, capacity building and exchanges.
  • Energy cooperation involves Indian national oil companies, Indian Strategic Petroleum Reserves Limited, JOGMEC and the Japan Bank for International Cooperation.
  • The Cooperative Biogas for Growth Initiative supports approximately 1,000 biogas and organic- fertiliser plants through dairy cooperatives.
  • The leaders supported the proposed clean-ammonia project in Odisha and recognised hydrogen and ammonia as important for decarbonisation and energy security.
  • The Joint Crediting Mechanism under Article 6.2 of the Paris Agreement can facilitate bilateral carbon- credit cooperation and low-carbon investment.
  • Cooperation will continue on the Mumbai– Ahmedabad High-Speed Rail project and Japan’s latest E10-series Shinkansen technology.
  • The Centre for Cellular and Molecular Platforms (C-CAMP) and RIKEN will cooperate in translational research, deep technology, start-ups, healthcare, agriculture and environmental applications.
  • The National Centre for Biological Sciences–Tata Institute of Fundamental Research and RIKEN will cooperate in biological and neuroscience research, researcher exchanges and joint projects.
  • The leaders welcomed research exchanges and progress in the ISRO–JAXA Lunar Polar Exploration Mission, or LUPEX, also called Chandrayaan-5.
  • India and Japan will celebrate 2027 as the Year of Shared Horizons, marking 75 years of diplomatic relations through cultural, academic, youth, business and public-diplomacy events.
  • Modi accepted an invitation to Japan for the 17th Annual Summit in 2027.
  • The leaders supported state: prefecture partnerships, including Yamanashi–Uttar Pradesh , and the India–Japan Governors’ Network for Friendship and Exchange.
  • Yamanashi (a leader in hydrogen technology) partnered with Uttar Pradesh (via UPNEDA) on hydrogen production, storage, and clean energy pilot projects. PM Modi’s State Visit to Uzbekistan Prime Minister Narendra Modi visited Uzbekistan on 29–30 August, 2026 at the invitation of President Shavkat Mirziyoyev. The two countries upgraded their Strategic Partnership (established in 2011) to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership. President Mirziyoyev conferr ed Uzbekistan’s highest state award, the “Oliy Darajali Do‘stlik” Order, on Modi.
  • Uzbekistan, a double: landlocked Central Asian country, remains strategically important to India because of its location and mineral resources.
  • Both countries discussed a framework for long-term uranium supplies to India and expanded cooperation in peaceful nuclear energy, geological exploration, mining, mineral processing and value-added products.
  • Uzbekistan produced approximately 7,000 tonnes of uranium in 2025, with proven reserves estimated at 139,000 tonnes. Cooperation also supports India’s National Critical Mineral Mission.
  • The countries set a bilateral trade target of US$5 billion by 2030, compared with trade exceeding US$1 billion previously.
  • Both sides supported multimodal transport corridors and reduced freight costs.
  • Iran’s Chabahar Port and the International North– South Transport Corridor (INSTC) offer alternative routes to overcome India’s limited overland connectivity with Central Asia.
  • An agreement between NPCI International Payments Ltd. (NIPL) and Uzbekistan’s National Interbank Processing Centre (NIPC) will enable Indian UPI applications to scan Uzbekistan’s UZQR codes for merchant payments.
  • Their joint military exercise DUSTLIK (7th edition) was last conducted in Uzbekistan’s Namangan Region in April 2026.
  • An MoU on Ayurveda and other traditional medicines was signed.
  • India announced 100 Lal Bahadur Shastri Hindi Scholarships and an ICCR Sanskrit Chair at Tashkent State University of Oriental Studies.
  • Both countries signed a Letter of Intent to conserve the ancient Buddhist sites of Fayaz Tepa and Kara Tepa near Termez.
  • India also announced a US$1 million grant for afforestation and ecological rehabilitation in the Aral Sea region.  India–Uzbekistan Business Forum 2026
  • The forum was attended by India’s Union Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal and Uzbekistan’s Minister of Investment, Industry and Trade, Laziz Kudratov.
  • Piyush Goyal called for doubling bilateral trade from approximately US$1.5 billion to about US$3 billion within three years.
  • The forum involved India’s Ministry of Commerce and Industry, Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Investment, Industry and Trade, and the Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FICCI).
  • Cooperation focused on mining, textiles, pharma- ceuticals, healthcare, agriculture, food processing, information technology, digital infrastructure and advanced manufacturing. India–Seychelles Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s State Visit to Seychelles from 27 to 29 June 2026 expanded bilateral cooperation following talks with President Dr Patri ck Herminie.
  • The visit coincided with the 50 th anniversary of Seychelles’ independence and diplomatic ties with India.
  • It was Modi’s second visit after March 2015 and advanced the February 2026 Joint Vision for Sustainability, Economic Growth and Security through Enhanced Linkages (SESEL).
  • SESEL covers defence, healthcare, education, digital transformation, renewable energy, capacity building and food security.
  • Cooperation also falls within India’s MAHASAGAR Vision—Mutual and Holistic Advancement for Security and Growth Across Regions.
  • The 19 outcomes comprised five development- assistance measures, five announcements and nine formal agreements, treaties or MoUs.
  • India gifted an indigenously built Fast Patrol Vessel, PS Lespwar, to the Seychelles Coast Guard, alongside ten utility vehicles, five sets of Laser Radial-class sailing boats, six ambulances, 500 metric tonnes of rice and 8,500 metric tonnes of cement. Seychelles decided to join the Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure.
  • MoUs covered preliminary preparations for a new Seychelles National Hospital and cooperation between HLL Lifecare Limited and Seychelles’ Ministry of Health under India’s Jan Aushadhi framework for affordable, quality medicines and medical products.

NPCI International Payments Limited and & Related Developments

  • NPCI International Payments Limited and the Central Bank of Seychelles signed an MoU to implement India’s Unified Payments Interface.
  • The Indian Council of Agricultural Research and Seychelles Agriculture Department signed an MoU with a 2026–2031 Work Plan.
  • Diplomatic training cooperation will facilitate exchanges between India’s Sushma Swaraj Institute of Foreign Service and Seychelles’ Ministry of Foreign Affairs. India–Cyprus Strategic Partnership India and Cyprus elevated their relationship to a Strategic Partnership during the State Visit of Cyprus President Nikos Christodoulides to India from May 20–23, 2026.
  • The 2026 visit was the first visit of President Christodoulides to India in his current capacity.
  • During the visit, he held talks with Prime Minister Modi in New Delhi, met President Droupadi Murmu, paid homage at Rajghat, and participated in a Business Forum in Mumbai.

  • They welcomed a five: year roadmap for defence cooperation for 2026–2031.
  • The joint statement noted the MoU between NPCI International Payments Limited and Eurobank Cyprus.
  • It also welcomed a framework for interoperability of India’s Unified Payments Interface with the Target Instant Payment Settlement (TIPS) system of the European Central Bank.

  • Both countries agreed to mark 2028, completing 80 years of diplomatic relations, as the “India–Romania Year of Innovation.” India-UK CETA and DCC The India–United Kingdom Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA) and Double Contribution Convention (DCC) became operational on July 15, 2026. They aim to expand trade and investment, facilitate temporary professional mobility and eliminate duplicate social-security contributions for eligible workers.
  • The Enhanced Trade Partnership and Roadmap 2030, launched in May 2021, laid their foundation.

After 14 negotiation rounds, CETA & Related Developments

  • After 14 negotiation rounds, CETA was concluded on 6 May 2025 and signed in London on 24 July 2025. DCC was signed on 10 February 2026.
  • CETA is a next: generation free trade agreement with 30 chapters covering goods, services, investment, digital trade, intellectual property, government procurement, competition, innovation, sustainability and MSMEs.
  • The UK provides zero: duty access to nearly 99 per cent of Indian tariff lines, covering almost the entire value of Indian exports to the UK.
  • Major beneficiary sectors include textiles, leather, footwear, gems, jewellery, marine products, engineering goods, pharmaceuticals, chemicals, processed food and automobile components.
  • India excludes dairy products, cereals, millets, apples, edible oils and oilseeds from major tariff concessions.
  • This protects small producers, domestic prices and rural livelihoods while balancing liberalisation with policy space for vulnerable sectors.
  • UK commitments cover 12 service sectors and 137 sub-sectors, including IT, finance, engineering, healthcare, education and telecommunications.
  • CETA facilitates temporary movement of business visitors, intra-corporate transferees, contractual service suppliers, independent professionals and investors.
  • It also creates opportunities for Indian chefs, yoga instructors and classical musicians.
  • DCC prevents dual social: security contributions for eligible temporarily posted or detached workers.
  • Ordinary overseas employees generally contribute in their country of employment.
  • It concerns contribution liability and does not automatically grant host-country pensions or other contributory benefits. International Events/Indices/Rankings/Reports WJP Rule of Law Index 2026 The World Justice Project (WJP) released the Rule of Law Index 2026 on October 21, 2026, ranking India 88th among 143 countries and jurisdictions, with an overall score of 0.48. India slipped two positions from 86th in 2025 , when its score was 0.49. Globally, the rule of law declined in 62% of countries, marking the ninth consecutive year in which deterioration exceeded improvement.  Key Highlights
  • About WJP: The World Justice Project is an independent, nonpartisan, multidisciplinary organisation promoting the rule of law worldwide.
  • Methodology: The Index uses eight factors and 44 sub-factors , drawing on household and expert surveys. Scores range from 0 (weakest) to 1 (strongest adherence to the rule of law).
  • Four Fundamental Principles: Accountability, Just Law, Open Government, and Accessible and Impartial Justice.
  • Regional Performance: India ranked 3rd among six South Asian countries and 6th among 33 lower-middle-income economies . Its strongest global factor ranking was in Open Government (45th), while its lowest was in Civil Justice (116th).  Global Rankings
  • Top Seven Countries: Denmark (1st; 0.90), Norway (2nd; 0.89), Finland (3rd; 0.87), Sweden (4th; 0.86), Luxembourg (5th; 0.83), Germany (6th; 0.83) and New Zealand (7th; 0.83).
  • Bottom Five Countries: Venezuela (143rd; 0.26), Afghanistan (142nd; 0.31), Haiti (141st; 0.31), Cambodia (140th; 0.31) and Nicaragua (139th; 0.32).
  • South Asian Rankings: Nepal (71st), Sri Lanka (74th), India (88th), Bangladesh (123rd), Pakistan (131st) and Afghanistan (142nd).
  • Other Major Economies: Singapore (14th), Japan (15th), United Kingdom (18th), United States (30th), South Africa (60th), Indonesia (75th), Brazil (76th), China (92nd) and Russia (121st).
  • Largest Improvements: Latvia (+1.6%), Trinidad and Tobago (+1.2%) and Guatemala (+1.1%).
  • Largest Declines: Haiti (−5.6%), Tanzania (−3.5%) and Sudan (−2.8%). These percentages represent annual changes in index scores. Nobel Prizes 2026 The 2026 Nobel Prizes were announced between October 5 and 12, 2026 in six categories—Physiology or Medicine, Physics, Chemistry, Literature, Peace and Economic Sciences. Nobel Prize 2026: Winners at a Glance Category Laureate(s) Institution / Af昀椀liation Awarded For Physiology or Medicine Karl Deisseroth Stanford University, USA; Investigator, Howard Hughes Medical Institute Discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics Peter Hegemann Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin, Germany – Experimental Biophysics Same Georg Nagel Julius-Maximilians-Universität Würzburg (JMU), Germany Same Physics Francis Halzen University of Wisconsin–Madison, USA Contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and discovery of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos Chemistry Henri B. Kagan Université Paris-Saclay, France – Professor Emeritus; research associated with Université Paris-Saclay/CNRS Non-linear effects in asymmetric organic synthesis Kenso Soai Tokyo University of Science, Japan – Professor Emeritus Asymmetric autocatalysis in organic synthesis Literature Anne Carson Canadian writer and classicist; University of Toronto alumna Innovative literary work engaging with the classical tradition Peace Navanethem “Navi” Pillay Former UN High Commissioner for Human Rights; former ICTR President and ICC judge; has served as an ad hoc ICJ judge Efforts to promote peace and international law Economic Sciences Robert E. Hall Stanford University, USA Microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation Michael Woodford Columbia University, USA – John Bates Clark Professor of Political Economy Same  Medicine: Optogenetics Revolution
  • Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel received the Medicine Prize on 5 October.
  • Hegemann and Nagel’s work on channelrhodopsins, light-sensitive ion channels found in microorganisms, helped provide the biological basis for optogenetics.
  • Deisseroth helped develop these discoveries into a technique that allows researchers to activate or inhibit selected neurons using light.
  • Optogenetics has transformed neuroscience by allowing scientists to examine how specific neural circuits influence memory, emotion and behaviour.  Physics: Opening a New Window on the Universe
  • Francis Halzen received the Physics Prize for his decisive role in the IceCube Neutrino Observatory.
  • IceCube uses about one cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice containing thousands of light sensors to detect extremely elusive neutrinos.
  • Its observations established the detection of high- energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin, helping create the field of neutrino astronomy.  Chemistry: Understanding Molecular Handedness
  • Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai jointly received the Chemistry Prize.
  • Kagan pioneered understanding of non-linear effects in asymmetric catalysis , while Soai demonstrated asymmetric autocatalysis, in which a reaction product helps produce more of the same handed molecular form.
  • Their discoveries improved understanding of chirality, an important concept in organic chemistry and pharmaceutical development.  Literature: Anne Carson
  • Canadian poet, essayist, translator and classicist Anne Carson received the Literature Prize on 8 October.
  • She was honoured for a body of work that combines poetry, prose, criticism, translation and ancient Greek literature in innovative forms.
  • Major works include Autobiography of Red, The Beauty of the Husband, Nox and Eros the Bittersweet.  Peace: Navi Pillay
  • South African jurist Navanethem “Navi” Pillay received the Nobel Peace Prize for her efforts to promote peace and international law.
  • Pillay served as UN High Commissioner for Human Rights (2008–2014) and held judicial positions at the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda (ICTR) and the International Criminal Court (ICC).
  • Her career has focused on accountability for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity.
  • Pillay was born in Durban into a family of Indian Tamil origin, making her award especially noteworthy from an Indian current-affairs perspective.  Economic Sciences: Stabilising Economic Fluctuations
  • Robert E. Hall of Stanford University and Michael Woodford of Columbia University received the Economic Sciences Prize on 12 October.
  • Their research connected the decisions of households and firms with economy-wide fluctuations in inflation, output and employment.
  • Their work provided theoretical foundations for modern macroeconomic stabilisation policies , including the use of fiscal policy, interest rates and central-bank communication.
  • Their models are widely used by central banks and finance ministries to analyse economic shocks. Global Hunger Index 2026 The Global Hunger Index (GHI) 2026 , released in October 2026 under the theme “No Security Without Food Security,” ranked India 100th among 122 countries , with a score of 24.1, placing it in the “serious” hunger category . India’s score improved from 38.1 in 2000 and 37.0 in 2006, but remained worse than the South Asian average of 23.5 and the global average of 18.1.  Key Highlights
  • About GHI: First published in 2006, the Global Hunger Index is an annual, peer-reviewed assessment jointly published by Concern Worldwide, Welthungerhilfe and the Institute for International Law of Peace and Armed Con昀氀ict (IFHV). The 2026 report is its 21st edition.
  • Four Indicators: The Index measures hunger using undernourishment (1/3 weight), child stunting (1/6), child wasting (1/6) and under- 昀椀ve mortality (1/3). Scores range from 0 (best) to 100 (worst).
  • Data Period: The 2026 Index combines undernourishment data (2023–2025), child wasting (2021–2025), child stunting (2024) and under- 昀椀ve mortality (2024), using international sources including FAO, WHO and UNICEF.
  • India’s Performance:  Undernourished population: 9.8%  Child stunting: 29.3%  Child wasting: 19.0%  Under-昀椀ve mortality: 2.7%
  • Child wasting remains India’s major nutritional concern, while stunting declined signi昀椀cantly from 50% in 2000 to 29.3% in 2026.  Top Performers: Twenty-four countries, including Armenia, Belarus, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bulgaria and Chile, recorded GHI scores below 5 and were jointly placed in ranks 1–24.  Lowest-Ranked Countries: Somalia (122nd; 47.0) recorded the highest hunger score, followed by the Democratic Republic of the Congo (121st; 39.5), Chad (120th; 38.0), Madagascar (119th; 36.5) and Haiti (118th; 34.4). Somalia was classi昀椀ed in the “alarming” category.  Global Findings: The global GHI score increased from 17.6 in 2018 to 18.1 in 2026, indicating stalled progress against hunger. South Asia scored 23.5 , remaining in the serious category. Burundi, South Sudan, Sudan and Yemen received provisional alarming designations because of incomplete data.  Major Challenges: Con昀氀ict, climate shocks, economic pressures and disrupted food systems continue to undermine global food security.
  • In India, inadequate dietary diversity, maternal malnutrition, poor sanitation and limited healthcare access contribute to persistent child undernutrition. WHO–UNICEF JMP Report 2026 On September 22, 2026 , the World Health Organization (WHO) and United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) released “Progress on Drinking Water, Sanitation and Hygiene in Schools 2015–2025” under their Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP). The report assesses school Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) services under Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) Indicator 4.a.1 and warns that universal coverage (over 99%) is unlikely by 2030.  Key Highlights  Global WASH Status (2025) Indicator Water Sanitation Hygiene Schools with basic services 78% 77% 72% Children lacking basic services 429 million 460 million 545 million Children with no service 258 million 244 million 362 million Projected 2030 coverage 84% 81% 79%
  • Required Acceleration: Fourfold for drinking water and 昀椀vefold for sanitation. WHO speci昀椀es fourfold for hygiene, while parts of the JMP report specify 昀椀vefold.
  • Important Distinction: Children lacking basic services include those with limited or no services.  India’s Performance
  • Basic Coverage: Drinking water 96.6% (2025) , sanitation 80.8% (2025) and hygiene 52.9% (2024).
  • No-Service Categories (2025): Approximately 50 million children lacked sanitation , 12 million lacked drinking water and 20 million lacked hygiene services.
  • Sanitation Gap: India accounted for nearly one- 昀椀fth of the global 244 million children without sanitation services.
  • Progress: During 2015–2025, schools without sanitation declined by 14 percentage points, while basic drinking water coverage increased by over four percentage points annually.
  • 2030 Outlook: India was among 28 of 62 countries on track for universal basic drinking water coverage. Academic Freedom Index 2026 The 12 th edition of Free to Think 2026, released by Scholars at Risk (SAR) on September 15, 2026, classi昀椀ed academic freedom in India as “severely restricted.” India’s Academic Freedom Index (AFI) score declined from 0.16 in 2024 to 0.14 in the latest assessment.
  • The report documented 382 attacks arising from 321 verified incidents involving higher-education communities across 59 countries and territories between 1 July 2025 and 30 June 2026.
  • Free to Think is an annual publication of the Scholars at Risk Academic Freedom Monitoring Project, examining threats to academic freedom, institutional autonomy and higher-education communities.
  • The Index measures actual levels of academic freedom across 179 countries and territories.
  • It is jointly implemented by Germany’s Friedrich- Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU) and the V-Dem Institute, using assessments from 2,357 country experts.
  • Five AFI Indicators: The Index evaluates: 1. Freedom to research and teach. 2. Freedom of academic exchange and dissemination. 3. Institutional autonomy. 4. Campus integrity. 5. Freedom of academic and cultural expression.
  • India was placed in the “severely restricted” category alongside Hong Kong, Indonesia, Pakistan, the West Bank and Ukraine.
  • SAR attributed India’s declining score partly to restrictions on research and teaching freedom.
  • It also raised concerns about university governance, leadership appointments, faculty dismissals, cancellation of academic events, student expression and changes in UGC regulations.
  • Afghanistan, China, Gaza, Iran, Russia, Türkiye, Syria, Venezuela and Zimbabwe were among the countries and territories identified as having completely restricted academic freedom. Global Gender Gap Index 2026 The World Economic Forum (WEF) released the 20 th Global Gender Gap Report on September 16, 2026, ranking India 131 st among 145 economies, with 64.5% gender parity.

India retained its 2025 ranking, & Related Developments

  • India retained its 2025 ranking, while its score improved marginally from 64.4% to 64.5%.
  • Globally, 69.2% of the gender gap has been closed, with full parity estimated to take another 120 years.
  • Launched by the WEF in 2006, the Global Gender Gap Index measures gender disparities rather than absolute development levels.
  • Its scores range from 0 (disparity) to 1 (full parity).
  • The Index assesses Economic Participation and Opportunity, Educational Attainment, Health and Survival, and Political Empowerment.  India’s Performance Dimension Gender Parity Economic Participation and Opportunity 41.2% Educational Attainment 96.6% Health and Survival 95.6% Political Empowerment 24.5% Overall 64.5%
  • Labour: force participation parity stood at 44.1%, while parity among professional and technical workers improved from 26.6% in 2006 to 49.9% in 2026.
  • Representation among legislators, senior officials and managers remained low at 13.1%.
  • India achieved full parity in secondary and tertiary enrolment, while adult literacy parity stood at 82.5%. Health and Survival parity improved to 95.6%.
  • India ranked 67th globally in Political Empowerment with 24.5% parity.
  • Parliamentary and ministerial representation parity stood at 16.1% and 5.9%, respectively, while the female head-of-state indicator reached 40.7%.
  • Top Five Economies: Iceland (93.0%) ranked first for the 17 th consecutive year, followed by Finland (87.2%), Norway (85.7%), Namibia (84.5%) and the United Kingdom (84.2%).
  • Other Top Ten Economies: New Zealand (6 th), Sweden (7 th), Australia (8 th), Germany (9 th) and Ireland (10th).
  • Lowest: Ranked Economies: Chad (145 th), Iran (144th) and Pakistan (143rd).
  • Global Dimension Scores: Educational Attainment (96.9%) and Health and Survival (96.2%) recorded the highest parity, followed by Economic Participation (61.7%) and Political Empowerment (22.1%).
  • Southern Asia ranked 7 th among eight regions, closing 64.5% of its gender gap. US–Denmark–Greenland Arctic Defense Agreement 2026 On September 22, 2026, the United States, Denmark and Greenland signed a new Arctic Defense Agreement at the United Nations Headquarters in New York, strengthening military cooperation and security in the Arctic and North Atlantic.
  • The agreement, signed by US President Donald Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenland’s Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen, expands US military access while recognising Denmark’s sovereignty and Greenland’s right to self-determination.
  • The agreement amends the 1951 Defense Agreement concerning Greenland and will enter into force after the necessary parliamentary procedures in Denmark and Greenland are completed.
  • The original US: Denmark Defense Agreement was signed on 27 April 1951 under the framework of the North Atlantic Treaty.
  • It was subsequently supplemented by the 1991 Memorandum of Understanding and the 2004 Igaliku Agreement.
  • The agreement permits the expansion and modernisation of US military activities at Pituffik Space Base, formerly known as Thule Air Base, in north-western Greenland.
  • The facility supports ballistic missile early warning, missile defence, satellite tracking and space surveillance.
  • The agreement also refers to the proposed US Golden Dome missile-defence system.
  • The agreement promotes greater North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) involvement in Arctic military planning, exercises, intelligence gathering, surveillance and interoperability.
  • It generally prohibits non: NATO countries from establishing military installations or maintaining a persistent military presence in Greenland without the parties’ agreement. 26th SCO Summit 2026 Prime Minister Narendra Modi attended the 26th meeting of the Council of Heads of State of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) in Bishkek, Kyrgyz Republic, on August 31–September 1, 2026. Chaired by President Sadyr Japarov, it marked the SCO’s 25th anniversary.

  • Measures for a Universal Centre for Countering Challenges and Threats and an SCO Anti-Drug Centre will complement the Regional Anti-Terrorist Structure (RATS) in Tashkent.
  • India’s approach centred on Security, Connectivity and Opportunity.
  • Modi called for dismantling the terrorist ecosystem, opposed double standards in counter-terrorism and stressed dialogue and diplomacy.
  • India linked Eurasian security with peace in Afghanistan and highlighted its humanitarian and development assistance.
  • It supported connectivity that promotes trade while respecting sovereignty and territorial integrity.
  • India supported English as an official SCO language alongside Russian and Chinese.
  • It announced that it would host the first SCO Civilisation Dialogue Forum later in 2026 and supported the Young Scientists Forum, Young Authors’ Conclave and youth cooperation.
  • Originating from the Shanghai Five of 1996, the SCO was established on June 15, 2001.
  • It has 10 full members. India and Pakistan joined in 2017, Iran in 2023 and Belarus in 2024.
  • Its Secretariat is in Beijing. Members cover approximately 36 million square kilometres, have over 3.4 billion people, and account for about one- fourth of global GDP and over 15% of international trade.

FAO Food Price Index The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) reported that the FAO Food Price Index (FFPI) averaged 131.1 points in July 2026, increasing by 0.7 points (0.6%) from June and 1.0% from July 2025. It reached its highest level since early 2023 but remained 29.1 points (18.2%) below its March 2022 peak. The increase was driven by higher cereal, vegetable oil and sugar prices, partly offset by declines in meat and dairy prices.

The FFPI measures monthly changes & Related Developments

  • The FFPI measures monthly changes in international prices of five globally traded commodity groups— cereals, vegetable oils, meat, dairy products and sugar—weighted by their average export shares during the 2014–2016 base period.
  • It reflects international commodity prices rather than domestic retail food prices.
  • The Cereal Price Index averaged 113.8 points, rising 3.4% monthly and 6.9% annually.
  • Wheat prices increased 5.8% due to Black Sea export disruptions, infrastructure damage and heatwaves affecting production.
  • Maize prices also rose amid hot, dry weather in parts of the United States and higher energy costs.
  • The Vegetable Oil Price Index increased 2.0%, reaching its highest level since June 2022.
  • Higher palm and soybean oil prices reflected strong biodiesel demand, rising crude-oil prices and increased consumption.
  • The Sugar Price Index rose 5.6%, driven by adverse weather in Europe and Asia and expectations of increased sugarcane diversion towards ethanol production in Brazil.
  • Meat prices declined 2.8% from their June record high, while dairy prices fell 0.7%, reflecting greater export availability and weaker demand for certain products.
  • Higher international food prices can contribute to domestic inflation and complicate the Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI) monetary policy management. World Investment Report 2026 The World Investment Report 2026, titled International Investment in a Turbulent Era, was released on July 7, 2026. Global foreign direct investment (FDI) rose by 6% to approximately US$1.6 trillion in 2025, ending two consecutive years of decline.
  • The report is the principal annual publication of the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), published since 1991.
  • UNCTAD is now publicly known as UN Trade and Development.
  • It examines investment flows, multinational enterprises, investment policies and sustainable development.
  • FDI is cross: border investment intended to establish a lasting interest and significant managerial influence. At least 10% of voting power generally indicates this relationship.
  • Unlike portfolio investment, it normally involves long-term influence, technology and capital transfers, and productive assets.
  • India’s inward FDI rose nearly 44%, from approximately US$27.1 billion in 2024 to US$38.9 billion in 2025, improving its rank from 13th to 11th.
  • Outward FDI increased from approximately US$24.3 billion to US$35.7 billion, improving its rank from 20th to 18th.
  • At the end of 2025, inward and outward FDI stocks were approximately US$559 billion and US$296.4 billion.
  • Outward growth indicates Indian companies’ international expansion.
  • Inward inflows remained below 2021 and 2022 levels.
  • UNCTAD publishes the World Investment Report, Trade and Development Report, Digital Economy Report, Technology and Innovation Report, Least Developed Countries Report, Economic Development in Africa Report, Review of Maritime Transport, and Commodities and Development Report.
  • The top five destination economies by FDI inflows are: Rank Economy FDI Inflows (2025) 1 United States $277 billion 2 Singapore $151 billion 3 Hong Kong, China $116 billion 4 China $105 billion 5 Brazil $77 billion
  • The top five investing nations driving India's FDI inflows: Rank Country of Origin Key Share & Characteristics 1 Singapore Dominates both cumulative inflows (~25%) and recent cycles, contributing up to 34%–37% of recent periodic equity. 2 Mauritius Historically the top source, holding ~23% of cumulative FDI, though newer fiscal rules have slightly adjusted its routing dominance. 3 United States Represents roughly 10% of total inflows, with concentrated investments in technology, IT, and startup ecosystems. 4 Japan Stays highly active, frequently combining with Singapore to supply substantial portions of quarterly capital for automotive and infrastructure. 5 Netherlands / UAE Trade places dynamically around the fifth spot, driven by heavy routing into manufacturing, green energy, and logistics channels. US–Saudi Arabia Civil Nuclear Cooperation Agreement 2026 The United States and Saudi Arabia signed a Section 123 Civil Nuclear Cooperation Agreement in July 2026. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright signed on 20 July (Washington) and Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman on 22 July (Riyadh).  Key Highlights
  • Legal Basis: Section 123 of the US Atomic Energy Act, 1954. Preliminary cooperation began in 2008, with negotiations concluding on 18 November 2025.
  • Duration: 30 years after entry into force, following completion of domestic procedures and exchange of diplomatic notes (Article 16).
  • Nuclear Safeguards: Restricts military use, unauthorised transfers, enrichment and reprocessing.
  • Uranium Enrichment: Article 7 provides for a two-year joint study ; subsequent enrichment requires written consent and safeguards.
  • Gold Standard: Unlike the 2009 US–United Arab Emirates agreement , Saudi Arabia has not renounced enrichment and reprocessing.
  • IAEA Protocol: The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) Additional Protocol is not mandatory. A separate bilateral safeguards agreement was signed. Saudi Arabia withdrew its Small Quantities Protocol on December 31, 2024.
  • Congressional Review: Trump submitted the agreement on 24 August 2026, triggering statutory 30- and 60-day review periods . Senators Jeff Merkley and Edward Markey introduced S.J. Res. 221 on 15 October seeking disapproval.
  • Abraham Accords: Trump publicly linked the agreement to Saudi participation, but the published text contains no such condition. Two con昀椀dential side letters remain undisclosed. US and Iranian Initial Peace Agreement On June 17, 2026, the United States and Iran signed a historic initial peace agreement—formalised via a 14-point Memorandum of Understanding (MoU)— aimed at ending the four-month West Asia war.
  • The agreement was signed electronically by US President Donald Trump and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian; the interim pact serves primarily as a comprehensive ceasefire to halt active military operations and stave off global economic depression.
  • However, the agreement is facing immense strain, highlighted by Iran’s declaration that it is closing the Strait of Hormuz due to ongoing Israeli strikes in Lebanon.  Key Terms of the 14-Point MoU
  • Termination of Hostilities: An immediate and permanent end to military operations on all fronts, explicitly including the conflict in Lebanon
  • Strait of Hormuz Reopening: Free, toll-free passage through the crucial energy shipping corridor is restored to full capacity within 30 days.
  • Sanctions Relief: The US Department of the Treasury must immediately issue waivers allowing Iran to export crude oil, petroleum products, and access associated banking and transportation services.
  • Reconstruction Fund: A framework with regional partners to develop an economic development plan for Iran worth at least $300 billion. White House officials noted that Gulf Arab nations are expected to finance the fund, and the US will not contribute directly.
  • Unfreezing Assets: The US commits to unblocking restricted Iranian funds and assets abroad, with Tehran seeking the return of approximately $24 billion.
  • Nuclear Constraints: Iran is required to halt further enrichment and “down-blend” (dilute) its existing highly enriched uranium stocks to 3.67% under IAEA monitoring.
  • The 60: Day Window: The initial arrangement sets up a 60-day technical negotiation period to secure a final, legally binding nuclear pact endorsed by the UN Security Council. IRan–ISRael ConflICT
  • On February 28, 2026 , joint U.S.: Israeli attacks pushed the conflict into a new phase.
  • The United States called it Operation Epic Fury, while Israel called it Operation Roaring Lion.
  • After these strikes, Iran presented its missile and drone attacks as successive waves of “Operation True Promise.”
  • Earlier, in June 2025, Israel had carried out a 12-day campaign called Operation Rising Lion targeting Iranian nuclear and military infrastructures including Tehran, Natanz, Tabriz, and Kermanshah.
  • The most inhuman face of the war was seen in the attack on Shajarah Tayyibeh Girls’ School in Minab, southern Iran, where a large number of girls were killed.
  • Iran targeted over 17 key U.S. sites in the Gulf region, including the 5th Fleet Headquarters in Bahrain.  Ali Khamenei
  • Ali Khamenei, Iran’s Supreme Leader since 1989, was assassinated in Tehran on February 28, 2026, during a joint US-Israeli strike.
  • Following this, his son, Mojtaba Khamenei , was announced as the new Supreme Leader on March 9, 2026, selected by the Assembly of Experts.
  • High: level U.S.–Iran talks took place in Islamabad on April 11–12, 2026, and ended without a deal.  Strait of Hormuz and Strait of Malacca:
  • The Strait of Hormuz, located between Iran and Oman, connects the Persian Gulf to the Arabian Sea.
  • It is the world’s most important oil transit chokepoint.
  • The Strait of Malacca, located between Malaysia, Indonesia, and Singapore , connects the Indian Ocean to the South China Sea.  It is the shortest sea route between the Middle East and East Asia.  Kharg Island
  • Another important dimension is Kharg Island , Iran’s principal oil export terminal in the Persian Gulf.  Handles nearly 90% of Iran’s crude oil exports.
  • On 17 April 2026 , the UK and France co-chaired an international meeting on the S trait of Hormuz Maritime Navigation / Freedom of Navigation Initiative, with 51 countries participating to support free navigation through the Strait of Hormuz.  U.S. Joins the Fray
  • In June 2025, in a dramatic escalation of hostilities, Israel launched Operation Rising Lion , a series of coordinated airstrikes and drone attacks targeting Iran’s nuclear and military infrastructure.
  • Key targets included in this operation were the Natanz uranium enrichment facility, a nuclear research center in Tehran; military bases in Tabriz; and an underground missile storage site in Kermanshah.
  • This pre: emptive operation aimed to halt Iran’s progress toward acquiring nuclear weapons.
  • In response, Iran launched Operation True Promise 3, firing ballistic missiles at Israeli targets, with explosions reported in Jerusalem and Tel Aviv, marking a major regional escalation.
  • The United States formally entered the conflict with precision airstrikes on Iran’s major nuclear installations—Fordow, Natanz, and Isfahan — using B-2 stealth bombers armed with bunker- buster bombs.
  • The official U.S. name for the strike on Iranian nuclear sites was Operation Midnight Hammer.
  • In response to growing tensions, the Government of India launched Operation Sindhu.
  • India has a strong track record in such operations, as seen during the 1990–91 Gulf War , the Libya crisis, and Operation Ganga in Ukraine (2022).  Modi Becomes First Leader Honoured by Israel and Palestine
  • PM Narendra Modi became the first leader to receive top honours from both Israel and Palestine.
  • He was awarded the Speaker of the Knesset Medal (Israel’s highest parliamentary honour) on February 25, 2026.
  • The award was presented by Amir Ohana at the Knesset in Jerusalem.
  • Earlier, in 2018, he received the Grand Collar of the State of Palestine from Mahmoud Abbas. The Global Risks Report 2026 The Global Risks Report 2026 is the 21st edition of the World Economic Forum’s annual report and was published on January 14, 2026, warns that the world is entering an “Age of Competition”—a phase where geopolitical rivalry, economic weaponization, technology disruption and climate stress are interacting and creating cascading crises.
  • The World Economic Forum defines a global risk as an event or condition that can cause a significant negative impact on:  Global GDP  World population  Natural resources and ecosystems
  • Such risks are cross: border, interconnected, and capable of triggering cascading crises.
  • The report is built mainly on:  Global Risks Perception Survey (GRPS) for global-level risk severity and interconnections.  Executive Opinion Survey (EOS) for country- level “national risk perceptions”.
  • The report uses three time horizons: immediate (2026), short-to-medium term (to 2028), and long term (to 2036).  Top 5 Global Risks ranked by severity
  • Short term (2 years):  Geo-economic confrontation  Misinformation & disinformation  Societal polarization  Extreme weather events  State-based armed conflict
  • Long term (10 years):  Extreme weather events  Biodiversity loss & ecosystem collapse  Critical change to Earth systems  Misinformation & disinformation  Adverse outcomes of AI technologies
  • Inequality is shown as the most interconnected global risk (linked strongly with economic and social risks).  India’s Risk Outlook
  • For India, EOS 2025 identifies the following five risks, in descending order of selection frequency, over the next two years.  Cyber insecurity ranks first.  Inequality of wealth and income ranks second.  Insufficient public services and social protections, including education, infrastructure and pensions, rank third.  Economic downturn, including recession or stagnation, ranks fourth.  State-based armed conflict ranks fifth. Asia Manufacturing Index, 2026 On January 12, 2026, the Asia Manufacturing Index (AMI) 2026, published by Dezan Shira & Associates, places India in 6th position among 11 Asian economies.  Performance of Other Asian Economies Rank Country Key Strength 1 China Strong industrial base and integrated supply chains 2 Malaysia Policy reforms and investor-friendly environment 3 Vietnam Export-driven manufacturing growth 4 Singapore Advanced infrastructure and innovation 5 South Korea High-technology manufacturing 6 India Market size and workforce strength The World Inequality Report 2026 In December 2025 , the World Inequality Report 2026 (3rd edition), published by the World Inequali ty Lab and edited by economists like Thomas Piketty and Lucas Chancel, revealed that global economic and environmental disparities remain at an extreme and persistent level.
  • The report highlights unprecedented concentration of wealth at the global level:  The top 10% of the global population controls nearly 75% of total wealth, while the bottom 50% owns only 2%.  The top 1% holds around 37% of global wealth, exceeding the combined wealth of the bottom half of the world.  The wealthiest 0.001% (about 60,000 individuals) possess three times more wealth than the poorest 50% globally.
  • The report identifies India as one of the most unequal countries globally.  The top 10% earns 58% of national income.  The bottom 50% receives only 15% of income.  The disparity has widened compared to earlier assessments.  The richest 10% owns about 65% of national wealth.  The top 1% alone holds around 40% of total wealth.  Average annual income per capita: €6,200 (PPP).  Average wealth per capita: €28,000 (PPP).
  • These figures highlight that while India has witnessed economic growth, wealth creation remains highly concentrated.
  • Globally, women earn 61% of men’s wages when unpaid work hours are excluded.
  • When unpaid care work is included, women earn only 32% of male income.
  • Women receive just 28.2% of global labour income, showing minimal progress over decades.
  • India’s female labour income share was 15.7% in both 2014 and 2024, reflecting structural barriers such as social norms, skill gaps, and unpaid care responsibilities.
  • The report introduces climate inequality as a major global concern:  The top 10% contributes 77% of emissions linked to private capital ownership.  The poorest 50% contributes only 3% of such emissions.  The wealthiest 1% is responsible for 41% of emissions, almost double that of the bottom 90%.
  • This indicates that those contributing least to climate change face the highest vulnerability, raising issues of climate justice and equity. C. International Conferences/Summits/Organisations
  • The report highlights systemic financial imbalances:  Approximately 1% of global GDP annually flows from poorer to richer nations through financial and investment mechanisms.  Developed countries benefit from lower borrowing costs and higher investment returns, reinforcing global economic hierarchy. Commitment to Development Index (CDI) 2025 The Commitment to Development Index (CDI) 2025, released by the Center for Global Development on November 20, 2025, measures how major economies support or hinder development in poorer countries through policies that go beyond foreign aid.

EU Signs Association Agreement with Andorra and San Marino On October 19, 2026, the European Commission, on behalf of the European Union (EU) , signed an Association Agreement with Andorra and San Marino in Brussels, Belgium . It aims to integrate these European microstates into the EU Single Market without granting EU membership.  Key Highlights
  • Nature and Scope: The Mixed Agreement involves the EU, its member states, Andorra and San Marino. It provides for the free movement of goods, services, capital and persons , subject to agreed conditions.
  • Financial Services: Market access will be phased in after regulatory assessments by the European Supervisory Authorities (ESAs) . Cooperation also covers research, education, environment and consumer protection.
  • Negotiation Timeline: Talks began in 2015 under December 2014 Council directives. Negotiations with Monaco were suspended in September 2023, while those with Andorra and San Marino concluded in December 2023.
  • Approval Process: The European Commission submitted proposals on 26 April 2024. The Council of the EU authorised signing and provisional application on 16 July 2026.
  • Legal Status: Under Article 112(3) , provisional application may begin separately with either country after prescribed procedures. Full implementation requires necessary approvals, including European Parliament consent . Provisional application remained uncon昀椀rmed as of 21 October 2026.
  • Monetary Agreements: Andorra ( 2011) and San Marino ( 2012) use the euro through monetary agreements without euro-area membership. They may issue limited national-design euro coins but not banknotes. Updated agreements were also signed.
  • EEA Plus: European Commission Executive Vice- President Maroš Šefčovič informally described the arrangement as “EEA Plus” in December 2023. EEA means European Economic Area; its of昀椀cial legal designation remains Association Agreement. FAO’s 28th Committee on Forestry Session 2026 The 28th Session of the Committee on Forestry (COFO) of the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) was held from 28 September to 2 October 2026 in Rome, Italy , under the theme “Forests for Food, Resilience and Prosperity.” The 10th World Forest Week was organised alongside it.  Key Highlights
  • About COFO: Established in 1971 at the 16th FAO Conference, it is FAO’s highest intergovernmental forestry body, comprising 128 members, including the European Union. It meets biennially and reports to the FAO Council on budgetary matters and FAO Conference on policy matters.

UN Scienti昀椀c Panel Releases First Global AI Assessment 2026 On July 1, 2026, the United Nations-established Independent International Scienti昀椀c Panel on Arti昀椀cial Intelligence (AI) released its 昀椀rst Preliminary Report: Evidence-based Assessment of Opportunities, Risks and Impacts of AI.

The assessment informed the inaugural & Related Developments

  • The assessment informed the inaugural UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance, held in Geneva, Switzerland, on 6–7 July 2026.
  • The report warns that AI capabilities are advancing faster than scientific understanding, independent evaluation and governance safeguards.
  • Created under UN General Assembly Resolution A/RES/79/325 of 26 August 2025, following the Global Digital Compact, the Panel comprises 40 independent experts from all five UN regional groups, appointed for three-year terms.
  • Co-Chairs: Yoshua Bengio (Canada), recipient of the 2018 Turing Award, and Maria Ressa (Philippines), recipient of the 2021 Nobel Peace Prize.
  • The Panel provides independent, non: prescriptive scientific assessments of non-military AI applications; it has no regulatory or enforcement powers.
  • In 2025, US institutions produced 59 notable AI models, China 35 and the rest of the world 13.
  • The private sector accounted for 91% of notable models.

  • On August 26, 2026, a catastrophic flash flood struck Nepal’s Rasuwa district near the Nepal–China border, sweeping through the Lhende Khola–Bhote Koshi–Trishuli river system.
  • The debris: laden flood damaged settlements, roads, bridges, hydropower projects and communication networks.
  • According to the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD), a slope failure on Langtang Lirung triggered a massive rock–ice avalanche that entered the Lhende Khola catchment.
  • The avalanche generated a debris: rich flood, potentially involving temporary river obstruction or displacement followed by sudden water release.
  • At Galchhi, the Trishuli River reportedly rose approximately nine metres within 30 minutes. Several monitoring stations were damaged or destroyed.
  • Initially considered a possible Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF) or earthquake-related disaster, the event was subsequently identified primarily as a rock–ice avalanche-induced cascading hazard, rather than a conventional GLOF.
  • India deployed NDRF teams in Bihar and Uttar Pradesh and provided specialised tunnel-rescue personnel and a 19-member forensic team for DNA identification, strengthening bilateral Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Relief (HADR) cooperation.
  • A GLOF occurs when a glacial lake suddenly releases water following the failure of its natural ice or moraine dam. Colombia Declares Emergency After 7.4-Magnitude Earthquake On August 10, 2026, a powerful 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck western Colombia, with its epicentre near San José del Palmar in Chocó Department, at a depth of approximately 103 km.
  • The Colombian Geological Service (SGC) described it as the country’s largest-magnitude earthquake of the 21st century.
  • Colombia lies in north: western South America, bordering both the Pacific Ocean and Caribbean Sea.
  • Its seismic activity is influenced by the interaction of the Nazca, South American and Caribbean tectonic plates.
  • Along Colombia’s Pacific margin, the oceanic Nazca Plate subducts beneath the continental South American Plate.
  • This convergence generates tectonic stress, causing earthquakes, crustal deformation and volcanic activity.
  • Colombia is part of the Circum: Pacific Belt, extending approximately 40,000 km around the Pacific Ocean.
  • This tectonically active region experiences frequent earthquakes and volcanic eruptions due to convergent plate boundaries and subduction zones.
  • The subduction of the Nazca Plate beneath the South American Plate produces compression, crustal folding and uplift, contributing to the formation of the Andes Mountains.
  • Fluids released from the descending plate also promote magma formation and volcanism. Fiscal & Monetary Affairs Strategic Restructuring of IDBI Bank On October 14, 2026 , the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA) , chaired by the Prime Minister, approved 10955230 Canada Inc., whose parent company is Fairfax Financial Holdings Limited, as the buyer for the strategic sale of a 60.72% stake in IDBI Bank Limited. The approved purchase consideration is approximately ₹52,878.08 crore. This decision marks an important stage in the transfer of the bank’s ownership and management control; completion of the transaction remains subject to compliance with further regulatory conditions.  Background of the Bank
  • IDBI was originally known as the Industrial Development Bank of India . It came into existence as a development 昀椀nance institution on 1 July 1964, and its undertaking was transferred to a banking company with effect from 1 October 2004.
  • IDBI Bank is a scheduled commercial bank regulated by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) . Following LIC’s acquisition of 51% of its paid-up equity capital , the RBI classi昀椀ed it as a private sector bank for regulatory purposes with effect from 21 January 2019. Indicative Shareholding Based on the Approved Main Transaction Shareholder Before the sale Stake to be sold After the main sale Government of India 45.48% 30.48% Approximately 15% LIC 49.24% 30.24% Approximately 19%  Key Features of the Approved Transaction
  • The strategic buyer is 10955230 Canada Inc., whose parent company is Fairfax Financial Holdings Limited.
  • The total approved stake is 60.72%, and the purchase consideration is ₹52,878.08 crore.
  • The Government of India will sell a 30.48% stake, while LIC will sell a 30.24% stake. The sale proceeds will be distributed in the corresponding proportion.
  • The approved bid is ₹81 per share, compared with the benchmark of ₹75.99 per share , calculated as the average of two independent valuations. 57th GST Council Meeting The 57th meeting of the GST Council was held in New Delhi on October 8, 2026 , chaired by Union Minister for Finance and Corporate Affairs Nirmala Sitharaman.
  • The Council recommended simplifying the registration application, FORM GST REG-01 , issuing clear guidelines on the documents required and making the portal more user-friendly.
  • Automatic approval of amendments to registration particulars, other than the Principal Place of Business (PPoB), has been proposed.
  • A simpli昀椀ed registration mechanism for small e-commerce sellers has been proposed under Rule 14B.
  • Reforms have been proposed to improve the reconciliation of tax liability and Input Tax Credit (ITC) across GSTR-1, GSTR-1A, GSTR-2B and GSTR-3B.
  • The Council recommended automating refunds of excess balances in the electronic cash ledger and reducing the time limit for issuing an acknowledgement or de昀椀ciency memo for refund applications from 15 days to 10 days.
  • The inclusion of ITC on input services received on or after 1 November 2026 has been recommended for eligible inverted duty structure refunds.
  • ITC on eligible capital goods received on or after 1 April 2027 is proposed to be included in the calculation of refunds of unutilised ITC arising from.
  • A minimum tax amount of ₹10,000 has been recommended for issuing a show-cause notice. Reserve Bank of India’s Monetary Policy (October, 2026)
  • The 63rd meeting of the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) was held from October 5 to 7, 2026, chaired by RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra.
  • The Committee unanimously decided to increase the repo rate under the Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF) by 25 basis points, raising it from 5.25% to 5.50%.   • In its October review, the RBI projected real GDP growth of 7.1% for FY 2026–27. This is a forecast for the full 昀椀nancial year. The base year of the current GDP series is 2022–23.  In昀氀ation and Major Risks
  • According to the data used in the policy review, CPI in昀氀ation rose from 4.5% in July 2026 to 4.8% in August.
  • The Committee projected CPI in昀氀ation at 5.2% and core in昀氀ation at 4.4% for FY 2026–27.
  • In a subsequent update, MoSPI released September CPI in昀氀ation data on 12 October 2026, reporting headline in昀氀ation of 5.54% and food in昀氀ation of 7.74%. Both 昀椀gures are provisional. The CPI base year is 2024=100. This release came after the October monetary policy decision.
  • For the period from 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2031, the in昀氀ation target is 4%, with a lower tolerance limit of 2% and an upper tolerance limit of 6%. The target was noti昀椀ed by the Government in consultation with the RBI.
  • The next MPC meeting is scheduled for 2–4 December 2026.Registration of Births and Deaths (Amendment) Act, 2026 The Registration of Births and Deaths (Amendment) Act, 2026 amended Section 13 of the Registration of Births and Deaths Act, 1969, specifying the competent authorities for cases reported more than one year after the event. The amendment came into force on October 1, 2026.  Key Details of the Act
  • It received presidential assent on August 6, 2026.
  • Section 2 of the Amendment Act substituted the existing Section 13(3) of the principal Act with new subsections 13(3) and 13(3A).
  • The Of昀椀ce of the Registrar General, India , under the Ministry of Home Affairs, appointed 1 October 2026 as the commencement date through Noti昀椀cation S.O. 5081(E), dated 16 September 2026. The noti昀椀cation was issued under Section 1(2) of the Amendment Act.  New Framework for Delayed Registration
  • Information reported after one year but within two years: Under Section 13(3) , registration may take place only on an order of the District Magistrate, Sub-Divisional Magistrate or an Executive Magistrate authorised by the District Magistrate.
  • Information reported after more than two years: Under Section 13(3A) , registration requires an order of a Judicial Magistrate of the First Class.
  • Jurisdiction: The Magistrate issuing the order must have jurisdiction over the place where the birth or death occurred.  Previous Framework and the Change
  • Following the 2023 amendment , registration of all births and deaths reported more than one year after the event required an order of the District Magistrate, Sub-Divisional Magistrate or an authorised Executive Magistrate. The 2026 amendment speci昀椀es different authorities for delays of more than one year but within two years, and more than two years.  Other Provisions
  • Births and deaths are ordinarily required to be reported within 21 days . Registration after the ordinary reporting period but within 30 days attracts a late fee. PMJDY Completes 12 Years The Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (PMJDY) completed 12 years on August 28, 2026, expanding access to formal banking and 昀椀nancial services among underserved and economically disadvantaged sections.  Key Facts and Background
  • Prime Minister Narendra Modi launched PMJDY on 28 August 2014 as India’s National Mission for Financial Inclusion.
  • India’s Financial Inclusion Index increased from 53.9 in 2021 to 67 in March 2025.
  • In January 2015, Guinness World Records recognised 18,096,130 bank accounts opened in a single week (from August 23-29, 2014) under the Department of Financial Services campaign.  Major Features and Bene昀椀ts
  • Eligible account holders receive a RuPay debit card, accepted at ATMs and most Point-of-Sale terminals. Banks had issued 41.29 crore cards by 19 August 2026, promoting digital payments.
  • Accident insurance cover increased from ₹1 lakh to ₹2 lakh for new accounts opened after August 28, 2018.
  • An overdraft of up to ₹10,000 is available to one eligible account holder per household, ordinarily after six months of satisfactory account operation and subject to prescribed conditions.  Progress so Far
  • Accounts increased approximately fourfold from 14.72 crore in 2015 to 59.09 crore by 19 August 2026. Rural and semi-urban areas held 45.95 crore accounts, or 77.8%, while urban and metropolitan areas held 13.14 crore.
  • Women held 32.92 crore accounts, or approximately 55.7% of the total, as of 19 August 2026, reflecting greater gender equality in formal financial access.
  • Deposits increased approximately twentyfold from ₹15,670 crore in March 2015 to ₹3,16,514 crore in August 2026. Average deposits reached ₹5,356 per account on 19 August 2026. CBDC-Based Food Subsidy Distribution under PMGKAY The Government of India has introduced a Central Bank Digital Currency-based Direct Bene昀椀t Transfer (CBDC-based DBT) system under the Pradhan Mantri Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana (PMGKAY) . Under this model, eligible bene昀椀ciaries receive food subsidies as programmable Digital Rupee tokens in their CBDC wallets instead of receiving the subsidy through conventional bank-account transfers.  Background
  • The Digital Rupee , also known as the e₹ or e-rupee, is a tokenised digital form of the Indian rupee issued by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) as a Central Bank Digital Currency.
  • Chandigarh was among the early adopters of food- subsidy DBT in September 2015 , when it shifted from physical distribution of subsidised foodgrains to direct subsidy transfers into bene昀椀ciaries’ Aadhaar-linked bank accounts.
  • CBDC based food subsidy was initiated on a pilot basis on February 15, 2026 by Home Minister Amit Shah in Gujarat and later on February 26, 2026 by Prahlad Joshi in Pducherry as a pilot initiative.
  • The Government launched CBDC: based DBT for PMGKAY bene昀椀ciaries in Chandigarh and Dadra & Nagar Haveli on August 14, 2026.
  • The initiative was launched by Union Minister for Agriculture and Farmers’ Welfare Shivraj Singh Chouhan. India’s Proposed `10 and `20 Polymer Banknotes The Government of India has approved a proposal by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) for 昀椀eld trials of ₹10 and ₹20 polymer banknotes.  Key Facts
  • The RBI proposed one billion notes of each denomination, totalling 200 crore notes with a face value of approximately ₹3,000 crore. The Government informed Parliament of the approval in 2026, when procurement remained at an initial stage. Regular issuance may be considered only after successful trials.
  • The RBI submitted the proposal under Sections 24 and 25 of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, following its Central Board’s recommendation. Section 24 covers the banknote denominations whereas Section 25 covers design, form and materials. Bharatiya Reserve Bank Note Mudran Private Limited (BRBNMPL), an RBI subsidiary, initiated polymer-substrate procurement.
  • Polymer banknotes use a non: fibrous, non-porous plastic film. Existing Indian paper banknotes use long cotton fibres from cotton comber and cotton linter.
  • Polymer notes will circulate alongside existing ₹10 and ₹20 paper notes, which will remain legal tender. Trials will assess cleanliness, security, handling and suitability for India’s cash economy.  Global Experience
  • Australia first issued a polymer banknote in 1988. More than 60 countries reportedly use polymer currency, including Canada, the United Kingdom, New Zealand and Singapore.  Currency in Circulation
  • According to the supplied RBI figures, currency in circulation rose 12% year-on-year to ₹41.23 lakh crore (banknotes alone excluding coins) at the end of March 2026 ( ₹40,814 coins in circulation). ₹500 notes represented approximately 86% of banknotes’ total value. Printing expenditure reportedly fell nearly 24% to ₹4,875 crore in 2025–26, mainly because of lower printing requirements. Bankers’ Books Evidence Act, 2026 The Bankers’ Books Evidence Act, 2026 came into force on October 1, 2026. The Act replaces the Bankers’ Books Evidence Act, 1891 with a technology-neutral framework recognising physical, electronic and digi tal banking records as evidence. The de昀椀nition of bankers’ books includes records at off site, virtual, cloud, backup and disaster recovery locations. Banks and bankers also include post of昀椀ce savings bank and money order of昀椀ces.  Legislative Background
  • The Lok Sabha passed the Bill on 5 August 2026 and the Rajya Sabha on 10 August. Presidential assent followed on 13 August 2026.  Major Provisions
  • The first schedule applies to copies of books maintained in written or physical form. The second schedule applies to copies of books maintained electronically, digitally or through other data storage mechanism.
  • Certification of Banking Records: Certificates must confirm accuracy and be authenticated manually, digitally or electronically by an authorised bank officer.
  • Conditions for Digital Records: Digital records are admissible if created and stored in the ordinary course of banking through regularly used, properly functioning systems.
  • Evidentiary Value: Certified copies are prima facie, not conclusive, evidence where original entries are legally admissible.
  • Extension to Financial: Sector Entities – The Central Government may extend coverage by notification. NBFCs, payment aggregators and fintech firms are covered only if notified or under another law.
  • Legal Proceedings and Production of Records
  • Proceedings include court cases, arbitration, investigations and inquiries. Indian Statistical Institute Bill 2026 Introduced in the Lok Sabha on 3 August 2026, the Indian Statistical Institute Bill, 2026 seeks to replace the 1959 Act (came into force on April 1, 1960). It would convert ISI into a statutory body corporate while retaining its status as an institution of national importance.  Change in Legal Status
  • Body: corporate status would provide clearer legal authority and institutional continuity. ISI would remain under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation.  Key Highlights
  • The President of India would be the Visitor, empowered to order reviews or inquiries and issue binding directions. The Visitor would nominate the Board’s Chairperson on the Centre’s recommendation.
  • Admission and Reservation: Admissions would follow transparent, merit-based criteria without discrimination.

Economic Affairs · Part 2

  • An 11: member Board would replace the 33-member Council as the principal policy-making and executive body, accountable to the Centre. It would comprise the Chairperson, government representatives, four external experts and four ISI representatives.
  • The Board would approve budgets, plans, fees and regulations, reorganise academic units and award degrees on the Academic Council’s recommendation.
  • The Director: led Academic Council would include Centre-Directors, all full-time Professors, selected faculty and the Dean of Academic Affairs.
  • Director: The Director would be the Chief Executive Officer, managing daily administration and implementing institutional decisions.
  • ISI may receive government grants after parliamentary appropriation, earn revenue, accept donations and maintain funds. VB – G RAM G Act, 2025 The Viksit Bharat – Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act, 2025, or VB-G RAM G Act, is India’s statutory framework for rural wag e employment and village development. It came into force across rural India on July 1, 2026, repealing the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, 2005 (MGNREGA).  About the News
  • Rural Development Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan released over ₹25,000 crore as the first installment, called the Mother Sanction, to support timely wage payments. A total ₹7.5 lakh crore (as on July, 2026) will be invested in 2.86 lakh Panchayats over the next five years. Wage rates have increased by around 10 percent on average.
  • The Act guarantees wage employment, strengthens village economies and promotes sustainable livelihoods. It links employment with productive public assets, transparency, convergence, climate resilience and local economic development, following “Rozgar Bhi, Samman Bhi”, or employment with dignity.  Key Features of the VB-G RAM G Act
  • The Act increases the employment guarantee from 100 to 125 days per financial year for rural households whose adult members volunteer for unskilled manual work.
  • The notified minimum wage floor for 2026–27 is ₹300 per day.
  • Wages should be paid weekly or within fifteen days of work and muster-roll closure measures delayed compensation.
  • Delays attract compensation of 0.05 percent of unpaid wages per day beyond the sixteenth day after closure.
  • Existing e: KYC-verified job cards remain valid until Gramin Rozgar Guarantee Cards are issued. Workers may register at Gram Panchayats, and pending e-KYC cannot justify denial of employment.
  • Work may be demanded orally, through Form-6 or digitally.
  • Failure to provide employment within the prescribed timeframe entitles workers to unemployment allowance of at least one-fourth of the notified wage for the first thirty days of the financial year and one-half for the remaining period.
  • Four Priority Areas: Water security; Rural infrastructure; Livelihood infrastructure; Climate resilience.
  • Funding Pattern: The Act operates as a Centrally Sponsored Scheme, with a 90:10 funding ratio for Northeastern and Himalayan States (like Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh and Jammu & Kashmir); and it is 60 : 40 for other States and UTs with legislatures.
  • UTs without legislatures receive full Central funding. Central allocations follow objective, rule- based parameters. States bear expenditure beyond normative allocations and must distribute funds transparently according to local needs.
  • Budgetary Commitment: For FY 2026–27, the Central share is ₹95,692.31 crore, described as the largest Budget Estimate allocation for a rural employment programme. Including the estimated State share, total outlay is expected to exceed ₹1.51 lakh crore. Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code Completes 10 Years The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 completed ten year milestone in 2026 (It was enacted on May 28, 2016 ). Over the last decade, the IBC has moved India’s insolvency regime away from delay-based liquidation towards corporate revival and preservation of enterprise value. The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India was established on October 1, 2016.  Resolution and Recovery Performance
  • As of March 31, 2026, a total of 1,419 cases had resulted in approved resolution plans under the IBC.
  • The IBC resolution process has facilitated realisation of more than `4 lakh crore for creditors.
  • The amount realised by creditors was around 95 percent of the fair value of the assets.
  • The amount realised was also around 167 percent of the liquidation value, showing that resolution under the IBC helped preserve enterprise value.
  • Till March 31, 2026, a total of 8,987 cases had been admitted under the IBC framework.
  • Out of these admitted cases, 7,102 cases had reached closure.
  • Among the closed cases, 4,099 companies were successfully rescued.
  • For Domestic Operations gross NPA ratio of the Scheduled Commercial Banks stood at 2.15 percent as of September 30, 2025.
  • Scheduled Commercial Banks recovered a total of `1.04 lakh crore through various recovery channels for FY 2024-25.

Out of this, nearly `0.54 & Related Developments

  • Out of this, nearly `0.54 lakh crore was realised through the IBC process.
  • This means that about 52.4 percent of total recoveries by Scheduled Commercial Banks came through the IBC route. 10 Years of UPI On April 11, 2026, the Uni昀椀ed Payments Interface (UPI) completed 10 years since its pilot launch in 2016. UPI has evolved from a digital payment experiment into the backbone of India’s digital economy. It recorded an all-time high of 22.64 billion transactions in March 2026 (It accounted for more than 81% of India’s volume of total retail payment transaction in FY 2024-25).
  • UPI recorded 24.51 billion transactions in August, 2026. The reform aims to modernise India’s tax system and make it more aligned with current economic realities. It simplifies language, structure and tax compliance while improving the efficiency of ta x administration.  Key Highlights  Operational and Structural Changes
  • The Central Board of Direct Taxes has notified the Income-tax Rules, 2026 to implement the provisions of the new Act.
  • A major procedural reform is the introduction of Form 130, which replaces the traditional Form 16 (TDS certificate issued by employers).
  • The act replaces the concepts of ‘Assessment Year (AY)’ and ‘Previous Year’ with ‘Tax Year’. The Financial Year (FY) continues to remain relevant in the Act.
  • A single unified concept called the “Tax Year” has been introduced for simplification.
