  • According to the Central Board of Direct Taxes, India’s gross direct tax collection for 2025–26 stood at `7.99 lakh crore. Report of the 16th Finance Commission (2026–31) The Finance Commission is a constitutional body under Article 280 of the Constitution, constituted by the President every five years (or earlier) to recommend the principles governing Centre–State fiscal relations.
  • The 16 th Finance Commission was constituted on December 31, 2023 under the Chairmanship of Dr. Arvind Panagariya (Article 280).  Key Highlights
  • The 16 th Finance Commission covers the period 2026–27 to 2030–31 . It submitted its report on 17 November 2025, and it was tabled in Parliament on 1 February 2026.
  • The Commission has not recommended three grant categories recommended by the 15th Finance Commission, namely revenue deficit grants, sector- specific grants, and state-specific grants.
  • The Commission has recommended that the States’ vertical share remain 41% of the divisible pool of Union taxes.  The weights are 42.5% for per-capita income distance (GSDP), 17.5% for population (2011), 10% for demographic performance, 10% for area, 10% for forest, and 10% for contribution to GDP .
  • The Commission has recommended total grants of about `9.47 lakh crore for 2026–31. Of this, about `7.91 lakh crore is for local bodies and `1.56 lakh crore is the Union share for disaster management grants.
  • The Commission has recommended a Special Infrastructure Component of `56,100 crore for selected urban local bodies for comprehensive wastewater management in urban growth centres.
  • It has also recommended an Urbanisation Premium of `10,000 crore for the full award period.
  • The Commission has recommended a total disaster management corpus of `2,04,401 crore for SDRF and SDMF together for 2026–31.
  • The Commission has recommended that the Centre reduce its fiscal deficit to 3.5% of GDP by 2030–31.
  • It has recommended that the States’ annual fiscal deficit ceiling remain 3% of GSDP excluding loans under Special Assistane to States for Capital Investment (SASCI).

Key Policy Documents/Events National Social Assistance Programme On October 14, 2026 , the Union Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi , approved the continuation of the National Social Assistance Programme (NSAP) from FY 2026–27 to FY 2030–31, with a total outlay of ₹53,428 crore over 昀椀ve years.
  • The programme provides basic assistance to elderly persons, widows and persons with disabilities from poor households, as well as families affected by the death of their primary breadwinner. It was launched on 15 August 1995.  Approved Changes
  • The following new names have been approved for the programme and its four sub-schemes: Previous name Approved name National Social Assistance Programme (NSAP) Pradhan Mantri Samajik Sahayata Yojana Indira Gandhi National Old Age Pension Scheme (IGNOAPS) Pradhan Mantri Vriddhavastha Pension Yojana Indira Gandhi National Widow Pension Scheme (IGNWPS) Pradhan Mantri Vidhwa Pension Yojana Indira Gandhi National Disability Pension Scheme (IGNDPS) Pradhan Mantri Divyangjan Pension Yojana National Family Bene昀椀t Scheme Pradhan Mantri Parivar Labh Yojana
  • Under the disability pension scheme, monthly central assistance of ₹375 for bene昀椀ciaries aged 0–79 years and ₹625 for those aged 80 years and above has been approved.
  • The disability eligibility threshold will be reduced from the previous 80% to benchmark disability of at least 40%. Eligibility will begin from birth.
  • The old age pension, widow pension and family bene昀椀t schemes have been approved for continuation in their existing form. National Family Health Survey-6 The fact sheets for the sixth round of the National Family Health Survey (NFHS-6) were released on May 29, 2026 by the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.   • Institutional deliveries increased from 88.6% in NFHS-5 to 90.6% in NFHS-6.

  • India’s Total Fertility Rate remained at 2.0.

The SRS Bulletin 2024 was released by the Of昀椀ce of the Registrar General of India.
  • SRS provides annual estimates of important demographic indicators in India.  It gives data on Birth Rate, Death Rate, Natural Growth Rate and Infant Mortality Rate.  Key Highlights
  • Birth Rate means the number of live births per thousand population in a year.
  • Birth Rate is an important indicator of fertility and population growth.
  • India’s Birth Rate declined from 36.9 in 1971 to 18.3 in 2024.
  • During the last decade, India’s Birth Rate declined from 21.0 in 2014 to 18.3 in 2024.
  • This shows a decline of about 13% in the last ten years.
  • The rural Birth Rate declined from 22.7 in 2014 to 20.2 in 2024.
  • The urban Birth Rate declined from 17.4 in 2014 to 14.7 in 2024.
  • In 2024, the Birth Rate was 20.2 in rural areas and 14.7 in urban areas.
  • Bihar had the highest Birth Rate at 26.8.
  • Andaman and Nicobar Islands had the lowest Birth Rate at 9.9.
  • Death Rate means the number of deaths per thousand population in a year.
  • India’s Death Rate declined from 14.9 in 1971 to 6.4 in 2024.
  • In 2024, India’s total Death Rate was 6.4.
  • The rural Death Rate was 6.8 in 2024.
  • The urban Death Rate was 5.6 in 2024.
  • The rural Death Rate remained the same in 2023 and 2024 at 6.8.
  • The urban Death Rate declined slightly from 5.7 in 2023 to 5.6 in 2024.
  • Chhattisgarh recorded the highest Death Rate at 8.4.
  • Chandigarh recorded the lowest Death Rate at 3.9.
  • The male Death Rate was 7.1.
  • The female Death Rate was 5.6.
  • The data shows that the male Death Rate was higher than the female Death Rate.
  • Male IMR was 24 and female IMR was 25.
  • Rural IMR was 27 and urban IMR was 17.
  • In rural areas, male IMR was 27 and female IMR was 28.
  • In urban areas, male IMR was 17 and female IMR was 16.
  • Natural Growth Rate is the difference between Birth Rate and Death Rate.
  • India’s Natural Growth Rate in 2024 was 11.9.
  • The rural Natural Growth Rate was 13.5.
  • The urban Natural Growth Rate was 9.0.
  • Bihar had a high Natural Growth Rate of 20.8.
  • Kerala had a low Natural Growth Rate of 3.9.
  • Infant Mortality Rate is commonly called IMR.
  • India’s IMR in 2024 was 24 infant deaths per thousand live births.
  • India’s IMR declined from 129 in 1971 to 24 in 2024.
  • India’s IMR declined from 39 in 2014 to 24 in 2024.
  • This shows a decline of about 38% in the last decade.
  • Rural IMR declined from 43 in 2014 to 27 in 2024.
  • Urban IMR declined from 26 in 2014 to 17 in 2024.
  • In 2024, rural IMR was 27 and urban IMR was 17.
  • Chhattisgarh recorded the highest IMR at 36.
  • Manipur recorded the lowest IMR at 2 (estimate covers 2022-24).
  • At the national level, about one in every 42 infants died before completing one year of life.
  • India’s maternal mortality ratio was 87 maternal deaths per 100,000 live births in SRS 2022-24, compared with 130 in 2014-16.  Sample Coverage
  • The SRS Bulletin 2024 covered 8,839 sample units across India.

  • The Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) unveiled its new logo and new mascot on 1 January 2026 to modernise its institutional identity, strengthen public outreach, and reinforce the role of official statistics in nation- building.

  • The design uses numbers and statistical symbols to indicate modern data systems and statistical science.
  • The upward growth bar conveys progress and explains how credible data supports sustainable economic growth.
  • The colour scheme: saffron, white, green, and deep blue–is used to represent national values such as growth, truth, sustainability, stability, and knowledge, strengthening the credibility of official statistics.

Industrial Sector Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development (Amendment) Act, 2026 The Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development (Amendment) Act, 2026 modernises the Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development Act, 2006. It seeks to address delayed payments, improve MSME liquidity, simplify digital registration, strengthen dispute-resolution institutions and rationalise compliance-related penalties.  Legislative Background and Present Status
  • The measure was introduced in the Rajya Sabha on 28 July 2026 by Union Minister for Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Jitan Ram Manjhi.  Rajya Sabha passed it on 3 August 2026.  Lok Sabha passed it on 7 August 2026.  It received Presidential assent on 13 August 2026.  It was published as Act No. 16 of 2026 in the Gazette of India.
  • The act seeks to address delayed payments, improve MSME liquidity, accelerate dispute resolution, simplify registration and compliance, and promote the Ease of Doing Business.
  • It amends speci昀椀c provisions of the MSMED Act, 2006 rather than replacing the entire principal legislation.  Key Provisions of the MSMED (Amendment) Bill, 2026
  • Filing of the memorandum will be free and voluntary for all MSMEs.
  • CPSEs must settle MSME invoices through TReDS, while States may impose the same requirement on their public enterprises and authorities.
  • TReDS, regulated by the RBI, enables MSMEs to obtain funds against unpaid invoices.
  • Discounted invoices increased from ₹40,000 crore in 2021–22 to ₹3.47 lakh crore in 2025–26.
  • States may establish multiple MSEFCs and provide them with adequate infrastructure, digital systems and trained personnel.
  • Mediation must be completed within 90 days of the 昀椀rst appearance.

Failed mediation must be referred & Related Developments

  • Failed mediation must be referred to arbitration within 30 days.
  • A buyer challenging an award must deposit 75% of the awarded amount.
  • If the case remains pending beyond six months , the court must release at least 50% of the award to the MSME supplier. The scheme has a budgetary outlay of ₹62,500 crore and seeks to strengthen India’s mobile phone manufacturing ecosystem.  About the Scheme
  • MPMS aims to expand mobile phone production, deepen domestic value addition, strengthen supply- chain resilience and improve global competitiveness.

  • IEMI 2025 is the second edition of the index. It was released on 16 September 2026 , covering the assessment period from January to December 2025. The 昀椀rst edition, IEMI 2024, was released on 4 August 2025.
  • The index has four principal objectives:  To identify states and Union Territories performing well in e-mobility.  To identify the key success factors in昀氀uencing progress in e-mobility.  To encourage states to adopt a more proactive and ambitious approach towards e-mobility.  To support evidence-based policymaking for sustainable EV growth.  Structure of the Index
  • IEMI 2025 comprises 16 indicators , classi昀椀ed as Outcome Indicators and Enabler Indicators, across three principal thematic areas. Global Multidimensional Poverty Index 2026 The Global Multidimensional Poverty Index, 2026, released on October 12, 2026, is jointly published by the UN Development Programme (UNDP) and the Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative (OPHI).  Key Highlights of the Report
  • The 2026 Global Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) report provides a statistical update of the Global Multidimensional Poverty Index, covering 108 countries.
  • The report highlights that, of the 6.3 billion people living in these countries, 1.2 billion people - or 18.9 per cent - are living in acute multidimensional poverty.
  • The number of people living in multidimensional poverty has risen for the 昀椀rst time since the index was launched in 2010.
  • This year’s update of the global MPI database includes new surveys from 13 countries.
  • The report identi昀椀es 33 countries that halved their MPI over the observed periods, including India.
  • China achieved the fastest halving in the available data–in four years, between 2010 and 2014.
  • The publication of the 2026 Multidimensional Poverty Index Report was supported by a 昀椀nancial contribution from the Republic of Korea.
  • Severe poverty: 534 million people , representing 44.6% of multidimensionally poor people , experience severe multidimensional poverty. Another 952 million people are vulnerable to multidimensional poverty.
  • A total of 617 million children under 18 years of age constitute 51.5% of all multidimensionally poor people. Approximately one in three children is poor, compared with one in seven adults.
  • 83.3% of poor people (998 million) live in rural areas, compared with 16.7% (200 million) in urban areas. Poverty incidence is 28.7% in rural areas, against 7.0% in urban areas.
  • Sub: Saharan Africa has both the highest poverty incidence (51.4%) and the largest poor population (616 million). South Asia follows with approximately 393 million poor people, with poverty incidence of 19.9%.
  • Approximately 65.1% of multidimensionally poor people–779 million–live in middle-income countries.
  • In 21 countries, more than half the population is multidimensionally poor; 18 of these countries are in Sub-Saharan Africa.  Countries at the top and bottom
  • Lowest poverty: Serbia, with a reported MPI of 0.000 and poverty incidence of 0.1%. The rounded MPI value does not mean poverty is entirely absent.
  • Highest poverty: Chad, with an MPI of 0.517 and a poverty incidence of 84.2%.
  • The 昀椀ve countries with the highest MPI values , arranged from highest to lowest, are: Country MPI value Poverty incidence Chad 0.517 84.2% Niger 0.470 79.9% Central African Republic 0.461 80.4% Burundi 0.409 75.1% Madagascar 0.386 68.4%  India Speci昀椀c Highlights
  • Based on its 2019: 2021 survey, India’s MPI is 0.069, poverty incidence 16.4%, and deprivation intensity 42.0%; 4.2% of the population is severely poor and 18.7% vulnerable.
  • Between 2005: 2006 and 2019–2021 , its MPI declined from 0.283 to 0.069 , while poverty incidence fell from 55.1% to 16.4%.
  • The report estimates that 237.849 million people (approximately 23.78 crore) as multidimensi- onally poor based on the 2024 population , the largest absolute number among the countries covered.
  • This is a population: based projection using the older survey poverty rate, not a new 2024 or 2026 poverty survey. About Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) Aspect Description About The MPI is a comprehensive measure that goes beyond income to capture the multiple and overlapping deprivations faced by individuals. It complements income-based poverty measures (like the USD 3.00/day threshold) by including non-monetary dimensions of poverty for better policy targeting. Structure 3 Dimensions → 10 Indicators (covering health, education, and living standards). Weighting System - Each dimension has equal weight (1/3 each). - Health (2 indicators) → 1/6 weight each. - Education (2 indicators) → 1/6 weight each. - Standard of Living (6 indicators) → 1/18 weight each. Range MPI values range from 0 to 1 . Higher values indicate greater poverty. Identi昀椀cation of the Poor A person is considered multi- dimensionally poor if their deprivation scores ≥ 33.3% (1/3).   • The EPI 2024 is a composite, evidence-based as - sessment that evaluates how prepared States/UTs are to build competitive export ecosystems through infrastructure, business conditions, governance sup- port, and export outcomes.
  • The first EPI was published in August 2020, and EPI 2024 is the 4th edition.
  • The index is aligned with India’s objective of achieving USD 1 trillion in merchandise exports by 2030 and the vision of Viksit Bharat @2047.
  • The four pillars and 13 Sub: pillars are follows – Export Infrastructure (20%) Utilities; Logistics Business Ecosystem (40%) Macro-economy; Cost competitiveness; Human capital; Finance and credit accessibility; MSME ecosystem; Industrial and innovation environment Policy & Governance (20%) State-level policy support and governance; Regulatory environment & compliance Export Performance (20%) State-level exports and trends; Export promotion and facilitation; Export portfolio and market access  Top performers in EPI 2024

Miscellaneous Women Towards Better Livelihoods Through Work and Enterprise The expansion of women’s economic participation in India is evident across employment, entrepreneurship, manufacturing and research. The government presented key 昀椀gures on women’s employment and entrepreneurship on October 15, 2026.  Women’s Employment
  • For women aged 15 years and above, LFPR based on usual status—principal and subsidiary activities—was 23.3% in 2017–18 . It stood at 40.0% in 2025 . The corresponding female WPR 昀椀gures for the same age group were 22.0% and 38.8%, respectively.
  • During 2025, an average of approximately 20 crore women aged 15 years and above were employed.  Women’s Role in Entrepreneurship
  • Approximately 3.69 crore registered women- owned MSMEs as of October 2026, representing a share of approximately 38% (October 15, 2026).
  • The MSME dashboard dated 17 October 2026 recorded 3,71,97,598 registrations in the women’s category, including those under Udyam Registration and the Udyam Assist Platform . Their calculated share of the total 9,89,02,198 registrations was approximately 37.61%.
  • As of 31 March 2026 , more than 1.07 lakh recognised startups had at least one woman director or partner , accounting for approximately 48% of all recognised startups.  Participation in Technical and Highly Skilled Fields
  • As of July 2026, women accounted for approximately 70% of the direct workforce in mobile phone manufacturing.
  • In civil aviation, women were reported to constitute approximately 15% of India’s pilots , one of the highest proportions globally. According to 昀椀gures reported in June 2025 , women accounted for 15% of air traf昀椀c controllers , 11% of 昀氀ight dispatchers and 33% of the Directorate General of Civil Aviation’s (DGCA) Flight Operations Inspectors.
  • According to Research and Development Statistics 2025–26 , women’s share in research careers in Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM) was 13% in 2000–01 , 18.6% in 2020–21 and 29% in 2023–24 . These 昀椀gures relate to the research workforce. NITI Aayog Report on Regulatory Reforms in Professional Services On August 10, 2026 , NITI Aayog Vice-Chairman Ashok Kumar Lahiri launched India’s Services Sector: Insights on Regulatory Regime in Professional Services . It is the third report under the Services Thematic Series; the related PIB release was published on August 14, 2026. It identi昀椀es reforms that could improve regulatory clarity, professional mobility, recognition of quali昀椀cations and international competitiveness.  Four-Pronged Strategy 1. Continuous Professional Development for Professionals: Structured CPD and lifelong learning can maintain professional competence as technology and industry practices change. 2. Adoption of Best Practices in Professional Services: Regulators should publish clear eligibility rules, contact details, processing timelines, decisions and review mechanisms and should hold regular consultations. 3. Elevate Professional Services within the Services Value Chain: India should move from routine, cost-based delivery towards research, engineering design, legal analytics, advanced 昀椀nancial modelling and strategic consulting. 4. Advance Emerging Trends in Professional Services: Professionals should build capabilities in arti昀椀cial intelligence, automation, ESG reporting, carbon accounting, climate-risk assessment, sustainable 昀椀nance and supply-chain advisory. The report cautions that adopting best practices d oes not mean mechanically copying foreign laws. SUMAN Roadmap 2030 Union Health Minister Jagat Prakash Nadda launched the roadmap on June 29, 2026, at the 16 th Conference of the Central Council of Health and Family Welfare.
  • The roadmap is an evidence: driven framework of the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, led by its Maternal Health Division under RMNCHA+N, integrating reproductive, maternal, newborn, child and adolescent health and nutrition.
  • It aims to achieve the SDG target of an MMR below 70 per 100,000 live births by 2030, reduce neonatal and infant mortality, ensure full service coverage across all States and Union Territories, and achieve zero preventable maternal and newborn deaths.
  • The SUMAN package promotes early registration, complete antenatal care, quality assessment and adequate institutional stay after delivery. Interventions target 130 districts across 13 States.
  • SUMAN Panchayats promote antenatal care, institutional delivery, immunisation and zero maternal and infant deaths. “Mothers’ Picnic” promotes awareness.
  • Digital measures include AI: enabled labour rooms, the JANANI portal and a centralised SUMAN Call Centre.
  • The roadmap strengthens maternal death surveillance, near-miss reviews, emergency obstetric care and referrals, including the use of Non-Pneumatic Anti- Shock Garment. Income Mobility in India (2014–2025)
  • The study is based on real per capita income data from the CMIE Consumer Pyramids Household Survey, using a balanced panel of households observed from 2014 to 2025.
  • The analysis classifies households according to their 2014 per capita income rank, into three groups: Top 10%; Next 40%; and Bottom 50%.
  • A household is considered:  Upwardly mobile if it moves to a higher group,  Downwardly mobile if it moves to a lower group,  Stable if it remains in the same group.
  • The share of households facing downward mobility rose from 14% in 2015 to 26.8% in 2025.
  • The share of households with no change fell sharply from over 70% to below 50%.
  • Upward mobility also increased, from 14.1% to 23.5%, but this improvement is gradual and trail in rise in downward movement.
  • Rural India shows the sharpest stress. By 2025, nearly 29% of rural households were worse off than in 2014.
  • By 2025, around one: fourth or more of households in these groups were worse off than in 2014. India's FDI In昀氀ow in FY 2024–25
  • According to government estimates, FDI inflows have seen a steady rise from USD 36.05 billion in FY 2013–14 to USD 81.04 billion (provisional) in FY 2024–25, marking a 14% increase from USD 71.28 billion in FY 2023–24.
  • The services sector emerged as the top recipient of FDI equity in FY 2024–25, attracting 19% of total inflows, followed by computer software and hardware (16%) and trading (8%).  FDI into the services sector rose by 40.77% to USD 9.35 billion from USD 6.64 billion in the previous year.
  • India is also becoming a hub for manufacturing FDI, which grew by 18% in FY 2024–25, reaching USD 19.04 billion compared with USD 16.12 billion in FY 2023–24.
  • Maharashtra accounted for the highest share (39%) of total FDI equity inflows in FY 2024–25, followed by Karnataka (13%) and Delhi (12%).
  • Among source countries, Singapore led with a 30% share, followed by Mauritius (17%) and the United States (11%).
  • Over the last eleven financial years (2014–25), India attracted FDI worth USD 748.78 billion, reflecting a 143% increase over the previous eleven years (2003– 14), which saw USD 308.38 billion in inflows. News in Shorts  First Soil Carbon Payments to Farmers in India

Arrangements for digital payments totalling more than ₹2.9 crore to 2,550 farmers in Punjab and Haryana were announced.
  • Grow Indigo launched the ‘Aadi’ farmer carbon programme in 2019 under ICAR’s technical guidance. During 2019–2022, participating farmers adopted practices such as direct-seeded rice, reduced tillage and crop residue management.  India Bans Sugar Exports

Union Budget 2026–27 Union Minister for Finance and Corporate Affairs, Smt. Nirmala Sitharaman, tabled the Union Budget 2026-27 in the Parliament on February 01, 2026. The highlights of the budget are as follows:  Core Theme: 3 Kartavyas
  • The Budget targets faster and more resilient growth by raising productivity and competitiveness amid global volatility.
  • The Budget aims to build people’s capacities so citizens become partners in prosperity.
  • The Budget seeks inclusive access to resources and opportunities for every region and section under Sabka Saath, Sabka Vikas.  Macro & Fiscal Snapshot (BE 2026–27)
  • Non: debt receipts are estimated at `36.5 lakh crore, and total expenditure is estimated at `53.5 lakh crore.
  • Centre’s net tax receipts are estimated at `28.7 lakh crore.
  • Gross market borrowings are estimated at `17.2 lakh crore, and net borrowings (dated securities) are estimated at `11.7 lakh crore.
  • Fiscal deficit is estimated at 4.3% of GDP, while RE 2025–26 keeps fiscal deficit at 4.4% of GDP.
  • Debt: to-GDP is estimated at 55.6% (BE 2026–27) versus 56.1% (RE 2025–26). PART-A: Interventions  Kartavya 1: Growth Push (6 Interventions) (1) Scale manufacturing in 7 strategic/frontier sectors
  • The Budget launches Biopharma SHAKTI with `10,000 crore (5 years) to build India as a global biopharma hub.
  • The Budget expands biopharma capacity via 3 new NIPERs, upgrading 7 NIPERs , and 1,000+ accredited clinical trial sites.
  • The Budget announces India Semiconductor Mission 2.0 for equipment/materials, full-stack IP , and supply-chain strengthening with industry-led R&D and training.
  • The Budget raises Electronics Components Manufacturing Scheme outlay to `40,000 crore.
  • The Budget proposes Rare Earth Corridors in Odisha, Kerala, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu for activities ranging from mining to manufacturing.
  • The Budget supports 3 Chemical Parks through a challenge-mode, cluster-based plug-and-play model.
  • The Budget strengthens capital goods manufacturing through Hi-Tech Tool Rooms, CIE equipment scheme, and a Container Manufacturing scheme with `10,000+ crore (5 years).
  • The Budget announces an Integrated Textile Programme, including the National Fibre Scheme, cluster modernisation, challenge-mode Mega Textile Parks, and Mahatma Gandhi Gram Swaraj for khadi/handloom/handicrafts. (2) Rejuvenate legacy industrial sectors
  • The Budget announces a scheme to revive 200 legacy industrial clusters through tech and infrastructure upgrades. (3) Create “Champion SMEs”

The Budget introduces an SME & Related Developments

  • The Budget introduces an SME Growth Fund of `10,000 crore to build future champion firms.
  • The Budget tops up the Self: Reliant India Fund by `2,000 crore for micro-enterprise risk capital.
  • The Budget proposes training ‘Corporate Mitras’ through professional institutes to provide support in Tier-II/III areas. (4) Infrastructure push
  • Public capex is raised to `12.2 lakh crore in FY 2026–27.
  • An Infrastructure Risk Guarantee Fund is proposed to improve private developer confidence.
  • CPSE real: estate recycling is proposed through dedicated REITs.
  • A new Dedicated Freight Corridor is proposed from Dankuni to Surat.
  • 20 new National Waterways are to be operationalised in 5 years, starting with NW-5 (Odisha).
  • Regional training centres and ship repair ecosystems at Varanasi and Patna are proposed.
  • A Coastal Cargo Promotion Scheme targets raising waterways/coastal shipping share from 6% to 12% by 2047.
  • A Seaplane VGF Scheme is proposed for tourism and remote connectivity. (5) Energy security
  • `20,000 crore (5 years) is allocated for Carbon Capture, Utilization, and Storage (CCUS) technologies. (6) City Economic Regions (CERs)
  • `5,000 crore per CER (5 years) is announced through challenge-mode, reform-cum-results based financing.
  • Seven High: Speed Rail corridors are proposed: Mumbai–Pune, Pune–Hyderabad, Hyderabad– Bengaluru, Hyderabad–Chennai, Chennai– Bengaluru, Delhi–Varanasi and Varanasi–Siliguri.  Banking & Investment Ecosystem
  • A High: Level Committee on Banking for Viksit Bharat is proposed.
  • The restructuring PFC and REC is proposed to improve scale and efficiency.
  • A review of FEMA (Non: debt Instruments) Rules is proposed for a user-friendly FDI framework.
  • An incentive of `100 crore is announced for a single municipal bond issuance above `1,000 crore.  Kartavya 2: Aspirations and Capacity
  • A high: powered Education to Employment and Enterprise Standing Committee is proposed with a services-sector focus.
  • Allied health capacity is expanded through new/ upgraded institutions and 1,00,000 Allied Health Professionals (AHP) in 5 years.
  • Five Regional Medical Hubs are proposed for medical tourism.
  • Three All India Institutes of Ayurveda are proposed.
  • Veterinary capacity is expanded by over 20,000 professionals, and a loan-linked subsidy supports private veterinary colleges/hospitals/labs.
  • AVGC labs are planned through IICT Mumbai in 15,000 schools and 500 colleges.
  • Five University Townships are proposed near industrial/logistics corridors.
  • A girls’ hostel in every district is proposed through VGF and capital support.
  • Tourism measures include upgrading NCHMCT, training 10,000 guides, and establishing a National Destination Digital Knowledge Grid.
  • 15 archaeological sites are proposed for experiential cultural tourism, and the Khelo India Mission is proposed for sports transformation.  Kartavya 3: Sabka Saath, Sabka Vikas (Targeted Areas)
  • The budget aims to enhance farmer’s through 500 reservoirs/Amrit Sarovars and support for high- value crops including coconut, sandalwood, cocoa and cashew, along with a Coconut Promotion Scheme.
  • Bharat: VISTAAR is proposed as a multilingual AI tool integrating AgriStack and ICAR practice packages.
  • Divyangjan Kaushal Yojana is proposed for job- ready roles in IT, AVGC, hospitality, and Food & Beverage services.
  • NIMHANS: 2 is proposed in North India, and mental health institutes in Ranchi and Tezpur are to be upgraded.
  • The Purvodaya/NER focus includes an East Coast Industrial Corridor, 5 tourism destinations, 4,000 e-buses, and a Buddhist Circuit Scheme in NE states.
  • `1.4 lakh crore is provided as Finance Commission grants for states in FY 2026–27 (as per 16th FC). PART –B : Overall Fiscal Framework
  • The Union Government is estimated to spend `53.47 lakh crore in 2026–27, representing a 7.7% increase over the Revised Estimates (RE) of 2025– 26.
  • Interest payments constitute about 26% of total expenditure and absorb nearly 40% of revenue receipts, highlighting persistent debt-servicing pressures.
  • Total receipts (excluding borrowings) are estimated at `36.51 lakh crore , marking a 7.2% increase over the RE of 2025–26, with tax revenue expected to grow by 8%.
  • The government has projected nominal GDP growth at 10% for 2026–27, reflecting expectations of sustained real growth and moderate inflation.  De昀椀cit and Debt Targets
  • The revenue deficit is targeted at 1.5% of GDP, unchanged from the revised estimate of 2025–26, indicating continued emphasis on fiscal consolidation.
  • The fiscal deficit is targeted at 4.3% of GDP , marginally lower than 4.4% of GDP in 2025–26 (RE).
  • The Centre has reiterated its commitment to reducing outstanding liabilities to around 50% of GDP by March 2031 , with liabilities estimated at 55.6% of GDP in 2026–27.  Taxation Proposals
  • Income tax slabs remain unchanged for Assessment Year 2026–27, maintaining stability in the personal tax regime.
  • A tax holiday until 2047 has been granted to foreign companies providing global cloud services using Indian data centres , subject to routing services to Indian customers through Indian resellers.
  • The tax holiday for IFSC units and Offshore Banking Units has been extended from 10 years to 20 years, with income taxed at 15% thereafter.
  • All share buybacks are proposed to be taxed as capital gains , with an additional buyback tax on promoters, raising the effective tax rate to 22% for corporate promoters and 30% for non-corporate promoters.
  • Securities Transaction Tax (STT) rates have been increased for options and futures , signalling a calibrated tightening in capital market taxation.
  • Interest expenditure deductions against dividend income or mutual fund income have been withdrawn.
  • Minimum Alternate Tax (MAT) rate has been reduced from 15% to 14% , while MAT credit accumulation is discontinued from April 2026.
  • A Foreign Assets Disclosure Scheme, 2026 has been introduced for small taxpayers, offering graded relief and immunity subject to compliance.
  • TCS rates on education and medical remittances, and overseas tour packages have been reduced to 2%, easing the burden on households.  Finance and Financial Sector Reforms
  • A High: Level Committee on Banking for Viksit Bharat will be constituted to review the banking sector.
  • The FEMA Non: Debt Instruments Rules will be simplified to facilitate foreign investment.
  • Persons Resident Outside India (PROI) will be allowed to invest up to 10% in listed Indian companies under the Portfolio Investment Scheme.
  • A market: making framework for corporate bonds and incentives for municipal bond issuance have been announced to deepen debt markets.  Industry, MSMEs, and Commerce
  • A scheme will be launched to revive 200 legacy industrial clusters through modern technology and infrastructure.   • The Economic Survey 2025: 26 urges a shift to entrepreneurial policymaking under uncertainty, where the State acts early, structures risk, learns through experimentation, and adapts without paralysis.
  • The Survey says governance is moving from compliance-driven regulation to capability- driven state capacity , signalling an emerging entrepreneurial State.
  • Despite post: COVID shocks, including global trade disruption and US tariffs in April 2025, the Indian economy has shown strong macroeconomic resilience.
  • The Survey anticipates real GDP growth above 7% in FY 2025–26 and expects growth to stay near this level in the following year.
  • It highlights a paradox in which India’s best macro performance in decades comes amid a global system that no longer reliably rewards discipline with currency stability, capital inflows, or insulation.
  • The Survey argues that India’s scale population of 145 crore, and democracy make it unrealistic to copy external development templates in a geopolitically uncertain world.
  • It states that global headwinds can become tailwinds if the State, private sector, and households align and sustain a national effort.
  • The Survey outlines three global scenarios for 2026: managed disorder, disorderly multipolar breakdown, and a low-probability, high-impact shock cascade worse that of 2008.
  • Across scenarios, it says India is relatively better placed due to a large domestic market, a less financialised growth model, strong reserves, and credible strategic autonomy, though insulation is not complete.
  • It warns of a common risk of disrupted capital flows and sustained rupee pressure that could last beyond one year.
  • The Survey says India must strengthen foreign currency earnings through exports and investor confidence to finance a rising import bill with rising incomes.
  • It recommends supply stability, strategic buffers, diversified trade routes, and alternative payment systems, calling for strategic sobriety over defensive pessimism.
  • It stresses that India must balance long-term growth with short-term shock absorption, captured in its “marathon and sprint” framing.
  • The Survey emphasises process reforms alongside policy reforms because administrative processes shape citizen-state interaction and reform outcomes.

Chapter 5

Science & Technology Affairs

Space exploration missions (JAXA MMX, Artemis II, ISRO LVM3), indigenous defence systems, health research, and AI.

JAXA Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) & Related Developments

  • JAXA Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) launched the Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission on 20 October 2026 aboard H3 Flight No. 10 from Tanegashima Space Center, Japan . It aims to achieve the world’s 昀椀rst sample return from the Martian system. Its planned duration is approximately 昀椀ve years.  Key Highlights
  • Mission objectives: Study Phobos and Deimos, Mars’s two moons, and return at least 10 grams of material from Phobos.
  • Timeline: Arrival at Mars is expected in 2027, and sample delivery to Earth in 2031.
  • Scientific significance: Determine whether the moons are captured asteroids or debris from a giant impact on Mars , improving understanding of planetary formation and the delivery of water and organic compounds.  Technical Features
  • Spacecraft: Three modules—propulsion, exploration and return—use solar panels for electricity and chemical propulsion for manoeuvres.
  • Orbit: A quasi-satellite orbit around Mars near Phobos supports surface mapping and landing-site selection.
  • Instruments: The spacecraft carries 13 mission instruments. TENGOO provides approximately 40 cm imaging resolution ; OROCHI captures images at multiple wavelengths; LIDAR measures surface distance using laser pulses.
  • Spectrometers: NASA ’s MEGANE (Mars-moon Exploration with Gamma rays and Neutrons) measures gamma rays and neutrons to determine elemental composition. MIRS (MMX InfraRed Spectrometer) operates at 0.9–3.6 micrometres , investigating minerals, water-related substances and organic matter.
  • Rover: IDEFIX, jointly developed by France’s CNES and Germany’s DLR, will assess surface conditions before the spacecraft lands.
  • Sampling: JAXA ’s C-Sampler collects subsurface material, while NASA ’s P-Sampler uses high- pressure nitrogen gas to gather surface particles.
  • Communication and return: NASA ’s Deep Space Network supports communication and navigation. A Sample Return Capsule will bring samples through Earth’s atmosphere; NASA will receive about 15% for research and curation. First GAGAN-Based Satellite In late June 2026, the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) supervised India’s 昀椀rst Satellite-Based Landing System (SLS) approach by a commercial jet using the indigenous GAGAN system. An IndiGo Airbus A321 conducted the demonstration using satellite-derived guidance instead of relying on a conventional Instrument Landing System (ILS).  Key Highlights
  • GAGAN (GPS Aided GEO Augmented Navigation) is India’s indigenous Satellite-Based Augmentation System developed by the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) and the Airports Authority of India.
  • It enhances GPS accuracy and provides integrity information for safer aircraft navigation. Certi昀椀ed to international standards, GAGAN supports satellite- based landing and serves sectors beyond aviation.  Key Elements of GAGAN
  • GAGAN operates through an integrated network of ground stations, communication systems, and geostationary satellites. These elements monitor GPS signals in real-time, calculate corrections, and broadcast enhanced navigation information to aircraft. Key Elements No. of Elements Deployed Role Indian Reference Stations (INRES) 15 Continuously monitor GPS signals across the country and detect any errors. A. Recent Astronomical Activities Indian Master Control Centres (INMCC) 2 Process data received from all reference stations, calculate signal corrections, and generate integrity information. Indian Land Uplink Stations (INLUS) 3 Transmit correction and integrity information from the ground to GAGAN satellites. Communication Networks 4 Connect all GAGAN stations and enable secure, real-time transmission of navigation data. Geostationary Satellites with GAGAN Payloads 3 Broadcast corrected navigation signals across the service area.
  • By enhancing navigation accuracy and seamless operations across the region, it continues to reinforce India’s leadership in satellite-enabled aviation services.  India’s Indigenous Navigation Ecosystem
  • The integrated architecture of GAGAN forms an important part of India’s broader satellite navigation programme.
  • Alongside GAGAN, India has developed the Navigation with Indian Constellation (NavIC), its indigenous regional navigation satellite system. While NavIC provides positioning, navigation and timing services, GAGAN enhances GPS signals to support precise aircraft navigation and landing. SOLAR-1 Space weather refers to changes in the space environment caused mainly by activity on the Sun. Powerful solar events can affect technological infrastructure and space missions. To strengthen it s forecasting and early-warning system, the United States made SOLAR-1 operational on June 10, 2026. It is the 昀椀rst U.S. satellite designed exclusively for continuous and operational space-weather observations. The satellite is operated by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) . Its observations are transmitted to NOAA ’s Space Weather Prediction Center (SWPC), which uses them to issue forecasts, watches, warnings and alerts.  Key Highlights
  • SOLAR: 1 stands for Space Weather Observations at L1 to Advance Readiness–1 . It was previously known as Space Weather Follow On–Lagrange 1, or SWFO-L1.
  • It was renamed SOLAR: 1 after reaching its intended orbit around the Sun–Earth Lagrange Point 1.  Launch and Journey to Deep Space
  • The spacecraft was launched on September 24, 2025, at 7:30 a.m. EDT from Launch Complex 39A at NASA ’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida.
  • It travelled aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket. NASA ’s Launch Services Program managed the launch.
  • After travelling for about four months and covering nearly one million miles, the spacecraft performed its final engine burn on January 23, 2026.
  • It then entered its planned orbit around L1 and was formally renamed SOLAR-1. Chandrayaan-3 Hop Experiment A team of scientists from the Indian Space Researc h Organisation (ISRO) on May 18, 2026 shared a report of the 昀椀ndings of the ‘Hop’ experiment conducted by the Vikram Lander of Chandrayaan-3 and the Chandra’s Surface Thermophysical Experiment (ChaSTE) on the Moon.
  • A new study conducted during the 昀椀nal phase of the Chandrayaan-3 missions when the Vikram lander performed a successful hop experiment, has offered fresh insights into the Moon surface.
  • During the 昀椀nal phase of its mission, Chandrayaan- 3’s Vikram lander reignited its engines to perform a controlled “hop” experiment (primarily to test ascent capabilities for future sample-return missions) and landed nearby , nearly 50 cm away from its initial position.
  • ChaSTE (Chandra’s Surface Thermophysical Experiment), a lunar thermometer was re-penetrated into the lunar regolith (soil) at the new location.
  • By analysing the ChaSTE data following this historic “hop” monoeuvre by the Vikram lander, scientists have discovered that the post-hop location at the Moon’s southern polar region possesses a complex, layered soil structure that was signi昀椀cantly altered by the lander’s brief 昀氀ight.  Key 昀椀ndings from the study have emerged, which include:
  • Layered Stratigraphy: analysis revealed a distinct two-layer structure within the top 6.5 cm of the post- hop site which means that the top few centimetres of the Moon’s surface aren’t just a uniform pile of dust; they are made of distinct layers with different properties,
  • Geotechnical Variability: the soil’s cohesion and density were found to increase signi昀椀cantly with depth which means that the Moon’s soil at the surface becomes more packed and sticky as we go deeper and Twilight Thermal Pro昀椀les: the data highlighted a “shadowing effect” where local craters and depressions caused temperatures to plunge faster than global models predicted.
  • Surface Erosion and Compaction: The engine 昀椀ring blew away the top 3 cm of regolith, exposing and slightly compacting the material underneath. India’s First Orbital Data Centre Satellite Path昀椀nder Recently on 4 May 2026 , Pixxel announced a strategic partnership with Sarvam to develop and build Path昀椀nder , described as India’s 昀椀rst orbital data centre satellite . Pixxel will design, build, launch and operate the satellite, while Sarvam will provide th e AI backbone for running full-stack language models, training and inference directly in orbit. The mission is important because it brings together remote sensing, high-performance computing and India-built AI on a single satellite platform.  Orbital Data Centre
  • An orbital data centre is a space: based computing system in which satellites carry high-performance processors such as data-centre-class GPUs.
  • These processors can run AI models in orbit, rather than depending entirely on ground-based data centres.
  • In ordinary satellite missions, satellites collect images or signals and send large volumes of raw data to Earth.
  • In an orbital data centre model, computation happens closer to where the data is generated. This is similar to edge computing, where data is processed near its source instead of being sent to a distant cloud server.

Path昀椀nder is a single & Related Developments

  • Path昀椀nder is a single: satellite demonstrator . Its purpose is to test whether powerful computing hardware, similar to that used in ground data centres, can work reliably in the space environment.  Role of Pixxel and Sarvam
  • Pixxel’s role:  Pixxel will design, build, launch and operate Path昀椀nder. It will also provide the hyperspectral imaging payload.  The satellite will be developed at Gigapixxel, Pixxel’s upcoming facility designed to scale satellite production to up to 100 units.
  • Sarvam’s role:  Sarvam will provide the AI backbone. Its full- stack sovereign AI platform, including models and inference infrastructure developed and governed in India, will run directly on the satellite’s GPU layer. Artemis II Mission Artemis II was not a Moon-landing mission; it was a crewed lunar flyby mission meant to prove that NASA ’s Space Launch System, Orion spacecraft, ground systems, recovery teams and mission procedures can safely carry humans beyond low Earth orbit and bring them back. NASA describes it as the first crewed Artemis flight and a key step toward long-term human return to the Moon and future crewed missions to Mars.
  • Artemis II lifted off from the Kennedy Space Center on April 1, 2026, sending the first humans to the Moon since 1972. (Note: The Apollo 17 mission in 1972 sent humans to land on the Moon, whereas Artemis II sent humans toward the Moon.)
  • During the mission, the crew completed a lunar flyby, returning humans to the Moon’s vicinity for the first time in 53 years after the final Apollo Mission to the Moon.  Engineering Focus of the Mission
  • The Artemis II Orion heat shield is the critical thermal protection system on the base of Orion Spacecraft. Orion heat shield protect the Capsule and Astronauts from searing temperatures and Extreme friction during high speed atmospheric re-entry.
  • During the flight, the astronauts tested Orion’s life- support, communications, control, navigation and manual operation systems in a deep-space environment.
  • The mission also tested how well astronauts could live and work inside Orion during a lunar-return flight.
  • This is important because Artemis is not only about reaching the Moon; it is about building the systems needed for repeated journeys, lunar surface work, and eventually Mars missions.
  • The Orion Spacecraft used in Artemis II was named Integrity by the crew.  Orion’s Heat Shield and Re-entry Lesson
  • One of the most important engineering lessons came from Orion’s heat shield. During Artemis I, NASA found unexpected cracking and shedding of heat-shield material.
  • NASA later explained that heat and gases had accumulated inside the Avcoat material, creating internal pressure and uneven shedding during re- entry, although the spacecraft would still have kept a crew safe.
  • For Artemis II, NASA closely monitored re-entry and the thermal protection system.
  • The spacecraft returned at extremely high lunar- return speed, and NASA ’s initial inspection found that the heat shield performed as expected and that heat-shield char loss was significantly reduced compared with Artemis I.
  • This result is important for astronaut safety in future Moon-landing missions.
  • Artemis III is now listed by NASA as a 2027 low- Earth orbit demonstration, mission to test one or both commerical landers from SpaceX and Blue Origin. India’s First Hydrogen-Powered Train Indian Railways is entering a new era of clean and sustainable transportation. Hydrogen fuel cell technology has emerged globally as a promising alternative to fossil fuel-based traction systems. India’s 昀椀rst indigenous hydrogen-powered train marks an important step in adopting this next-generation technology. It is a locomotive that generates its own electricity onboa rd using hydrogen. With the inauguration on the Jind- Sonipat section ( Haryana) of the Northern Railway on 17 July 2026 by PM Narendra Modi ,the hydrogen fuel cell-powered train is begin its operations.
  • The project combines advanced propulsion technology with dedicated hydrogen storage, refuelling and operational infrastructure.

It will demonstrate the feasibility & Related Developments

  • It will demonstrate the feasibility of clean rail transportation in India.  Inside India’s First Hydrogen Train
  • The hydrogen train project has been developed in accordance with design approval and technical speci昀椀cations prepared by the Research, Designs & Standards Organisation (RDSO) . Designed and developed entirely in India, the project demonstrates the vision of Atmanirbhar Bharat.  Key Features of the Hydrogen Powered Train on the Jind- Sonipat Section-
  • The Train has two 1200 kW power cars, totalling 2400 kW hydrogen fuel cell propulsion system.
  • Approved to operate at a maximum speed of 75 kmph with a design speed of 110 kmph.
  • Capacity of Around 2,600 Passengers.
  • Developed from the design stage through prototype manufacturing.
  • It will connect Jind Junction, Gohana Junction and Sonipat while serving intermediate stations.  Technology Behind the Train
  • Hydrogen fuel cell technology produces electricity through a chemical reaction using hydrogen.
  • The primary energy source is a Proton Exchange Membrane Fuel Cell (PEMFC) . This is a fuel cell that generates electricity by reacting hydrogen and oxygen across a proton-conducting Per昀氀uorosulfonic Acid (PFSA) polymer membrane.
  • The process produces only water vapour and heat as byproducts. Hydrogen is a high-energy fuel, 120 MJ/Kg (megajoules per kilogram) in comparison to diesel, which is 43 MJ/Kg.  Hydrogen Infrastructure
  • The country’s largest railway hydrogen storage and refuelling facility has been established at Jind, Haryana.
  • The indigenous facility stores nearly 3,000 kg of hydrogen at a time. It will support hydrogen-powered train operations.
  • The train consists of two Hydrogen Driving Power Cars (DPCs) and eight Trailer Coaches (TCs).
  • Each DPC houses fuel cells, lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries and hydrogen storage cylinders. JAMA Blood Group in Humans The International Society of Blood Transfusion (ISBT) has recognised JAMA as the 49 th human blood group system, numbered ISBT 049. The discovery followed a joint investigation by researchers in the United Kingdom and Israel into unusual blood samples from a woman and her brother. ISBT rati昀椀ed the system at its Kuala Lumpur Congress in 2026 and announced it on September 14, 2026. The 昀椀nding adds to the understanding of rare blood characteristics and the ir possible importance in transfusion medicine.  Key Highlights
  • Blood plays a vital role in the human body, carrying oxygen and essential nutrients to cells. For years, A, B, AB and O have been the blood groups most familiar to people.
  • Now, scientists have identi昀椀ed a new blood group system called JAMA, taking the total number of recognised blood group systems to 49.
  • The International Society of Blood Transfusion (ISBT) has of昀椀cially recognised JAMA as the 49th blood group system.
  • The discovery came from a joint investigation by researchers from the UK and Israel. It began when scientists examined the blood of an Israeli woman and her brother.
  • The woman was found to have an antibody that reacted with the red blood cells of most people.
  • However, the same reaction did not occur with her own red blood cells or those of her brother.
  • This unusual result caught researchers’ attention because the antibody did not correspond to any previously identi昀椀ed blood group antigen.
  • JAMA should not be viewed as another category alongside A, B, AB and O. Instead, it is a separate blood group system involving a speci昀椀c antigen.
  • This antigen is found on the red blood cells of most people. In the woman and her brother, however, it was absent.
  • Their blood also contained a corresponding antibody, helping scientists identify the unusual blood group characteristics. WHO Global Tuberculosis (TB) Report 2025 Recently, WHO released the Global Tuberculosis Report 2025 on November 12, 2025, giving an updated assessment of the TB epidemic and response at global, regional and country levels based mainly on data up to 2024. Data from 184 countries and areas cover more than 99% of the world’s population and TB cases, giving the report very strong global representativeness.
  • Tuberculosis (TB) is described as the world’s leading cause of death from a single infectious agent, and remains among the top 10 causes of death worldwide.
  • TB is an airborne, contagious disease; since 2000, global efforts to combat TB have saved an estimated 83 million lives.  Global TB Burden
  • In 2024, an estimated 10.7 million people developed TB, corresponding to 131 new cases per 100,000 population worldwide.
  • Top eight countries (≈ two: thirds of global TB burden):  India (25%), Indonesia (10%), Philippines (6.8%), China (6.5%), Pakistan (6.3%), Nigeria (4.8%), Democratic Republic of the Congo (3.9%), Bangladesh (3.6%).  TB Incidence in India
  • TB incidence in India has fallen by 21%, from 237 per lakh population in 2015 to 187 per lakh population in 2024 , almost double the global decline of 12%; this is described as one of the highest declines globally among high-burden countries.
  • TB mortality in India (TB deaths in HIV-negative people) has reduced from 28 per lakh population in 2015 to 21 per lakh population in 2024 , with India achieving a higher reduction than the global reduction.
  • India’s treatment coverage rose from 53% in 2015 to over 92% in 2024 , ahead of global universal health coverage and other high-burden countries.
  • In 2024, 26.18 lakh TB patients were diagnosed in India, out of an estimated 27 lakh incident cases, reducing the “missing cases” from 15 lakh in 2015 to less than one lakh in 2024, with no signi昀椀cant increase in MDR-TB cases.   • High Thrust FFSC Rocket Engines: FFSC engines route fuel and oxidiser through separate pre-burners before the main combustion chamber. Chapter 6

Environmental Affairs

UNEP Emissions Gap Report 2026, Ramsar wetlands tally (103), COP30 climate negotiations, and biodiversity initiatives.

UNEP’s Emissions Gap Report 2026 & Related Developments

  • UNEP’s Emissions Gap Report 2026 UNEP’s Emissions Gap Report 2026: 17th edition of the Emissions Gap Report 2026 (titled The Point of Return) was released by the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) on October 21, 2026.
  • Global emissions: Greenhouse gas emissions reached 58.4 gigatonnes of CO 2 equivalent (GtCO2e) in 2025, against a revised 58.5 GtCO2e in 2024; uncertainty prevents confirming a decline or peak.
  • G20: Excluding the Afrizcan Union, members contributed 76% of global emissions; their emissions excluding land use, land-use change and forestry rose 0.7% in 2025.
  • National commitments: By 1 September 2026 , 124 Parties, representing 76% of global emissions, had submitted updated nationally determined contributions (NDCs).
  • Warming threshold: Exceeding 1.5°C above preindustrial levels is unavoidable; stronger mitigation can reduce its magnitude and duration.
  • Lowest overshoot pathway: Peak warming can be limited to 1.7–1.8°C with 66% probability , with around 50% probability of returning to 1.5°C by 2100.
  • Required reductions: Against 2025 levels , emissions must fall 18% by 2030, 45% by 2035, and 69% by 2040.
  • Commitment shortfall: Full NDC implementation delivers only 5–8% reductions by 2030 and 11–15% by 2035.
  • Emissions gap: Even with conditional commitments implemented, the gap against the lowest overshoot pathway remains 5 GtCO 2e in 2030 and 16 GtCO2e in 2035.  Emissions Gap Report 2026: India-speci昀椀c facts
  • Third: largest emitter: India’s greenhouse gas emissions were 4.5 billion tonnes of CO 2 equivalent in 2025, placing it third after China and the United States. This estimate excludes land use, land-use change and forestry (LULUCF).
  • Low per capita emissions: India emitted 3.1 tonnes of CO 2 equivalent per person in 2025 , compared with the global average of 6.4 tonnes— the lowest among the six largest emitters assessed. These figures also exclude LULUCF.
  • Decadal emissions trend: During 2016–2025, India’s total greenhouse gas emissions increased by an annual average of 3.5%, while per capita emissions increased by 2.6% annually.
  • 2035 emissions: intensity target: India’s updated nationally determined contribution (NDC) seeks to reduce greenhouse gas emissions per unit of GDP by 47% from 2005 levels by 2035.
  • 2035 non: fossil electricity target: India aims for about 60% of cumulative installed electricity capacity from non-fossil sources by 2035 , conditional on technology transfer and international finance.
  • 2035 carbon: sink target: India aims for a cumulative increase of 3.5–4 billion tonnes of CO2 equivalent in carbon sinks through forest and tree cover , relative to 2005 levels. Emissions- Gap-Report-2026
  • Progress towards 2030 commitments: India is among six G20 members likely to achieve their unconditional 2030 targets under existing policies, alongside China, Indonesia, Russia, South Africa and Türkiye . The report also projects India to achieve its conditional 2030 target.
  • Projected emissions under NDCs: Under full implementation of its NDC targets, India’s annual emissions in 2035 are projected to be 1,254 million tonnes of CO 2 equivalent higher than in 2030 , with per capita emissions of 3.6 tonnes. Emissions- Gap-Report-2026
  • Coal: power construction: India and China together account for 95% of coal-power capacity currently under construction worldwide . This figure concerns construction, rather than existing installed capacity. Total Ramsar sites in India & Related Developments

  • Total Ramsar sites in India at Present: 103
  • State having the most number of Ramsar sites: Tamil Nadu (20)
  • Largest wetland under the Ramsar convention (in India): Sundarbans, West Bengal.
  • Smallest wetland under the Ramsar convention (in India): Vembannur Wetland Complex Tamil Nadu
  • First wetland under the Ramsar convention (in India): Chilika Lake and Keoladeo National Park (Rajasthan) (1981) Major Ramsar Sites in India 1. Sukhna Wetland (March 16, 2026)  Key Highlights Background
  • The Montreal Protocol (1987) was adopted to phase out CFCs and other ozone-depleting substances.
  • Countries have since eliminated nearly 99% of controlled ozone-depleting substances, helping the ozone layer recover.
  • HFCs became widely used in refrigeration and air- conditioning because they do not damage the ozone layer.
  • However, many HFCs have hundreds or thousands of times the warming impact of CO 2 over 100 years.
  • As HFC use expanded, the Federated States of Micronesia and Mauritius proposed bringing them under the Montreal Protocol in 2009.
  • The Kigali Amendment entered into force in January 2019 . It establishes binding schedules to reduce HFC production and consumption, while developing countries receive longer compliance periods.
  • Since limited HFC use can continue after reductions, it is called a phase-down rather than a phase-out.  India’s Kigali Commitments
  • India ratified the Kigali Amendment in 2021.  2028: Freeze HFC production and consumption at the agreed baseline.  2032: Reduce HFCs by 10% below the baseline.  2047: Achieve an 85% reduction.
  • The limits are calculated according to the gases’ warming impact.
  • Equipment purchased before the first reductions may remain in use well into the 2030s. Cabinet approves Green Energy Corridor Phase-III scheme On 30 September 2026, the Union Cabinet approved Green Energy Corridor Phase III to strengthen renewable electricity transmission and add battery storage.  Key Highlights  Green Energy Corridor
  • A Green Energy Corridor is a network of transmission lines and substations that carries electricity from renewable energy plants to the power grid.
  • Power evacuation means moving the electricity generated at a plant into this network.
  • Phase III will strengthen the Intra: State Transmission System (InSTS) within States and Union Territories.  Objectives and Key Features

It aims to support evacuation & Related Developments

  • It aims to support evacuation of up to 135 gigawatts (GW) of renewable energy and deployment of 50 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) by FY 2032–33.  Key Highlights  103rd Ramsar Site: Sauj Lake
  • Sauj Lake, located in Mainpuri district of Uttar Pradesh, is a shallow lake surrounded by farmland in the floodplain of the Ganga River.
  • It forms part of a larger network of wetlands, contributing to ecological connectivity in the wider landscape, and is close to Saman Bird Sanctuary.  102nd Ramsar Site: Sukhna Wetland
  • Located at the edge of the city of Chandigarh and at the base of the Outer Himalayas , Sukhna Wetland is a peri-urban reservoir that plays an important role in regulating sediment and water flows from the surrounding catchment.  101st Ramsar Site: Glaw Lake
  • Glaw Lake in Arunachal Pradesh was announced as India’s 101st Ramsar Site on 3 August 2026.
  • It became the first wetland from Arunachal Pradesh to be included in the List of Wetlands of International Importance.
  • Glaw Lake, locally known as Glaw Tuwi, is a natural freshwater wetland in Lohit district.
  • As of August 2026, India ranked third globally by number of Ramsar Sites, behind the United Kingdom with 176 sites and Mexico with 144 sites.  100th Ramsar Site: Jai Prakash Narayan Bird Sanctuary (Surha Tal)
  • On 5 June 2026, the Jai Prakash Narayan Bird Sanctuary, also known as Surha Tal, located in Ballia district of Uttar Pradesh, was recognised as India’s 100th Ramsar Site. India’s 昀椀rst petroglyph conservation park inaugurated in Leh PM Modi inaugurated India’s first Petroglyph Conservation Park on October 15, 2026 at Sindhu Ghat in Leh to protect Ladakh’s ancient rock art and archaeological heritage.  Key Highlights
  • A petroglyph conservation park is a dedicated open- air facility designed to protect, preserve, and showcase ancient rock carvings (petroglyphs) that are at risk from natural erosion, infrastructure expansion, and unregulated tourism. The Kigali Amendment marked its 10th anniversary The Kigali Amendment to the Montreal Protocol marked its 10th anniversary on October 15, 2026 . Adopted in Kigali, Rawanda on October 15, 2016. It seeks to phase down HFCs, which are used in cooling. Full implementation could avoid about 0.3 – 0.5°C global warming by 2100.
  • The scheme will strengthen transmission networks so that more renewable electricity can reach consumers.  Financial Outlay and Implementation
  • Target Completion: FY 2032–33.
  • Total Project Outlay: ₹1,86,405 crore.  Intra-State Transmission System development under GEC-III: ₹1,36,378 crore.  Deployment of 50 GWh of battery storage: ₹50,000 crore.
  • Total Central Financial Support: ₹54,082 crore.  Central Financial Assistance (CFA) will reduce intra- state transmission charges and help keep electricity costs affordable.  Expected Bene昀椀ts and Signi昀椀cance
  • Support India’s target of 900 GW installed non- fossil fuel capacity by 2035.
  • Enhance national energy security and promote environmentally sustainable development by reducing carbon emissions.
  • Generate direct and indirect employment in the power, manufacturing, construction and energy storage sectors.
  • Create long: term skilled jobs in grid management, operation and maintenance.

Improve renewable energy utilisation and & Related Developments

India’s Net Zero Portal and the NAPCC Dashboard Union Minister of State for Environment, Forest and Climate Change, Shri Kirti Vardhan Singh, on 16 September, 2026 launched India’s Net Zero Portal and the National Action Plan on Climate Change (NAPCC) Dashboard on the occasion of World Ozone Day 2026 in Mumbai. The two digital initiatives mark an important step towards strengthening transparency, coordination and evidence-based climate action.  Key Highlights
  • Net Zero emissions refer to a state where anthropogenic greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions by an entity (organization / industry / government) over a period of one year are compensated by GHG removals through anthropogenic interventions over the same period of time.  The Net Zero Portal
  • The Net Zero Portal is a centralised digital platform for voluntary registration and disclosure of Net Zero commitments by Indian entities across sectors.
  • Participating entities can disclose their greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, declare Net Zero targets and provide annual progress updates.  The NAPCC Dashboard
  • The NAPCC Dashboard provides a consolidated digital view of implementation and progress across the National Missions under the NAPCC.
  • It brings together mission: related information and identified indicators on a common platform, facilitating systematic monitoring by concerned Ministries and Departments.  Indian climate goals in 2015
  • India’s 2015 Intended Nationally Determined Contribution (INDC) contained eight goals. Three were quantitative targets, shown in the comparison below.
  • The remaining five concerned sustainable lifestyles, cleaner development, adaptation, finance and technology .  NDC updates in 2022 and 2026
  • A Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) is a country’s climate action plan under the Paris Agreement.
  • The 2022 Updated First NDC strengthened India’s targets for 2030 and explicitly supported Lifestyle for Environment (LiFE). India submitted its NDC for 2031–2035 on 24 April 2026, raising all three quantitative targets. Quantitative goal 2015 INDC By 2030 2022 update By 2030 2026 NDC By 2035 Reduction in GDP emissions intensity from the 2005 level 33–35% 45% 47% Share of cumulative installed electric power capacity from non-fossil sources About 40% About 50% About 60% Forest and tree carbon sink in billion tonnes of CO2 equivalent Additional 2.5–3.0 Additional 2.5–3.0 3.5–4.0 relative to 2005  Progress and future milestones
  • 2019: The original GDP emissions-intensity goal reached a 33% reduction from 2005, eleven years before the 2030 deadline.
  • 2021: The original 40% non-fossil installed-capacity target was achieved nine years early.
  • June 2025: The revised 50% non-fossil installed- capacity target was achieved five years early.
  • India’s Progress on Climate Commitments  India reduced the emissions intensity of GDP by 37.38% in 2022 compared with the 2005 level.  During 2005–2022, India created an additional carbon sink of 2.44 billion tonnes of CO2 equivalent through increased forest and tree cover.  This reflects India’s continued progress towards achieving its Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) targets.
  • Expansion of Non: Fossil Electricity Capacity  As of 30 September 2026, non-fossil fuel sources accounted for about 55% of India’s total installed electricity capacity.  India’s total installed electricity capacity stood at 558.8 GW , of which 308 GW came from non-fossil sources.  The growing share of non-fossil capacity highlights India’s transition towards a cleaner and low-carbon energy system. Swachh Sagar Surakshit Sagar 2026 The 昀椀fth edition of Swachh Sagar, Surakshit Sagar was held from 12 to 19 September 2026. The “Swachh Sagar, Surakshit Sagar/Clean & Related Developments

  • The “Swachh Sagar, Surakshit Sagar/Clean Coast Safe Sea “campaign is a citizen-led campaign for improving ocean health through collective action.

Project GIB Adds Three Chicks Project Great Indian Bustard (GIB) has added three more chicks to the conservation breeding programme in the last couple of days, taking the total number of chicks hatched so far in the fourth year of captive breeding to 26, Union Minister for Environment, Forest and Climate Change Shri Bhupender Yadav said on 14 June 2026 . The captive stock has now grown to 94 birds, with more chicks expected this season.
  • As per the report in the fourth year of GIB captive breeding, 26 chicks have hatched so far, including 18 through artificial insemination, four through natural breeding and four from wild-collected eggs.
  • As per the report in exchange for the wild eggs, three chicks have hatched in the wild in Rajasthan through a jumpstart intervention to improve founder genetic diversity and mitigate predation risk.
  • Project Great Indian Bustard (Project Bustard) was launched by the Chief Minister of Rajasthan on 5 June 2013 to conserve the Critically Endangered Great Indian Bustard ( Godawan; Ardeotis nigriceps), the State Bird of Rajasthan. Rajasthan became the first state to launch a dedicated conservation project for the species, initially in the Desert National Park (DNP), Jaisalmer.
  • The Great Indian Bustard is a flagship grassland bird and an indicator of healthy grassland ecosystems.
