Pradhan Mantri Surya Sarovar Yojana The Union Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, approved the Pradhan Mantri Surya Sarovar Yojana (PM-SSY) to accelerate 昀氀oating solar development. It combines Floating Solar Photovoltaic (FSPV) projects with co-located Energy Storage Systems (ESS) to support land-ef昀椀cient generation, grid 昀氀exibility and peak-demand management.  Background and Need
  • The National Institute of Solar Energy estimates floating-solar potential at approximately 102.18 GWp across reservoirs and suitable inland water bodies. With only around 700 MW operational when PM-SSY was approved, the scheme seeks to expand generation without increasing competition for scarce land.  Key Highlights
  • PM-SSY covers all States and Union Territories and seeks to add 5,000 MW of floating-solar capacity. Eligible projects will receive Central Financial Assistance of ₹1 crore per MW after successful commissioning. Feasibility studies, including bathymetry, hydrography and environmental studies, may receive up to ₹50 lakh per project.
  • The scheme is expected to reduce annual carbon dioxide emissions by approximately 10 million tonnes, create 16,000–17,000 full-time-equivalent employment opportunities and promote domestic flotation-system, solar-PV and storage manufacturing.  Solar Growth in India
  • Installed solar capacity increased more than 58 times, from 2.82 GW in March 2014 to 164.59 GW on 31 July 2026, making solar the largest individual component of renewable capacity. This included 122.57 GW ground-mounted, 30.74 GW grid- connected rooftop, 4.77 GW in hybrid projects and 6.51 GW off-grid solar.  Record Growth in FY 2025 to 2026
  • India added 44.61 GW of solar capacity in FY 2025–26, compared with 23.83 GW in FY 2024–25. Total non-fossil capacity reached 283.46 GW , including 274.68 GW renewable capacity, following a record annual non-fossil addition of 55.29 GW . Solar-module manufacturing capacity rose from about 2.3 GW in 2014 to around 172 GW by 31 March 2026. On 29 July 2025, renewables met a record 51.5% of electricity demand of 203 GW .  Enabling Infrastructure  Solar Parks Scheme and Bhadla Solar Park
  • The Solar Parks Scheme provides land, transmission connectivity and common infrastructure. Its initial 20 GW target expanded to 40 GW in 2017. By February 2026, 54 parks with 39,188 MW sanctioned capacity had been approved, including an inter-state floating solar park spanning Jharkhand and West Bengal. Rajasthan’s Bhadla Solar Park, developed during 2015–2020, covers nearly 5,700 hectares and has approximately 2,245 MW installed capacity.  Production Linked Incentive Scheme
  • The PLI Scheme for High: Efficiency Solar PV Modules began in 2021 with an initial outlay of ₹4,500 crore, followed by a ₹19,500 crore second tranche. By March 2026, reported cumulative investment was approximately ₹64,873 crore and direct employment 14,794. By 10 June 2026, domestic module and cell manufacturing capacities reached about 192 GW and 30 GW respectively. Module capacity enlisted under the Approved List of Models and Manufacturers (ALMM) crossed 200 GW in August 2026; this category differs from total manufacturing capacity.  Current Solar and Non Fossil Capacity Snapshot
  • On 31 July 2026, renewable capacity including large hydro was 291.73 GW . Total non-fossil capacity was 300.50 GW , comprising solar 164.59 GW , wind 58.14 GW , large and small hydro 57.24 GW , bio- power 11.75 GW and nuclear 8.78 GW . The nuclear figure excludes 100 MW under prolonged outage, temporarily removed from installed-capacity calculations from 31 May 2025. Non-fossil sources exceeded 54% of approximately 552 GW total capacity. A rounded 27 August update placed non- fossil capacity at 302–303 GW and solar at around 165 GW . The detailed 31 July break-up remains the source-wise statistical reference available up to 30 August 2026. India launched its 昀椀rst-ever Guide to Grasslands India launched its first-ever Guide to Grasslands and Other Open Natural Ecosystems (ONEs) of India on August 17, 2026 at an official side event of the 17th Conference of the Parties (COP17) to the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD) in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia.  Key Highlights
  • The Guide was launched under the aegis and guidance of the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change.
  • Its publication and the launch event were organised by the Ashoka Trust for Research in Ecology and the Environment (ATREE).  The event brought together representatives of the government, research institutions, international organisations and civil society.  Need for the Guide

Grasslands, scrublands and ravines have & Related Developments

  • Grasslands, scrublands and ravines have often been assessed mainly on the basis of their lack of dense tree cover and consequently described as “wastelands”.
  • However, these ecosystems provide habitats to specialised and endemic species and sustain pastoral and livestock-dependent communities.
  • Major Open Natural Ecosystems covered in the Guide  Himalayan and Terai grasslands  Thar and Banni landscapes  Deccan savannas  Rocky plateaus  Ravines and scrublands  Coastal ecosystems  Desert landscapes UNCCD COP17
  • Mongolia hosted UNCCD COP17 in Ulaanbaatar from 17–28 August 2026 under the theme “Restoring Land, Restoring Hope.” International Year of Rangelands and Pastoralists 2026
  • The UN General Assembly proclaimed 2026 as the International Year of Rangelands and Pastoralists (IYRP) through Resolution 76/253, adopted on 15 March 2022.
  • The proposal was spearheaded by Mongolia, while the Food and Agriculture Organization is the lead agency for its implementation. India’s First Dedicated Urban Night Safari The Supreme Court on 15 July 2026 permitted Uttar Pradesh to proceed with the proposed Kukrail Night Safari and Zoological Park Project in Lucknow.However, this is only conditional prior permission from the Court. It is not a blanket environmental clearance, and every separate statutory approval must be obtained before the related work begins. The order also remains subject to further directions of the Supreme Court.
  • The project had faced years of scrutiny because it is to come up inside the ecologically sensitive 2,027-hectare Kukrail Reserve Forest on the outskirts of Lucknow, which is also home to Uttar Pradesh’s first gharial rehabilitation centre, established in 1975.
  • The Rs 1,510: crore project will come up over 855 acres within the Kukrail Reserve Forest and will be developed in two phases:  Phase I: Night Safari and Eco-tourism Zone  Phase II: Day Zoo Prakriti Café Union Minister Prataprao Jadhav inaugurated Prakriti Café at Ayush Bhawan, New Delhi, on 22 July 2026. Prakriti Café is a workplace food outlet that brings the principles of Ayush Ahaar into everyday meal choices.  Key Highlights
  • The idea behind Prakriti Café is to bring the principles of Ayush closer to everyday life. A healthy lifestyle is built through simple and consistent choices, and mindful eating is an important part of that journey.
  • The café offers a range of fresh and wholesome food options inspired by the Ayush Ahaar initiative, which seeks to promote nutritious dietary practices rooted in India’s traditional knowledge systems. Ethanol Blending in India Ethanol is a renewable alcohol fuel. India’s Ethanol Blended Petrol (EBP) Programme mixes domestic ethanol with petrol to reduce crude-oil dependence, support farmers and rural industry, and lower road transport’s environmental impact.  Meaning and Present Status
  • E5, E10 and E20 contain about 5%, 10% and 20% ethanol by volume. E20 combines anhydrous ethanol with 80% petrol. Since November 2023, the Ethanol Supply Year (ESY) runs from 1 November to 31 October. India first achieved 20% blending in 2025; the November 2025 – August 2026 average was 20%. Public-sector outlets normally supply E20; premium grades XP100, poWer100 and Speed100 remain ethanol-free. From 1 April 2026, notified blended petrol requires a minimum Research Octane Number of 95.  Evolution of the Programme
  • Pilots began in 2001, and the EBP Programme launched in 2003 in nine States and four Union Territories. The 2018 National Policy on Biofuels targeted E20 by 2030; the 2022 amendment advanced it to ESY 2025–26. E10 was achieved in June 2022, and phased E20 rollout began on 6 February 2023.  Scale and Measurable Outcomes
  • Capacity grew from 421 crore litres in 2014 to about 2,000 crore litres in 2026. Procurement was about 38 crore litres in ESY 2013–14 and was projected to exceed 1,200 crore litres in ESY 2025–26. The 10 July 2026 update reported cumulative gains since ESY 2014–15: foreign-exchange savings exceeding ₹1.97 lakh crore, nearly 316 lakh tonnes of crude substitution, around 952 lakh tonnes of CO 2 reduction and farmer payments exceeding ₹1.66 lakh crore.
  • Why Ethanol Blending Matters  Energy Security  Farm and Rural Economy  Environment and Fuel Quality  Major Government Measures  Vehicle Compatibility and Mileage  International Perspective
  • E10 predominates in the United States; E85 contains about 51–83% ethanol and is intended for flex-fuel vehicles. Brazil mandated E30 from 1 August 2025. Brazil temporarily introduced E32 in ordinary and additivated petrol from August 1, 2026 for 180 days with one possible equal extension. Japan targets direct E10 by FY 2030 and E20 by FY 2040. India helped launch the Global Biofuels Alliance in September 2023 to promote sustainable biofuels, standards and best practices. Tamil Nadu’s 3D-Printed Arti昀椀cial Reef pilot under PMMSY Tamil Nadu has begun deploying advanced 3D-printed arti昀椀cial reef modules off Rameswaram in Ramanathapuram district. The pilot forms part of Phase II of Tamil Nadu’s arti昀椀cial-reef programme supported under the Pradhan Mantri Matsya Sampada Yojana (PMMSY) . It combines digital manufacturing with marine habitat restoration, 昀椀sheries development and coastal-community resilience.
  • Each module weighs about 1 tonne and has been developed by Chennai-based startup Tvasta, an IIT Madras-incubated company, in collaboration with the Visakhapatnam Regional Centre of the ICAR- Central Marine Fisheries Research Institute.
  • The project is being led by Principal Scientist and Head Dr Joe K. Kizhakudan.
  • Unlike conventional artificial reefs made from reinforced concrete structures, these modules feature complex geometries with multiple crevices, folds and attachment surfaces.

The initiative aims to restore & Related Developments

  • The initiative aims to restore fish habitats and strengthen the resilience of coastal communities.
  • The project is jointly funded by the Central and State governments in a 60:40 ratio. Sustainable Development Report 2026 and SDG Progress in India The Sustainable Development Report, 2026, released by the Sustainable Development Solutions Network (SDSN) on June 23, 2026, places India 94 th among 169 ranked countries with a score of 68.3 out of 100. On the SDSN scale, a score of 100 would indicate achievement of all the SDGs. India has climbed 18 places, from 112th in 2015 to 94 th in 2026 , making it one of the largest movers since the SDGs were adopted. East and South Asia have recorded the strongest regional progress since 2015. Among major economies, India improved by 18 places, while China improved by 14 places.  Key Highlights
  • India’s higher score has not yet placed the country on course to meet the 2030 Agenda. According to the 2026 assessment.
  • A calculation from the official 2026 data set finds trends for 75 available indicators for India :  Of these 25 are on track or maintaining achievement (33.3%).  Eight are moderately improving (10.7%), 33 are stagnating (44.0%) and Nine are decreasing (12.0%)  Thus moderate improvement and stagnation together account for 54.7%.  These are indicator shares, not shares of all 169 targets.  Zero Hunger and India’s Double Burden of Malnutrition
  • SDG 2: Zero Hunger remains one of India’s most serious development challenges. India’s overall performance under this goal is largely stagnating.
  • Of the 9 indicators assessed under SDG 2, 4 remain in the “significant challenges” or “major challenges” categories.
  • The only SDG 2 indicator presently on track is cereal yield, which reached 3.6 tonnes per hectare of harvested land in 2023 . Progress on nutrition- related indicators has been much slower.  Child stunting
  • Stunting, which refers to low height for age and usually reflects long-term undernutrition, declined from 37.9 per cent in 2015 to 35.5 per cent in 2020 in the series used by the SDG report.  Child wasting
  • Wasting, or low weight for height, indicates acute undernutrition.
  • The series used in the Sustainable Development Report shows that child wasting increased from 16.9 per cent in 2017 to 18.7 per cent in 2020.  Undernourishment and obesity
  • India is also off track in reducing undernourishment. The proportion of undernourished people declined from 12.1 per cent in 2015 to 10.5 per cent in 2018, but subsequently increased to 12 per cent in 2023 . The trend is classified as stagnating.
  • At the same time, adult obesity increased from 4.91 per cent in 2015 to 7.27 per cent in 2022.  Health, Climate and Governance Pressures
  • India faces major difficulties under SDG 3: Good Health and Well-being . Half of the 14 monitored health indicators are either stagnating or deteriorating.
  • The death rate associated with air pollution increased marginally from 131.72 deaths per 100,000 population in 2019 to 132 deaths per 100,000 in 2023.
  • Similarly, the probability of death from heart disease, cancer, diabetes and chronic lung disease among adults aged 30–70 increased from 22.6 per cent in 2015 to 23.6 per cent in 2021.
  • India’s carbon dioxide emissions from fossil-fuel combustion and cement production also continued to increase. Per capita emissions rose from 1.69 tonnes in 2015 to 2.21 tonnes in 2024.  Global SDG Outlook and Why India Matters
  • The global outlook remains difficult. In SDSN’s goal-level assessment, none of the 17 Sustainable Development Goals is fully on course for achievement by 2030.
  • Progress has been especially weak in sustainable cities, environmental protection, food systems and peaceful institutions. SDG 11, SDG 14, SDG 15 and SDG 16 are among the goals furthest off track, while some of the most poorly performing indicators are connected with SDG 2 and SDG 16.

Disaster & Related Developments

  • Disaster: related deaths fell by 65 per cent when comparing 2015-2024 with 2005-2014 (excluding COVID-19).
  • In 2025, global temperatures reached 1.43°C above pre-industrial levels , while atmospheric carbon dioxide reached its highest concentration in 2 million years. Centre of Excellence on Human- Wildlife Con昀氀ict Union Minister for Environment, Forest and Climate Change Bhupender Yadav inaugurated the Centre of Excellence (CoE) on Human–Wildlife Conflict at WII– SACON, Coimbatore, Tamil Nadu, on July 10, 2026.The Minister launched the National Human–Wildlife Conflict Portal and released the first edition of the publication series Current Status of Human–Wildlife Conflict in India: An Overview.  Key Highlights
  • Wildlife Institute of India’s premier research institute Salim Ali Centre for Ornithology and Natural History (SACON), Coimbatore, got a shot in the arm with the establishment of a national-level Centre of Excellence (CoE) on human - wildlife conflict. Namo Oxygen Parks Marking World Environment Day 2026, Union Environment Minister Bhupender Yadav and Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta on June 5 , 2026 inaugurated 18 Namo Oxygen Parks across the national capital and launched a series of green initiatives under the nationwide ‘Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam’ campaign.
  • The origin of these parks traces back to an act of environmental vandalism. In 2024, the Delhi Development Authority (DDA) illegally axed over 1,100 mature trees in the Southern Ridge, a protected reserve forest often called the ‘lungs of the capital’. E85 Fuel Rollout in India India’s launch of E85 fuel marks a shift from ordinary ethanol blending in petrol to a wider 昀氀ex-fuel mobility ecosystem. The policy is important for energy security, import reduction, farmer income, cleaner mobility and India’s long-term climate commitments.  Key Highlights
  • Union Minister for Petroleum and Natural Gas Shri Hardeep Singh Puri launched E85 fuel at an IndianOil retail outlet in New Delhi on the occasion of World Environment Day 2026 (June 5, 2026).
  • E85 is a high: ethanol blended fuel comprising 80–85 per cent ethanol and 14–19 per cent petrol, speci昀椀cally designed for use in 昀氀ex-fuel vehicles.
  • The initiative aims to facilitate the adoption of Flex- Fuel Vehicles (FFVs), which are capable of operating on ethanol blends from E20 to E100, without restricting consumers to a single blend.
  • Ethanol blending has increased from 1.53 per cent in 2014 to 20 per cent as of June 5, 2026, with the target achieved 昀椀ve years ahead of schedule.  Bene昀椀ts of E85:
  • E85 is priced nearly `20 per litre lower than conventional petrol to ensure that the economic bene昀椀ts of domestically produced ethanol are passed on to consumers.
  • Flex: fuel vehicles operating on E85 can reduce lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions by around 61 per cent compared to conventional petrol vehicles.  Flex-fuel vehicles
  • A 昀氀ex: fuel vehicle is typically understood as the one which holds the capability to run on different variants of fuel.
  • In the present context, the FFVs should be able to run on E20, E85, and E100 types of fuel.
  • The vehicle’s engine and fuel system automatically detect the ethanol content and adjust fuel injection and ignition timing accordingly. Andaman & Nicobar Islands Set Guinness World Records In May 2026, the Andaman and Nicobar Administration created two underwater Guinness World Records at Swaraj Dweep. The records were linked with the Administration’s larger effort to promote the islands as a global centre for scuba diving, marine tourism and responsible adventure tourism. Guinness World Records lists the Andaman and Nicobar Administration as the record holder for both underwater achievements.  Location: Swaraj Dweep
  • Swaraj Dweep, earlier known as Havelock Island, is one of the important tourist destinations of South Andaman.  Sequence of the Achievements

  • The second achievement followed with the creation of the “Tallest human stack underwater” at Swaraj Dweep. First International Conference on Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels The First Conference on Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels was an important step in global climat e governance because it focused specifically on how countries can reduce their dependence on coal, oil and gas in a just, orderly and equitable manner. The background to the conference lies in the COP28 Global Stocktake decision.  Guiding Principles
  • The Conference was guided by three key principles:  Participation by those ready to move forward.  Implementation as the guiding star, based on the shared scientific certainty.  Focus on solutions that meaningfully support the transition rather than delay it. India’s 1st Satellite-Tagged Ganges Soft-shell Turtle India’s first satellite-tagged Ganges soft-shell turtle, an endangered species, was released in the 1,302 sq. km Kaziranga National Park and Tiger Reserve in Assam on May 15, 2026.  Key Highlights

The Ganges soft & Related Developments

  • The Ganges soft: shell turtle ( Nilssonia gangetica ), a Schedule I animal under the Wildlife Protection Act of 1972, can be differentiated from other riverine turtles by its distinct arrowhead-shaped markings on the top of the head.
  • Ganges softshell turtle (Nilssonia gangetica) can be differentiated from other riverine turtles in having distinct arrow head shaped markings on top of head. India Ranks Third Globally in Renewable Energy Installed Capacity India ranks third in renewable electricity install ed capacity in IRENA ’s end-2025 international comparison, ahead of Brazil and behind China and the United States. The 昀椀gures below incorporate the July 2026 IRENA revision, the latest veri昀椀ed MNRE capacity snapshot and CEA ’s later generation data, checked on 18 October 2026.
  • IRENA ’s Renewable Capacity Statistics 2026 originally placed India at 250.52 GW . Its July 2026 Renewable Energy Statistics revised this estimate to 250.50 GW without changing India’s third position.
  • The revised end: 2025 country comparison places China first with 2,258.02 GW and the United States second with 466.45 GW .
  • Brazil follows India with 228.20 GW , followed by Germany with 200.90 GW , Japan with 134.95 GW and Canada with 110.39 GW .
  • The revised world renewable capacity total is 5,155.01 GW , compared with 5,149.28 GW in the March edition.
  • MNRE’s latest verified capacity figures are for 30 September 2026. Renewable capacity stood at 299.247 GW , and nuclear capacity of 8.780 GW raised total non-fossil capacity to 308.027 GW .
  • Renewable capacity comprised 171.051 GW of solar, 59.201 GW of wind, 11.748 GW of bio- power, 5.182 GW of small hydro and 52.065 GW of large hydro.
  • At the earlier 31 March 2026 milestone, India had 283.46 GW of non-fossil capacity, comprising 274.68 GW of renewable capacity and 8.78 GW of nuclear capacity.
  • The renewable component comprised 150.26 GW of solar, 56.09 GW of wind, 11.75 GW of bioenergy, 5.17 GW of small hydro and 51.41 GW of large hydro.
  • India achieved its 2030 NDC target of about 50% non-fossil share in cumulative installed electric power capacity in June 2025, five years ahead of schedule. This share reached 54.18% on 30 June 2026.
  • India’s NDC for 2031: 2035 raises the capacity-share target to about 60% by 2035, with technology transfer and low-cost international finance. India also targets 500 GW of non-fossil installed capacity by 2030 and net-zero emissions by 2070.
  • CEA ’s March 2026 Executive Summary gives an actual FY 2025–26 generation aggregate of 1,847.941 BU, including 7.831 BU imported from Bhutan. Total generation grew by 1.04%.
  • Fossil or thermal generation was 1,307.131 BU, accounting for a calculated 70.73% of this aggregate and declining by 4.10% from the preceding year.
  • Calculated non: fossil generation, including imports, was 540.811 BU or 29.27%; renewable generation including large hydro and imports was 485.620 BU or 26.28%.
  • Using the previous: year baseline published with the earlier provisional series, these updated totals imply growth of about 16.1% for non-fossil sources and 18.7% for renewables including hydro and imports.
  • CEA ’s renewable generation report records 310.585 BU from renewables excluding large hydro in FY 2025–26, an increase of 21.79%.
  • Wind generation reached 106.700 BU, growing by 28.02%, while solar generation reached 174.757 BU, growing by 21.23%.

Together, wind and solar generated & Related Developments

  • Together, wind and solar generated a calculated 281.456 BU, equivalent to 15.23% of the Executive Summary aggregate including Bhutan imports.
  • The 8 April 2026 provisional release reported coal generation of 1,250.189 BU, a 67.7% share and a decline of 3.69%. These coal figures belong to that earlier provisional series and should retain that qualification.
  • CEA ’s domestic generation series excludes Bhutan imports. On this basis, FY 2025–26 generation was 1,840.110 BU, including 532.980 BU from non-fossil sources and 477.789 BU from renewables.
  • Installed capacity and electricity generation measure different things. Renewable capacity is part of non- fossil capacity, which also includes nuclear power. Reaching a 50% capacity share therefore does not mean that non-fossil sources generate 50% of annual electricity. COP 15 of the Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species Migratory species are animals that move across countries, continents, oceans, rivers and skies for food, breeding, climate suitability or survival. Their protection cannot be done by one country alone because their routes cut across political boundaries. This is why the Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals (CMS) , also known as the Bonn Convention, is important for global biodiversity governance.
  • The 15 th Meeting of the Conference of the Parties to CMS (CMS COP15) was held in Campo Grande, Brazil, from March 23 to March 29, 2026, under the theme “Connecting Nature to Sustain Life.”  Major Outcome
  • The biggest outcome of COP15 was the decision to provide new or upgraded treaty protection to 40 species, subspecies and populations of birds, aquatic wildlife and terrestrial animals.
  • These were added to or upgraded within CMS Appendices I and II. With this, the Convention now covers over 1,200 unique species.  Brazil’s Role and Next COP
  • With the conclusion of COP15, Brazil holds the CMS COP Presidency for the next three years . The focus during this period will be on implementing the decisions taken in Campo Grande.
  • The next CMS COP , COP16, will be held in Bonn, Germany, in 2029 . It will coincide with the 50th anniversary of CMS , making it symbolically important because Bonn is the city where the treaty was signed in 1979. Project Him Sarovar Project Him Sarovar is a new water-security initiative of the Ladakh Administration. It has been designed for Ladakh’s cold desert conditions, where water is a lifeline for agriculture, settlements and livelihoods. The project focuses on scientific snow harvesting , conservation of snowmelt and glacial melt , and creation of small water bodies so that seasonal water, which usually flows away, can be stored and used during lean periods.  Key Highlights
  • Project Him Sarovar was launched on April 10, 2026 by Vinai Kumar Saxena, LG of Ladakh.
  • Under Phase I, 50 water bodies were proposed with 30 in Leh and 20 in Kargil covering nearly 25% of Ladakh’s villages. As of June 12, 2026. 5 reservoirs had already been completed and the target was to create 100 such water bodies by next year. Congo 50.2 India’s National Repository for Deep-Sea Fauna India has taken an important step in marine biodiversity conservation by designating the “Bhavasagara” Referral Centre at the Centre for Marine Living Resources & Ecology (CMLRE), Kochi, Kerala, as the National Repository for Deep-Sea Fauna on March 24, 2026. The designation was made by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC), while CMLRE functions under the Ministry of Earth Sciences (MoES).  About Bhavasagara Referral Centre
  • The Bhavasagara Referral Centre is a specialised national facility dedicated to deep-sea biodiversity. It acts as a repository for deep-sea faunal collections from India’s Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ).
  • Bhavasagara maintains over 3560 taxonomically identified and geo-referenced voucher specimens.
  • The repository will also support capacity building in deep-sea taxonomy. State of India’s Environment (SOE) 2026 Report The State of India’s Environment 2026 report was released by the Centre for Science and Environment (CSE) and Down to Earth Magazine on February 25, 2026 at the Anil Agarwal Dialogue 2026 in Nimli near Alwar Rajasthan. The annual SOE series began in 2014, though CSE’s longer environmental reporting tradition goes back to the 1982 Citizen’s First Report.  Key Highlights
  • The report states that 2025 recorded the highest rise in the frequency and impact of extreme weather events in India during the last four years.
  • These events included heatwaves, cold waves, heavy rainfall, and 昀氀oods.
  • From January 1 to November 30, 2025 , extreme weather events occurred on 99% of the days in India, causing 4,419 deaths and affecting at least 17.41 million hectares of crop area.
  • In comparison, 2024 saw such events on 88% of the days, with 3,393 deaths and 3.61 million hectares of crop damage, while 2023 recorded them on 89% of the days , causing 3,208 deaths and affecting 2.09 million hectares.
  • Among the States, Himachal Pradesh was the worst affected with extreme weather on 267 days, followed by Kerala with 173 days and Madhya Pradesh with 162 days.  Air Pollution, Freshwater Stress, and Novel Entities
  • On air pollution, CSE’s analysis shows that only 15% of India’s population, about 200 million people, lives within 10 km of a continuous air quality monitor.
  • This means that 85% of the population, or over 1.2 billion people, lives beyond 10 km of a continuous monitor in CSE’s February 2026 analysis.
  • The report notes that ocean acidity has increased by 30–40% since the industrial era , threatening marine ecosystems, including corals and shell- forming organisms , and weakening the ocean’s ability to absorb carbon. International Renewable Energy Agency Recently, the Sixteenth Session of the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA) Assembly concluded on 12 January 2026 in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates (UAE) , marking a signi昀椀cant milestone in global deliberations on sustainable energy transition. The Assembly was held under the theme “Powering Humanity: Renewable Energy for Shared Prosperity”.

India’s First Indigenous Designed Pollution Control Vessel
  • Marking a major step forward in India’s pursuit of Aatmanirbharta in shipbuilding and maritime capability development, Raksha Mantri Shri Rajnath Singh commissioned Indian Coast Guard Ship (ICGS) ‘Samudra Pratap’, the 昀椀rst of two Pollution Control Vessels built by Goa Shipyard Limited (GSL), in Goa on January 05, 2026.
  • With over 60% indigenous content, ICGS Samudra Pratap is India’s 昀椀rst indigenously designed pollution control vessel and the largest ship in the ICG 昀氀eet to date.

  • The report was launched on 17 November 2025 during COP30 in Belém, Brazil.

UNEP states the GMP includes & Related Developments

  • UNEP states the GMP includes 159 countries + the European Commission.
  • The report notes that (as of April 2025) those members covered about 57% of global anthropogenic methane emissions.
  • Sector shares of global anthropogenic methane are about 42% agriculture, 38% energy, 20% waste.
  • G20+ countries are responsible for about 65% of total anthropogenic methane emissions and hold 72% of global technicale methane mitigation potential by 2030. 30th Conference of the Parties to the UNFCCC: COP30 COP30, held in Belém in the Amazon region, became strongly associated with an “implementation-昀椀rst” framing. Alongside the political track, COP30 also showcased a large- scale implementation architecture through the COP30 Global Climate Action Agenda (GCAA)—a renewed framework built on the Marrakech Partnership and the Global Stocktake response, organized into six thematic axes and driven by 30 activation groups (482 initiatives).  Key Highlights
  • COP30 took place in Belem from November 10-22, 2025.
  • In parallel, the COP30 Global Climate Action Agenda (GCAA) operationalized this “implem- entation turn” through a four-step activation cycle–Coordinate, Measure, Showcase, Scale.
  • Coordinate: 30 activation groups with 482 initiatives aligned toward 30 key objectives.  COP30’s “Implementation Shift” and the Belém Package
  • Unlike earlier COPs that leaned heavily toward announcing new pledges, COP30 marked a clear shift toward implementation.
  • The central political outcome was widely described as the Belém Package —around 29 decisions functioning less as a new “target set” and more as an implementation toolkit to deliver the Paris Agreement.
  • The package’s conceptual foundation was the Global Mutirão decision.
  • “Mutirão” (a Brazilian term) implies the community coming together for shared work—similar in spirit to India’s concept of “Shramdaan.”  Accelerating Action: Mitigation, Adaptation, and Finance (with Finance the Most Contested) (1) Climate Finance: reinforcing obligations + tracking and delivery tools
  • A major achievement attributed to COP30 was strengthening the interpretation of Paris Agreement Article 9.1 (developed countries “shall provide” 昀椀nancial resources to developing countries).
  • A two: year “Climate Finance Work Programme” was launched.
  • Tropical Forest Forever Facility (TFFF): Brazil- led blended 昀椀nance mechanism targeting USD 125 billion, designed like a “scholarship for forests,” delivering performance-based payments for protecting tropical forests (monitored via satellite data). (2) Adaptation: operationalizing the GGA and scaling resilience delivery
  • COP30 decisions treat the Baku Adaptation Road Map as an ongoing work stream with a de昀椀ned 昀椀rst phase (2026-28). (3) Mitigation & Transition: the Belém 4x Pledge and sectoral scaling
  • To curb emissions and accelerate system transitions, COP30 advanced the implementation of the Belém 4x Pledge. The pledge was launched at the Pre- COP .  Target: quadruple the use of sustainable fuels by 2035 relative to 2024 (including green hydrogen, advanced biofuels, and e-fuels).  Tracking: IEA to track progress.
  • 23 countries of昀椀cially endorsed the pledge, with broad non-state support (including major industry actors).  Just Transition
  • Belém Action Mechanism (BAM): adopted to support a socially fair transition away from fossil fuels—focused on worker reskilling and social dialogue, though without a large dedicated fund.
  • The Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative announced its 18th nation-state supporter (Cambodia) and presented a PAS with next steps through the Climate Action Agenda.  Health
  • Belém Health Action Plan: launched to build climate-resilient health systems to tackle heatwaves and vector-borne diseases.
  • The Belém Health Action Plan is described as the world’s 昀椀rst international climate adaptation plan dedicated entirely to health , launched with an initial USD 300 million investment from a coalition of 35+ philanthropies, funding research, policy, solutions for extreme heat/air pollution/ infectious diseases, and strengthening health systems via climate-data integration.
  • COP30 also marked “Race to Zero for health care hits 100”: The campaign has reached 100 institutions representing 14,000+ hospitals/ health centers across 28 countries.  India’s position at COP30 (as reflected in negotiations and blocs)  Finance is an obligation: India emphasized that under Article 9.1, climate 昀椀nance is a legal obligation, not charity, and demanded USD 1.3 trillion/year.  Opposition to CBAM: India strongly opposed unilateral trade measures like the EU’s CBAM, arguing they violate CBDR-RC and resemble “green protectionism.”
  • Looking ahead: COP31 (Türkiye, 2026) and the “Belém Mission to 1.5°C”

  • The Uttar Pradesh Budget for 2026: 27 was presented by Finance Minister Suresh Kumar Khanna on February 11, 2026 . This is a large, expansionary budget with a strong focus on growth, infrastructure, welfare, and technology-led development.
  • The budget combines higher expenditure , continued revenue surplus , and a fiscal deficit kept at 3% of GSDP, which indicates that the state is trying to balance development spending with fiscal discipline.  Economic Background of Uttar Pradesh
  • The Gross State Domestic Product (GSDP) of Uttar Pradesh for 2026–27, at current prices, is projected at ₹39.8 lakh crore . This implies a 28% increase over the revised estimate for 2025–26.
  • In 2024: 25, Uttar Pradesh’s GSDP at constant prices is estimated to grow by 9%, which is higher than the estimated 6.5% GDP growth for India in the same year.
  • The structure of the state’s economy in 2024–25 shows that agriculture contributes 27% , manufacturing contributes 26% , and services contribute 47% of the economy. This means services remain the largest sector, but agriculture continues to hold a very significant share in Uttar Pradesh’s economy.
  • Uttar Pradesh’s per capita GSDP in 2024–25 is estimated at ₹1,24,366, which is an increase of 11.6% over 2023–24. It is noted that India’s per capita GDP is estimated at ₹2,34,859 in 2024–25.  Overall Size of the Budget
  • The total expenditure proposed in the budget for 2026–27 is ₹9,12,696 crore . This is 27% higher than the revised estimate for 2025–26.
  • Out of this, debt repayment is estimated at ₹61,795 crore. Therefore, net expenditure , which is the more meaningful measure for policy analysis, stands at ₹8,50,901 crore.
  • Total receipts are budgeted at ₹8,48,233 crore , while net receipts excluding borrowings are estimated at ₹7,32,420 crore. The difference is to be partly met through borrowings.   • The budget estimates a revenue surplus of ₹64,458 crore, which is 1.6% of GSDP , in 2026–27. This means the state expects its revenue receipts to exceed its revenue expenditure.
  • However, this revenue surplus is lower than the revised estimate for 2025–26, when revenue surplus was estimated at ₹74,348 crore, or 2.4% of GSDP. This suggests that while the state remains in surplus on the revenue account, the cushion is becoming smaller.
  • The fiscal deficit for 2026: 27 is budgeted at ₹1,18,481 crore, which is 3% of GSDP. This is the same ratio as the revised estimate for 2025–26 and aligns with the 16th Finance Commission’s recommended annual limit of 3% of GSDP for states for 2026–31.
  • The primary deficit is estimated at ₹49,560 crore, or 1.2% of GSDP, in 2026–27. This is significantly higher than the revised estimate for 2025–26, indicating a larger gap even before interest payments are considered.  Expenditure Pattern
  • Revenue expenditure in 2026: 27 is proposed at ₹6,64,471 crore , which is 31% higher than the revised estimate for 2025–26. Revenue expenditure mainly includes salaries, pensions, interest payments, grants, and subsidies.
  • Capital outlay is budgeted at ₹1,77,744 crore , which is an increase of 11% over the revised estimate of 2025–26. Capital outlay is important because it creates assets such as roads, buildings, and infrastructure.
  • The rise in revenue expenditure is being driven by higher spending on pension, general education , rural development , grants to local bodies and Panchayati Raj institutions, and energy.  Receipts Structure
  • Revenue receipts for 2026: 27 are estimated at ₹7,28,928 crore , which is 26% higher than the revised estimate for 2025–26.
  • Of the total revenue receipts, roughly 50% will be raised by the state from its own resources and the remaining 50% will come from the Centre , either as the state’s share in central taxes or as grants.
  • State’s own tax revenue is estimated at ₹3,34,491 crore in 2026–27, which is 48% higher than the revised estimate for 2025–26.
  • State’s own non: tax revenue is estimated at ₹26,754 crore , which is almost double the revised estimate for 2025–26. The budget attributes this mainly to increases in concession fees, rent, royalty, share capital receipts from Uttar Pradesh Power Corporation for rural electrification, and interest income.
  • The state’s share in central taxes is estimated at ₹2,68,911 crore, while grants from the Centre are estimated at ₹98,772 crore.  Tax Revenue and Tax Trends
  • Among own tax sources, State GST is projected to be the largest source , contributing 45% of the state’s own tax revenue in 2026–27. State GST is budgeted at ₹1,49,956 crore, which is 79% higher than the revised estimate for 2025–26.
  • State excise is estimated at ₹71,278 crore, or 17% higher than the revised estimate for 2025–26.

Sales tax/VAT is projected at & Related Developments

  • Sales tax/VAT is projected at ₹48,115 crore , showing a 43% increase over the revised estimate of 2025–26.
  • Stamp duty and registration fees are estimated at ₹43,802 crore, while taxes on vehicles are budgeted at ₹15,808 crore.
  • The revised estimates for most own: tax revenue heads in 2025–26 were lower than the original budget estimates, which suggests that revenue projections have recently been difficult to realise fully.  Debt, Liabilities, and Guarantees
  • At the end of 2026: 27, the state’s outstanding liabilities are estimated at 23.1% of GSDP, which is lower than the revised estimate of 27.6% of GSDP for 2025–26. This indicates an expected improvement in the debt burden relative to the size of the economy. Rupee Comes In, 2026-27 (B.E.) Rupee Goes Out, 2026-27 (B.E.)   • It is noted that as of 31 March 2025, Uttar Pradesh’s outstanding government guarantees were estimated at ₹1,71,924 crore , which is 5.8% of GSDP. These are contingent liabilities that may become actual obligations in the future.  Sector-Wise Expenditure Priorities
  • The sectors listed account for 60% of the total sectoral expenditure budgeted by the state in 2026–27.
  • Education, Sports, Arts, and Culture have been allocated ₹1,08,154 crore, which is 28% higher than the revised estimate of 2025–26.
  • Energy has been allocated ₹56,621 crore , an increase of 17% over the revised estimate of 2025–26.
  • Health and Family Welfare has been allocated ₹53,326 crore, which is 24% higher than the revised estimate for 2025–26.
  • Transport has been allocated ₹50,391 crore, while Rural Development receives ₹49,044 crore , with rural development showing a sharp 59% increase over the revised estimate.
  • Social Welfare and Nutrition has been allocated ₹42,263 crore , Police gets ₹41,898 crore , Agriculture and Allied Activities gets ₹30,938 crore, and Urban Development gets ₹27,532 crore.  Important Scheme Allocations by Sector
  • In education, Rs. 55,792 crore has been allocated towards assistance to non-government primary schools, and ₹7,738 crore has been allocated for primary education under Samagra Shiksha Abhiyan.
  • In energy, ₹21,500 crore has been allocated towards power subsidy.
  • In health, ₹5,793 crore is allocated for urban health services (Allopathy) and ₹6,818 crore for rural health services (Allopathy).
  • In transport, ₹38,592 crore has been allocated towards capital outlay on roads and bridges.
  • In rural development, ₹6,102 crore is allocated for Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana-Rural , ₹5,544 crore for MGNREGS, and ₹4,580 crore for Ajeevika Mission.
  • In social welfare, ₹8,950 crore has been allocated towards old age/farmer pensions , and ₹3,500 crore towards Nirashrit Mahila Pension Yojana.
  • In agriculture, ₹2,400 crore is allocated for subsidy for power supply to private tubewells , and ₹638 crore for the conversion of diesel pumps to solar pumps.
  • In urban development, ₹6,842 crore is allocated towards Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana-Urban.
  • In agriculture, the state will launch a programme to encourage agriculture marketing and exports.
  • For ease of doing business, industrial requirements such as licensing and registration will be simplified in the next phase under the principle of Jan Vishwas. Uttar Pradesh Economic Survey 2025–26 On February 9, 2026 , the Government of Uttar Pradesh presented the Uttar Pradesh Economic Survey 2025–26.
  • With the vision of rapid development, the state has set a target of becoming a one trillion dollar economy.
  • According to quick estimates at current prices, the Gross State Domestic Product (GSDP) of Uttar Pradesh increased from `13.30 lakh crore in 2016– 17 to `26.67 lakh crore in 2023–24.
  • In 2024: 25, advance estimates placed it at `29.62 lakh crore , while revised estimates placed it at `29.78 lakh crore.
  • With a 13.4% growth over the previous year , the GSDP is estimated at `30.25 lakh crore , higher than both earlier estimates.
  • In 2025: 26, the state economy is estimated to reach approximately `36 lakh crore.
  • According to the research report ‘Ecowrap’ by State Bank of India , India is moving towards becoming the third-largest economy in the world by 2027, surpassing Japan and Germany, and Uttar Pradesh is expected to play a decisive role in this achievement.
  • Uttar Pradesh’s GSDP at current prices increased from `13.30 lakh crore in 2016–17 to `30.25 lakh crore in 2024–25 (quick estimates) , registering a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 10.8% over 8 years.
  • In 2024: 25, the state contributes about 9.1% to India’s GDP.  Structural Changes in Economy

From 2017 & Related Developments

  • From 2017: 18 to 2024–25 , structural changes are visible in the state economy:  The primary sector remained almost stable (from 25.9% to 25.8%).  The secondary sector increased significantly (from 25.4% to 27.2% ), indicating growth in industrial production, manufacturing, and infrastructure.  The tertiary sector declined slightly (from 48.8% to 47.0%), indicating a balanced restructuring of services.  Comparison with National Economy
  • At the national level:  The Primary sector declined from 20.4% to 19.7%  The Secondary sector declined from 27.0% to 25.3%  The Tertiary sector increased from 52.5% to 54.9% Sector-wise Contribution in 2024–25 Sub-sector Share Agriculture, forestry and 昀椀sheries 24.9% Construction 12.9% Real estate and professional services 13.9% Manufacturing 11.7% Trade and hotels 8.3% Transport and communication 7.4%  Agriculture and Allied Sector
  • The agriculture and allied sector has shown continuous progress.
  • Its Gross Value Added increased from `2.96 lakh crore in 2016–17 to `6.95 lakh crore in 2024–25 , growing at a CAGR of 11.2% , which is nearly a doubling of value.
  • Advance estimates placed it at `6.86 lakh crore , while revised estimates placed it at `7.12 lakh crore.
  • Crops remain the main component , contributing the highest share of 67.4% in the Gross Value Added (GVA) of the agriculture and allied sector.
  • Livestock contributes 24.7%, forestry contributes 4.5%, and fisheries and aquaculture contribute 3.5%.
  • In 2024: 25, the total foodgrain production in the state increased by 9.9% over the previous year , reaching 737.4 lakh metric tonnes , and the state continues to hold a leading position in the country.
  • Within this, oilseed production increased by 57.9%, total cereals increase by 11%, including a 23.6% increase in paddy and a 6.3% increase in wheat production.
  • Milk production increased by 33.6%, placing the state at the first position in the country.
  • Egg production increased by 167%.
  • In 2025: 26, fish production is estimated to increase further by 15.7%, reflecting efforts towards sustainable agriculture and diversification.  Forestry and Land Use
  • It increased from 23,437.53 sq. km in 2021 to 23,996.72 sq. km in 2023, registering an increase of 559.19 sq. km (2.39%).
  • Uttar Pradesh ranks second in the country in terms of increase in forest and tree cover.  Secondary Sector (Industry and Infrastructure)
  • The Gross Value Added (GVA) of the secondary sector increased from `3.34 lakh crore in 2016–17 to `7.60 lakh crore in 2024–25, growing at a CAGR of 10.8%.
  • Within the secondary sector:  The construction sector leads with a 47.4% share, reflecting rapid expansion of infrastructure and urban development.  The manufacturing sector contributes 42.9%, indicating strong industrial capacity and investment.  The electricity sector contributes 9.6%, ensuring energy availability and continuity of industrial activities.
  • According to the Annual Survey of Industries 2023–24, the Gross Value Added of industries in the state increased by 25% over the previous year, which is the highest among major states and more than double the national growth rate of 11.9%.  Infrastructure Development
  • In Varanasi, the country’s first urban ropeway project is under construction, which is considered a major step in urban transport.
  • The state is developing as the capital of expressways, with:  7 operational expressways  3 expressways under construction  12 proposed
  • At present, the state has 12 domestic and 4 international airports (Lucknow, Varanasi, Kushinagar, and Ayodhya).
  • With the start of operation at Noida International Airport at Jewar (Gautam Buddha Nagar), the state will become the first in India with 5 international airports.
  • The total road network includes 12,123 km of National Highways, and 90 National Highways pass through the state.  Energy and Digital Connectivity
  • Uttar Pradesh achieved a leading position in power generation, producing 126.50 thousand gigawatt- hours by December 2025–26.
  • The state also ranked first in the country in terms of the number of internet subscribers, with 13.82 crore subscribers as of September 2025–26.  Service Sector
  • The service sector contributes 47.0% to the state economy.
  • The Gross Value Added (GVA) of the service sector increased from `5.95 lakh crore in 2016–17 to `13.10 lakh crore in 2024–25 (quick estimates) , growing at a CAGR of 10.4%.
  • The progress of the service sector in Uttar Pradesh has been remarkable in 2024–25 compared to 2016–17, as the Gross Value Added (GVA) of all sub-sectors has almost doubled.  State Finances
  • The total state budget increased from `3.47 lakh crore in 2016–17 to `8.33 lakh crore in 2025–26 , recording an increase of `4.86 lakh crore over nine years.
  • The public debt: to-GDP ratio declined from 29.3% in 2016–17 to 28.0% in 2024–25 , which is significantly lower than the national level (81.3%) and the global average (92.8%) , indicating fiscal stability and discipline.  Per Capita Income

The per capita income (net) & Related Developments

  • The per capita income (net) increased from `54,564 in 2016–17 to `1,09,844 in 2024–25 , growing at a CAGR of about 9.1%.
  • During the period 2020: 21 to 2024–25, the growth rate was higher at 14.7%.
  • The per capita income (gross) was estimated at `1,26,304 in 2024–25.  Population and Demographic Trends
  • As per March 2026 estimates, Uttar Pradesh has a population of 25.19 crore, which is:  17.8% of India’s population (141.51 crore)  3.0% of the world’s population (830 crore)
  • India contributes about 17% of the global population.
  • If Uttar Pradesh were a country, it would rank 5th in the world in population , after India, China, the United States (33.5 crore), and Indonesia (27.7 crore).  Population Growth and Fertility
  • The population growth rate declined from 1.85% per year in 2011 to 1.70% in 2021, and is expected to decline further to 0.58% during 2026–2051.
  • The Total Fertility Rate (TFR) declined from 2.7 (NFHS-4, 2015–16) to 2.4 (NFHS-5, 2019–21) and is expected to reach the replacement level of 2.1 soon.  Life Expectancy and Social Indicators
  • Life expectancy is expected to increase as follows :  Males: from 62.5 years (2011) to 73.2 years (2051)  Females: from 65.0 years (2011) to 77.1 years (2051)  Sex Ratio and Age Structure
  • The sex ratio at birth in Uttar Pradesh was 111 boys per 100 girls in 2011.
  • The age pyramid shows clear demographic changes:  2011: wide base (high child population)  2026: higher proportion of the working-age population (20–34 years)  2046: decline in the 0–14 age group and an increase in the population aged 40 and above.  Dependence on Central Taxes
  • The state’s dependence on central taxes has been continuously declining.
  • It was 56.0% in 2016: 17, and is estimated to decline to 46.4% in 2025–26.
  • The State’s Own Tax Revenue increased from `0.86 lakh crore in 2016–17 to `2.09 lakh crore in 2024–25 (advance estimates), which is about 2.5 times growth.
  • The capital expenditure increased from `69.79 thousand crore in 2016–17 to `147.72 thousand crore in 2024–25 (advance estimates) , reflecting development-oriented priorities.
  • The public debt: to-GDP ratio declined from 29.3% in 2016–17 to 28.0% in 2024–25 , which is significantly lower than the national level (about 81.3%) and global average (about 92.8%) , indicating fiscal discipline and stability.  Budget and Receipts
  • Over the last nine years, the total budget increased at a CAGR of about 10.3%, reaching approximately `8.09 lakh crore in 2025–26.
  • During the same period, total receipts increased at 10.2% CAGR, reaching about `7.79 lakh crore.
  • As per the 2025: 26 budget:  Revenue expenditure: `5.83 lakh crore
  • Compared to 2024: 25 revised estimates:  Revenue receipts increased by 21.0%  Revenue expenditure increased by 19.2%
  • Over the last nine years (2016: 17 to 2025–26):  Revenue receipts grew at a CAGR of 11.1%  Revenue expenditure grew at a CAGR of 11.9%
  • The ratio of revenue expenditure to revenue receipts declined from 92% (2016–17) to 89.2% (2024–25) and is estimated at 87.9% in 2025–26.  Composition of Revenue Receipts
  • Revenue receipts represent income from regular government operations.
  • The main components include:  The state’s own resources (tax and non-tax revenue)  Transfers from the Central Government (share in the divisible pool and grants)
  • Revenue receipts increased from `2.57 lakh crore (2016–17) to `6.63 lakh crore (2025–26 BE).
  • Over nine years:  State tax and non-tax revenue grew at 12% a CAGR  Central transfers grew at a CAGR of 10.3%.  Breakup of Revenue
  • State Tax Revenue  2016: 17: `0.86 lakh crore  2025–26: `2.95 lakh crore  Growth rate: CAGR of 14.7%
  • Share in Central Taxes  Estimated at `2.55 lakh crore in 2025–26  Growth rate: 9.9%
  • Non: Tax Revenue  State non-tax revenue: `0.25 lakh crore (2025–26)  Grants from the Centre: increased at a CAGR of 11.7% to about `0.88 lakh crore (2025–26).

Bihar Current Affairs

Bihar state current developments, data centres, GSVA growth rates, agriculture milestones, and governance portals.

 Bihar’s First AI & Related Developments

  •  Bihar’s First AI: Ready Data Center
  • Chief minister Samrat Choudhary on October 13,2026 inaugurated a Rs 400-crore data centre of CtrlS Data centers Ltd in Patliputra industrial area in Patna with an initial IT load capacity of 12 MW .
  • Along with it CtrlS Data Centers has also signed a letter of intent (LoI) with the Bihar government to invest ₹10,000 crore in a proposed 150 MW hyper- scale AI factory in Bodh Gaya.  Sankalp Dashboard and Samanvay Portal
  • Recently on October 13,2026, Bihar chief minister launched the Sankalp Dashboard and Samanvay Portal.
  • The Sankalp dashboard brings the work of all 48 state departments onto one digital platform to improve transparency and accountability.  Cabinet clears Bihar’s 昀椀rst tech park at Gardanibagh, Patna
  • The state cabinet on 12 October ,2026 approved Bihar’s first tech park at Gardanibagh in Patna, to anchor an IT and IT-enabled services (ITES) ecosystem in the capital.
  • NBCC (India) Ltd, a central public sector enterprise, will build it, and the state is authorised to sign an MoU with it.  Bihar MSME Policy, 2026
  • The policy was unveiled on 8 October 2026 , alongside the inauguration of MSME centres in all districts to support entrepreneurs.
  • It aims to promote industrialisation, investment and employment, and develop Bihar as a manufacturing hub of Eastern India.
  • Major Targets in the Draft:  Formalise 1 crore MSMEs across manufacturing and services.  Generate over 1 crore direct and indirect jobs.  Integrate 500-plus MSMEs into Global Value Chains (GVCs).  Train 1 lakh MSMEs annually in Industry 4.0 and sector-specific skills.  Establish four Technology/Extension Centres in Kosi, Bhagalpur, Munger and Purnea.
  • Incentives Proposed in the Draft:  Capital subsidy: Provide 25% in Category A districts and 30% in Category B districts, capped at ₹25 lakh, ₹1.5 crore and ₹5 crore for micro, small and medium enterprises, respectively.  Additional support: Provide 10% additional capital subsidy to women, SC, ST, BC, Divyang and transgender entrepreneurs.  Employment support: Reimburse employers’ EPF contributions for three years, capped at ₹24,000 per employee annually, subject to employment thresholds.  Electricity subsidy: Reimburse 20% of eligible low- tension power charges for three years.  Rooftop solar subsidy: Provide 25% of installation cost, capped at ₹5 lakh, for systems up to 300 kW .  Stamp duty: Provide 100% reimbursement on land purchases by new manufacturing enterprises. Note: These detailed targets and incentives are from the July 2026 draft.  Rising Bihar - Investor Summit 2026
  • Rising Bihar: Investor Summit 2026 was organised on the theme Bihar – The Emerging Investment Destination of India on 1st October 2026 at Hotel Taj City Centre, Patna.
  • The summit served as a premier platform to showcase the Government of Bihar’s vision for industrial growth.  Vinay Kumar appointed as the Chief Information Commissioner
  • 1991: batch IPS officer Vinay Kumar has taken Voluntary Retirement Scheme (VRS) from the post of Bihar Director General of Police (DGP) and has been appointed as the Chief Information Commissioner (CIC) of Bihar.  Bihar Cabinet gives nod to Bihar Green Hydrogen Policy, 2026
  • Intended to reduce carbon emissions, the Bihar cabinet on September 30, 2026 gave its nod to the draft “Bihar Green Hydrogen Policy, 2026” to promote renewable energy and reduce dependence on imports of natural gas.
  • A target has been set to produce 0.10 million metric tonnes, or 1,00,000 tonnes of green hydrogen per year by 2031.
  • The vision is to establish 1 GW of electrolyser capacity and achieve approximately 2.5 GW of renewable energy capacity through green hydrogen and its derivative projects.  PM Modi’s Silicon Statue Installed in Motihari
  • On the occasion of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s birthday on 17 September, 2026 , a silicon statue of PM Modi was installed at the newly constructed Deendayal Bhawan in Motihari, Bihar.  Surbhi Sundaram Wins ‘Miss Beautiful Smile’ Title
  • Surbhi Sundaram, a resident of Kishanganj, won the ‘Miss Beautiful Smile’ title at the Jewel of South 2026 competition held in Bengaluru.  Darbhanga Scientist Imtiaz Ahmed Leads ISRO’s EOS-05 Mission
  • Imtiaz Ahmed, a scientist from Revada village in Jale block, Darbhanga, has brought recognition to Darbhanga and the Mithila region by serving as the Project Director of ISRO’s EOS-05 mission.  Bihar Partners with Google India for AI Teacher Training
  • The Government of Bihar signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Google India to train school teachers across the state in Artificial Intelligence (AI) skills and practical tools.  Bihar Launches ‘Bihar Vidya Saathi’ for 24- Hour Online Learning Support
  • The Bihar Government launched ‘Bihar Vidya Saathi’, a 24×7 one-on-one interactive learning platform for eligible students in approximately 700 designated model school across Bihar, covering classes 9-10 and the science stream in classes 11-12, integrating teacher support, digital study resources and AI-powered learning tools.
  • Students can connect with teachers based on their academic needs and queries at any time.  Bihar Approves Incentive for Creators Promoting Government Schemes
  • The Bihar Cabinet, chaired by Chief Minister Samrat Choudhary, approved amendments to the Bihar Social Media and Other Online Media Rules, 2024 through the 2026 amendment rules.
  • Financial Incentive: Eligible creators will receive Rs. 10,000 per one lakh views for qualifying videos.
  • The incentive is capped at Rs. 1 lakh per video.
  • Videos must achieve at least 10 lakh views to qualify for the maximum incentive.
  • Eligibility: The benefit will be available only to registered and empanelled influencers, social media pages and channels.  New Chief Justice of Patna High Court
  • Justice V . Kameswar Rao was sworn in as Chief Justice of the Patna High Court on September 13, 2026.  Bihar to Get Skill India International Centre in Patna
  • The Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepre - neurship approved a Skill India International Centre in Patna to support Bihar’s youth seeking overseas employment.  Tarapur to Get Grand Adiyogi Centre
  • The Bihar Government approved a yoga, spiritual and tourism centre at Ghazipur village in Tarapur block, Munger district.
  • Around 15.01 acres of government land will be leased to the Isha Foundation for 99 years at a token annual rent of Rs. 1.  Patna Launches ‘Nagar Netra’
  • Patna Smart City is set to launch the Civic Services Surveillance and Monitoring Project, using 19 AI powered e-scooters called ‘Nagar Netra’.
  • The e: scooters will monitor civic conditions across all 75 wards of Patna Municipal Corporation, with approximately one e-scooter covering four wards.  Bihar’s First Fish Brood Bank
  • Bihar’s first Fish Brood Bank has been established at Raghopur Bakhri in Dumra, Sitamarhi, under the Pradhan Mantri Matsya Sampada Yojana (PMMSY).
  • Objective: To produce genetically improved brooders and disease-free, quality fish seed using scientific methods.  Prashant Kishor Wins Bankipur Assembly By-Election
  • Prashant Kishor, founder of the Jan Suraaj Party, won the Bankipur Assembly by-election in Bihar.
  • Prashant Kishor secured 64,151 votes and defeated BJP candidate Neeraj Kumar by 19,324 votes.  AIIMS Patna Launches AVBODHAN 2026
  • AIIMS Patna launched AVBODHAN 2026, a three- day national hands-on training programme on endoscopic skull base surgery, described as the first comprehensive programme of its kind in Eastern India.  Film Kakori won 72nd National Film Award

The historical film Kakori, directed & Related Developments

  • The historical film Kakori, directed by Kamlesh Mishra from Gopalganj, Bihar won the 72nd National Film Awards.
  • It won the Award in the Best Historical Reconstruc - tion/Compilation in Film Non-Feature film category.
  • Award ceremony was held on September 22, 2026.  Lithium-Ion Battery Manufacturing Plant
  • Lithium: ion battery manufacturing and assembly plant will be established in Hathua Industrial Area (Phase III), Gopalganj.
  • The establishment involves an investment of Rs. 87.55 crore, marking a major boost to Bihar’s clean energy and manufacturing ecosystem.
  • The plant will be set up by Shri Shirdi Sainath Power Infratech Private Limited.  India’s First Indoor Botanical Garden to be Developed in Patna
  • The Bihar Government announced the development of India’s first Indoor Botanical Garden in Patna, aimed at promoting environmental conservation, biodiversity, and tourism.
  • The indoor botanical garden will be developed on 5 acres of land near JP Ganga Path (Jaypee Ganga Path) in Patna.  Three Traditional Products of Bihar Receive GI Tag
  • Three distinctive traditional products of Bihar — Nalanda’s Bawan Buti Sari and Fabric, Gaya’s Pattharkatti Stone Craft and Bhojpur’s Pidhiya Painting — have been awarded the geographical indication (GI) tag.  International Ayush Conclave 4.0 (Nepal Edition)
  • The three: day international conclave was held in Kathmandu, Nepal .
